As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have passed through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Since measure itself is fundamentally non-existent, how could one possibly...
What constitutes the time for preaching the Dharma?
△ Seventh, regarding the provisional and the real concerning the Pure Land: Now, the essence and attributes of the Vairocana Dharmadhātu encompass as many realms as there are motes of dust;

the wondrous gates of the Vaipulya scriptures intermingle purity and impurity throughout the infinite. It is simply that, according to the karmic functions cultivated by each individual, the perceived realms differ.

This causes the sacred teachings to appear contradictory, as they rely on indeterminate faculties. Sometimes, as a provisional expedient, the Pure Land is divided among other lands, pointing to the defiled realm as Sahā;
or this place is treated as a site of transformation, while the upper direction is designated as the land of true retribution.

Thus Mañjuśrī comes from the Eastern Land, and Avalokiteśvara arrives from Sukhāvatī; such provisional manifestations differ according to the occasion. For those who have newly awakened their faith, there is no [fixed] distinction.
Now, relying on this, I shall briefly synthesize the various approaches by presenting them in ten categories.
First, the Pure Land of Amitābha Buddha is for those ordinary beings who grasp at signs and have not yet gained faith in the true principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*).

By means of focused mindfulness—because the mental recollection is concentrated—the mind becomes partially purified and one attains birth in the Pure Land; this is a provisional skillful means, not yet the ultimate reality.

Second, regarding the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*’s Pure Land: for those who do not yet believe in the true principle of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) and who delight in wondrous forms and appearances, it causes them to visualize those physical images.
Because the visualization is perfected, they are born in the Buddha-land; this is a provisional skillful means, not yet the ultimate reality.
Third is the Pure Land of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra. When the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe and applied his supernatural power, it was manifested for a moment and then vanished again;
this is the land of true retribution (*vipākabhūmi*). It has not yet been fully described in detail; thus, it is truly not yet extensive.

In the *Four Brahma-Net Sūtras* regarding the Pure Land, the description of the thousand-petaled lotus and the ten billion four-continent worlds is presented as a partial manifestation of the retributive realm for the sake of bodhisattvas of the three vehicles whose vision is not yet extensive; thus, it is not yet perfected and remains provisional rather than ultimate.
The pure land of the five Maheśvara devas is taught for the sake of bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching whose distinction between defilement and purity has not yet been extinguished;
it is said that this Jambudvīpa of the desire realm is outflowing (sāsrava), while those Maheśvara heavens are retributive fruition (vipākaphala). Yet even these are provisional and not ultimate.
The *Six Nirvāṇa Sūtras* speak of a Pure Land of True Reward located to the west, beyond lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers.

This present trichiliocosm is entirely a land of defilement; it is taught for those within the provisional vehicles who have not yet eliminated the distinction between the defiled and the pure. Thus, it is provisional and not ultimate.

The sevenfold Pure Land of the Lotus Sūtra involves the three transformations of the relocation of devas and humans; this is also taught for those who have not yet transcended the dichotomy of defilement and purity, and is thus provisional rather than ultimate.
The Pure Land indicated by the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is such that those of the three vehicles may know this very land is eternally pure despite its defilement;
while the multitude may believe this, they are unable to see it for themselves. This is the reality, not a provisional teaching.
Ninth is the Pure Land of Mind-Only. When one realizes that one’s own mind is, in its very essence, non-mind, its nature is solely true wisdom.

One does not dwell on purity or impurity; one accords with reality and follows one's nature, and the mind is free from anger and obstruction. To benefit and bring peace to sentient beings—this is the true pure land.
Because one is purified oneself, others are also purified. Thus it is said: "According to the purity of one's mind, so is the purity of the Buddha-land."
The ten Vairocana pure lands are the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*). They encompass both the pure and the impure; they are neither impure nor pure.
They are devoid of the characteristics of high and low, this and that, or self and other. Each and every Buddha-land fills the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);

inexhaustible Buddha-lands do not transcend a single mote of dust. Taking the Dharma as their boundary, they are not limited by perimeters. Their oceans of marks are both uniform and diverse in their forms and appearances.
Layer upon layer. This constitutes the realm of true recompense (śuddhāvāsa-niṣyanda).

△ Eighth, regarding the realm of gathering and transforming beings: Now, the Buddha-realm is boundless, pervading the entire dharma-dhātu; yet according to the capacity and breadth of sentient beings' dispositions, there appear differences in perception.
Here, based on the provisional and the real, I shall briefly indicate five gates. I only hope that you will abandon the branches and return to the root.
Returning to the source, may you swiftly realize Bodhi without delay.
As for those who see the Buddha within themselves, this refers only to seeing Him within a single Jambudvīpa.
Second, as for the various devas seeing the Buddha, they likewise see Him according to their own perceived realms; this is just as with Śakra, Brahmā, and the other [devas].
The Heavenly King occupies the rank of a bodhisattva; thus, the extent of what he perceives is assigned according to that bodhisattva rank, rather than being that of an ordinary celestial being.
Among the three vehicles, great arhats, by the power of their divine eye, perceive the Buddha’s gathering and transformation of beings throughout the trichiliocosm. As...
Aniruddha said: "With my divine eye, I see the trichiliocosm of Śākyamuni Buddha’s land as clearly as looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of one's hand.

As for a lesser arhat, his vision is not fixed; though he may have long cultivated the power of patience (*kṣānti*) and be able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), he may not yet possess supernatural powers such as transformations.
Alternatively, he may perceive the transformation and conversion of a single Jambudvīpa, as is the case with a subsequent-level arhat."
Alternatively, one may see the Buddha manifesting worlds equal in number to the four continents and so forth.

This is the realm of the Buddha perceived by Bodhisattvas of the four provisional teachings: those at the first stage see a hundred Buddhas; those at the second stage, a thousand Buddhas; and they increase accordingly with each successive level.
Regarding the five types of Bodhisattvas of the True Teaching: those of the first stage see many hundreds of Buddhas; those of the second stage see many thousands of Buddhas.

"Many hundreds" and "many thousands" refer to inexhaustible hundreds and inexhaustible thousands. To speak in terms of ultimate reality, those of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages all see them equally, like the net of Indra.
Within the Dharma-realm and empty space, all are entirely equal, without distinction between small and large. However—
Within the sequential progression [of the stages], there are levels of rank and descent.
△ Ninth, regarding the extension or brevity of cause and effect: Now, the Dharma-realm has neither beginning nor end; the essence of wisdom is neither cause nor fruit.

It is only for the sake of the measure of sentient beings that these names are provisionally applied. Like splitting bamboo or climbing a ladder, one proceeds according to the speed or slowness of their faculties. As for the measure...

When passion is severed, the self perishes; how then can a name subsequently be established? Therefore, the extension or brevity of cause and effect is like the tracks of a bird in the sky or a child born to a stone woman.
Now, based on the distinctions among the faculties (*indriya*), ten gates are established for the sake of exposition.
First, those who attain the fruit of arhatship through the "Come hither" (ehibhikṣu) ordination of the Hīnayāna;
second, those who attain the fruit of arhatship after one more birth in the Hīnayāna;
third, those who attain the fruit of arhatship after three more births in the Hīnayāna.
1. Those of the Four Lesser Vehicles attain the fruit of Arhatship after sixty kalpas.
2. Pratyekabuddhas attain the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood after four births.
3. Slow-acting Pratyekabuddhas attain the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood after passing through one hundred kalpas.
Seventh, the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings must necessarily pass through three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

Eighth, the *Lotus Sūtra* of the true teaching unifies the three vehicles into one, enabling the dragon girl to attain Buddhahood in an instant, thereby shattering the prolixity and stagnation of the three vehicles.
The nine sons of the Tuṣita Heaven attain the fruit of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) in three lifetimes;
Sudhana attains Buddhahood in one lifetime. As for "one lifetime": at the limit of a single kṣaṇa, mental activity ceases and views subside;

the three periods of time become a single thought-moment, and there is nothing further to be born. This is called "one lifetime. Thus, through non-arising, one immediately attains the fruit of Buddhahood, as in the original [text].

Because they have been born [into this state], they are called "born once. This is identical to the Dragon Girl, who, at the limit of a single kṣaṇa, when her emotions were exhausted and her temporal existence vanished, was named a Buddha.
△ Regarding the beginning and end of the teachings in the tenth assembly: Now, the World-Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, shines universally throughout the Dharma-realm. His wisdom...
Encompassing the myriad beings, he shares the same reality as both ordinary and sagely beings. The ten locations and ten assemblies are as layered as Indra’s net;

the ten lands and ten bodies are like reflections in a mirror, mutually penetrating. When one gate is opened, all gates are simultaneously revealed; when one chapter is discussed, all chapters are harmonized.
When the Way-tree first sprouted, the nine heavens arrived together; when the Universal Radiance was gathered in one place, those from the ten locations ascended all at once. Now...

In antiquity there was no differentiation. Within a single thought-moment—whether old or new—one does not depart from a single station, yet one immediately distinguishes the gates of the five stations.

Within a single practice, one establishes an ocean of practices as numerous as motes of dust, desiring to bring about resonance within a single thought-moment so that the course of cultivation is not in vain.
Now, ten dharmas are divided to summarize the governing principles.
First is the *Vairocana-buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, which is precisely the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lord" (*Lokendrarāja-vyūha*).

Regarding the phrase "initially attaining perfect enlightenment" (*prathama-abhisambuddha*): "initial" (*prathama*) refers to the mutual penetration of past and present; "attaining" (*abhisambuddha*) refers to acceding to the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

To act in accordance with this suchness without mental fabrication is termed "perfect" (*samyak*); for wisdom to penetrate this principle is termed "enlightenment" (*bodhi*). This sutra consists of thirty [chapters].

There are nine grades. As stated in the *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* (*Yíngluò jīng*), regarding the eleven stages (*bhūmi*) taught in the "Buddha-Flower" chapter (*Fóhuā pǐn*) of the Third Dhyāna Heaven, there are in total ten locations and ten assemblies comprising forty chapters.

All were spoken simultaneously in a single instant at the time of his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, through the Ocean-Seal Dharma-gate (*sāgaramudrā-dharmaparyāya*). Because the nature of the Dharma is such that it constitutes both before and after, they are arranged as three successive assemblies.

Regarding those who gather at the Hall of Universal Radiance (Puguang-dian), it is because they all rely on conceptual calculations, which deviate from the fundamental Dharma. It is for the sake of sentient beings that the events of the three periods of time are manifested within a single thought-moment;
it is not that the three periods of time exist within the fundamental Dharma itself. To clarify the fundamental Dharma, how could it ever follow from its derivative manifestations?

As stated in the "Ten Samādhis" (Shiding-pin) and the "Detachment from the World" (Lishi-jian-pin) chapters, one attains perfect enlightenment for the first time within the Bodhimanda. Thus, [it is said] universally...

In the Hall of Universal Radiance, he enters the Samādhi of the Limit of the Kṣaṇa. Although the arrangement of the written words is not without sequence, when one examines the intent of the sūtra, it is entirely a comprehensive teaching on the wisdom that encompasses a single time, a single limit, and a single dharma-realm. It is merely that the names of the Bodhisattvas differ according to their respective dharma-positions;
it is not that the Buddha departs and returns again. Thus, the Hall of Universal Radiance is taken as the fruit of the virtues of the dharma-realm.

The Great Abode is the capital of wisdom. The ten gates of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) constitute the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), while Samantabhadra’s practice of transcending the world constitutes its function.
Therefore, the three assemblies, the single location, and the entirety are but one time and one gathering; they cannot be conceived by the intellect as having temporal sequence or spatial movement.
Although there are nine other assemblies, they are all likewise contained within this single assembly, at this single time, within this single Dharma-realm, and within this single ocean of wisdom.
The Dharma-gates are layered and inexhaustible; they appear and vanish simultaneously without obstruction or hindrance.

Therefore, this sutra contains five types of pervasive causes and effects: the first assembly’s six chapters demonstrate the pervasiveness of the causes and effects for attaining Perfect Enlightenment;

the second through sixth assemblies’ twenty chapters demonstrate the pervasiveness of the causes and effects for faith and progressive cultivation; [the seventh through tenth assemblies] the ten concentrations, the ten supernatural powers, and the ten...

The Chapter on Forbearance and the Like constitutes the pervasive totality of the essential body (*dharmakāya*); the Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra and the Chapter on Leaving the World constitute the pervasive totality of the ocean of practices;
and the Chapter on the Dharma Realm constitutes the pervasive totality of the inconceivable ocean of great perfect wisdom of the dharma realm.
Therefore, at the beginning of each of these five sections, it is stated that "the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha," etc., clarifying that these five dharmas are one.

At that time, the single locus, the single dharma-realm, and the single essence-function—the identical dharma of all Buddhas—is equally pervasive and perfectly complete, devoid of the meaning of before and after.

It is like a king’s precious seal, which stamps everything simultaneously and suddenly, such that the resulting inscription has no sequence of first or last. This is to be seen for oneself through the principles of the six aspects—totality and particularity, sameness and difference, formation and destruction—and their integration via the ten mysterious gates. The Ten Mysterious Gates: 1. The Gate of Simultaneous Arising and Non-arising 2. The Gate of Mutual Interpenetration of One and Many 3. The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of Phenomena and Principle 4. The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of All Phenomena 5. The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of Time and Space 6. The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of Causes and Conditions 7. The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of the Three Times 8. The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of the Pure and the Impure 9. The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of the Great and the Small 10. The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of the Hidden and the Manifested.

These are: the gate of simultaneous fulfillment and correspondence; the gate of unimpeded mastery over the vast and the narrow; the gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without confusion;
the gate of the sovereign interpenetration of all phenomena; the gate of the simultaneous accomplishment of the secret and the manifest;

the gate of the subtle containment and establishment; the gate of the realm of Indra’s net; the gate of generating understanding by relying on events to reveal the Dharma; and the gate of the ten periods of time separated...
The Gate of the Differentiation of Dharmas; the Gate of the Perfect Fusion of the Principal and its Retinue Endowed with Virtue.
These six characteristics and ten mysteries pervade all phenomena, all times, and all places. Principle and phenomenon are perfectly fused; essence and appearance are without obstruction.
Now, within a single dharma-realm, according to the modes of practice for cultivating and purifying expedient means, we provisionally establish stages to represent the Dharma and distinguish them.

There are ten locations and ten assemblies: first, the site of enlightenment; second, the Hall of Universal Radiance; third, the summit of Mount Sumeru; fourth, the Yāma Heaven; fifth, the Tuṣita Heaven;
sixth, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; seventh, the Third Dhyāna Heaven; eighth, the Jeta Grove; ninth, to the east of the City of Enlightenment.

The ten universal buddha-fields, as well as all the empty space within their atoms and throughout the entire dharma-realm—such assemblies as these are all contained within the great mansion of the dharma-realm, the Hall of Universal Radiance.

For this reason, this sutra establishes six locations for the "Gate of Unifying Cause and Effect into a Single Boundary": first, in the initial assembly, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the Tathāgatagarbha.

The Samādhi of the Body. By means of the Dharma-gate of the Vortex of the Ocean of Worlds, it reveals the gate of the causes, conditions, beginning, end, and karmic fruition of the Flower Treasury Ocean of Worlds, the fundamental source of the Buddha. Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) is its practice; the Tathāgata’s Treasury Body is its essence.

This clarifies that through function one enters the essence, such that principle and phenomena penetrate one another. [It further reveals] the two types of Tathāgata jewel thrones, their circular terraces, foundations, and steps—all of them.

From within the ornaments emerge the multitude of Bodhisattvas. The great wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) constitutes the essence of the Buddha’s seat, while the ten thousand practices of Samantabhadra serve as its functional adornment;
this clarifies how principle and phenomenon, cause and effect, essence and function, mutually benefit one another.

Third is the Dharma-gate of the Single Limit of Perfectly Attaining Enlightenment, expounded three times in the Hall of Universal Radiance; this clarifies the gathering of the branches back into the root. Fourth is the Appearance of the Tathāgata.

In this chapter, the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows to moisten the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, and light from his mouth to moisten Samantabhadra’s mouth, causing the two to engage in mutual dialogue to expound the Dharma-gate of the fruits and virtues of the Buddha’s appearance. Mañjuśrī represents the essence of wisdom, while Samantabhadra represents the function of practice;
thus, it is shown that the aspects of wisdom and practice are mutually penetrating. This state of penetration is precisely what is called "Buddha. [This occurs] in the first assembly.
The Buddha is precisely the Buddha who has realized Buddhahood by himself. The Buddha appearing in the "Chapter on Manifestation" is one reached through the Bodhisattva’s own power;
because of faith in the Buddha, he initiates practice and makes progress, and upon realizing the fruit of Buddhahood for himself, he is no different from the previously believed-in Buddha.
Fifth, in the Jeta Grove, the World-Honored One entered the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi, while Samantabhadra spoke verses. This samādhi is...
*Li* (principle) is Samantabhadra, and *xing* (practice) is Mañjuśrī; this clarifies the union of practice with principle.

The emission of light from between the eyebrows that universally illumines all signifies that light is the function of practice, while Mañjuśrī is principle; this clarifies the union of principle with practice.
Within the pavilion of Maitreya, the six Sudhanas bring together Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya to harmonize the beginning and end, cause and effect. In total—
It constitutes a single boundary, for its essence and function are thoroughly pervasive.

Second is the demonstration of the fruit and the exhortation to practice; this comprises five chapters of the sutra, from the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata" to the "Chapter on Vairocana.
The Tathāgata’s oral radiance summons the assembly to gather. Samantabhadra, as the eldest son of the Buddha, upholds the dharma of the Buddha's household and enters [the state of realization].
The "Buddha Samādhi" section elevates the meritorious virtues of the Buddha-fruit, causing the assembly to develop reverence, affection, faith, and joyful practice.
Once the three types of faith are fully perfected, this corresponds to the six chapters of the sutra from the "Tathāgata Name" chapter to the "Worthy Head" chapter.

These six chapters collectively constitute the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*). Since Mañjuśrī is the teacher of those who have awakened from ignorance, he brings forth the fundamental source of one's own mind.
The Buddha of Moving Wisdom establishes the gateway of perfected faith. If there were a Buddha external to the mind, faith would not be perfected;
for to perceive [a Buddha] as external to the mind is itself a false view.
The fourth is the realization of the true reality. This consists of six chapters, from the "Ascending Mount Sumeru" chapter to the "Clarifying the Dharma" chapter.

It clarifies that by ascending from the stage of faith to the mountain peak of the Ten Abodes of the Dharma King, one’s wisdom shines forth without obstruction. Furthermore, the mountain symbolizes meditative concentration (*samādhi*); concentration is able to give rise to wisdom.
From this point onward, one acts in accordance with the Dharma without effort; beginning and end are both Buddha-nature. One does not attain full perfection only upon reaching the eighth stage.
Merit. Within the stream of the Dharma, the initial water and the subsequent water are of one nature because the Buddha as cause and the Buddha as fruit are of one nature.

There is no beginning, middle, or end, for there is no interval between moments; there is no moment that can be separated. Thus, cause and effect reach their consummation in a single thought-moment, for it is a single Buddha corresponding in each thought.
One need not discuss the marks and signs or supernatural powers; these marks, signs, and powers arise from this very [realization].

It is attained within awakening. If one realizes perfect awakening, one does not cling to any marks; because one is constantly in accord with the path of awakening, the miraculous transformations and the primary and secondary marks arrive spontaneously without being sought.
Even when reaching the ultimate limit of merit and wisdom, the three periods of time are simultaneous without shifting by even a hair’s breadth of thought.
It is like a royal jewel-seal: it stamps all at once, forming characters without sequence.
The fifth is the practice of setting forth and cultivating, which comprises four chapters from the "Ascending to the Palace of Yāma Heaven" chapter to the "Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries" chapter.
Yāma is a heaven that dwells in space. This clarifies the progression from the summit of Mount Sumeru to the limit where characteristics cease;
it is the realization of the Buddha’s wisdom-body by relying on the dharma-emptiness of fundamental wisdom, thereby practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Sixth is the mutual interpenetration of principle and phenomena. This refers to the three chapters from the "Ascending to Tuṣita" chapter to the "Ten Dedications" chapter.

By means of the ten practices of phenomena, one dedicates them into the principle of the ten abodes, thereby rendering principle and phenomena unimpeded and allowing essence and function to penetrate one another.

Tuṣita is located within the five heavens of the desire realm; it symbolizes the integration of fundamental wisdom and discriminative wisdom, wherein wisdom and compassion are harmoniously fused, and [the Bodhisattva] dwells therein.
The Middle Way.

The virtue accomplished through the cultivation of the seven aggregates corresponds to the single grade of the tenth stage within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

This is because the dharma-gates of the ten stages are accumulated and perfected within the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications; they then mature spontaneously until the ultimate wisdom of the fruit is attained.
It is full. Abiding in the Palace of the Fundamental Dharma (*dharmadhātu*), it is eternally and universally present throughout all things; there is no further advancement.
The Buddha is always manifest and does not newly arrive; therefore, there are no chapters on ascending to heaven or welcoming and praising him.

This deva relies upon the manifestation of others to achieve his own bliss, signifying that at this stage he practices compassion and wisdom by relying upon sentient beings, free from any thought of self.
Eighth, "Unimpeded according with Conditions" refers to the Buddha-flower Samādhi of the devas and humans of the third dhyāna in the seventh assembly.

It explains the Dharma-gate of Samantabhadra within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) among the eleven stages (*ekādaśabhūmi*). This clarifies that the path of self-perfection (*svabhāva-mārga*) of the ten stages has reached its conclusion;

within the stage of Equal Enlightenment, one universally pervades the Dharma-realm through the practices of Samantabhadra in a state of profound, non-obstructive interpenetration. Here, the devas lose their feelings of sorrow and joy, signifying equality.

Awakening brings stability and the cessation of turbulent emotions; through wisdom and compassion alone, one benefits the world. The text for this assembly is not yet complete; according to the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Śrī-mālā-sūtra*), it concludes at the stage of the nine causes and effects.

This refers specifically to the twelve chapters of the sūtra, beginning from the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (*Daśa-samādhi-paṭala*) up to the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgatotpatti-paṭala*) and including the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokātīta-paṭala*). This is because [the sequence] proceeds from the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" to the "Chapter on Transcending the World."

This is because it comprehensively encompasses the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the stage of Buddhahood, as well as the gates of cause and effect from beginning to end throughout the myriad practices of Samantabhadra;

thus, the initial sections of both the "Ten Samādhis" (*Daśadharmasamādhi*) and the "Leaving the World" (*Lokottara*) chapters all introduce the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, being identical to the first and second assemblies.
This is because the Ten Samādhis represent the essence of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom, while Leaving the World represents Samantabhadra.
The great function of abiding in the world is entirely contained within the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall, where all are gathered at once.
It is simply according to their respective positions that the names of the assembly of Bodhisattvas differ; it is not that they have departed and then returned.

It is like hundreds of thousands of precious mirrors in the sky with a single Buddha image placed on the ground, surrounded and adorned by the assembly of Bodhisattvas, appearing simultaneously within those hundreds of thousands of mirrors.
They appear instantaneously. Within each individual mirror, the reflections interpenetrate one another without any coming or going. It is the same with the Tathāgata:

at the moment he first attains perfect enlightenment, the heavens, the human world, and the lands of the ten directions all appear simultaneously and instantaneously, mutually penetrating one another without any coming or going.
Tenth, to cause ordinary beings to realize the truth: this refers to the single stage of the Dharma-realm in the Śītavana forest.

When the Tathāgata enters the Lion-Stretching Samādhi, he manifests the vast sphere of the fruit-virtues of the Dharma-realm, universally adorned, so as to inspire faith and joy in beings and lead them to penetrate the true reality of the Buddha.
By establishing the six stages—faith and the others—within the nature of the Dharma-realm as skillful means for progressive cultivation, one does not depart from the essence.

By employing unimpaired skillful means, their wisdom becomes ever more sublime while their conduct becomes ever more humble. They establish themselves in accordance with their practice and knowledge, remaining undeluded regarding cause and effect.
This causes the awakened ones to clearly discern both the general and the specific, achieving success according to their stages, neither stagnating at the beginning nor departing from the source.

For instance, there were six thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). In the presence of Mañjuśrī, they suddenly attained clarity regarding the ten ears and ten eyes, and their bodies pervaded the ten directions as they accomplished the Buddha-dharma, yet they did not depart from beneath Mañjuśrī’s feet.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand nāgas, five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred boys, and five hundred girls, all of whom were likewise ordinary worldlings.
Indeed, all those who believe in the Buddha-fruit of the Dharma-realm ascend through the ten abodes and ten stages; among them, Sudhana is cited as an example of this commonality.
Just as Sudhana first resolved his mind toward enlightenment because of Mañjuśrī, he later beheld Mañjuśrī again once his wisdom was perfected.

Because all phenomena within the *dharmadhātu* are collectively divine, collectively true, and collectively inconceivable, they are expounded through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.
Because the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is the single identity of ordinary beings and sages, it is expounded among human beings.

Those who have faith and understanding, as well as those who have realized and entered this Dharma-gate, are like the cubs of the lion king; although at the time of their first birth they are still [unformed],...
Just as the lion king possesses sovereign power and majesty while his lion-like form remains entirely unchanged, so too are all beasts already struck with fear;

likewise, it is with those who have faith and those who have realized the truth. Although they may not yet be able to exercise the same power and function as the Buddha, those who have faith have already planted the seed of the Buddha, and those who have realized the truth have already been born into the Buddha’s family, becoming true sons of the Buddha. And...

The Buddha’s wisdom is identical; it transcends the views of those in the provisional vehicles, as well as the bodhisattvas of the nine stages who have attained supernatural powers. Therefore, it is said:

"Even if a bodhisattva were to recite the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma and attain the six supernatural powers, if they do not hear or believe in this Dharma-gate, they shall not understand it.
It is further stated that even non-retrogressive bodhisattvas likewise cannot know it. This is because [this Dharma] is that which brings one out of birth and death.
It is not non-retrogression in the sense of having reached the stage of fundamental wisdom by penetrating fundamental ignorance;
rather, it is merely the establishment of a thatched hut outside the gate of the great dwelling of the ocean of dharmadhātu-wisdom, provisionally intended to avoid the calamity of fire.
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "Great" (*mahā*) signifies the meaning of being boundless; "direction" (*ava*) signifies the meaning of dharma-rules;

"vast" (*taṃsa*) signifies the meaning of the all-pervasive nature of wisdom and principle. "Buddha" signifies the meaning of the essence of wisdom that dwells in no dependence, and the meaning of the sovereignty of wisdom.

"Flower" (*avaṃsaka*) signifies the meaning of inexhaustible practices that pervade the Dharma-realm, for through these practices one is able to bring to full bloom the fruits for oneself and others. "Adornment" (*sūtra*) signifies the meaning of embellishment.

Because within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) there are the blossoming flowers of conditioned practice (*saṃskṛta-caryā*), which serve as the fruit of the subtle principle and wisdom in the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*), there further arise ten kinds of unconditioned practice (*asaṃskṛta-caryā*) flowers. These constantly adorn one another, constituting the path of self-benefit and benefiting others;
thus, "practice" (*caryā*) carries the meaning of "ornamentation. This sutra [reveals] that the fundamental essence of the Dharmadhātu of Vairocana’s great wisdom is inherently quiescent.

Taking as its primary tenet the Buddha’s own vehicle—the nature and characteristics of the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya, which are the fruition of perfected virtues and are characterized by the non-obstruction of phenomena and their essence—it causes those who have first resolved upon the path to aspire toward the vast.
Thus, they recover the fundamental immovable wisdom of the nature of their own minds, which abides without dependence;
because this is non-dual and one with the wisdom of all Buddhas, this sutra constantly takes the fruit of Buddhahood as the path for cultivation and progress.
This is the trace of the Buddha’s fundamental great wisdom; it is because one cultivates the wisdom of distinctions based upon this ancient trace that [enlightenment is attained].

If there were progress and cultivation apart from the Buddha’s ancient trace, there would be no principle of attaining Buddhahood. For example, while those of the three vehicles may temporarily escape a portion of the coarse suffering of birth and death, they are not practicing the Buddha-vehicle by relying on the ancient trace of the essence of the Buddha-wisdom. Furthermore, this sutra [addresses] the faculties and capacities of all sentient beings...

The Buddha’s single perfect sound, in a single thought-moment, constantly turns the wheel of Dharma throughout the three periods of time—without beginning and without end—as the very essence of his teaching.

To state the essential point: it encompasses the ocean of afflictions of all sentient beings, as well as the roots of goodness possessed by all sentient beings according to their respective capacities.
The fruits of happiness for humans and devas; the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas;

liberation, nirvāṇa, and the collections of names, phrases, and syllables, as well as vocal karma and so forth; and all the retributions of good and evil, the void, the dharma-realm, speech and silence—all phenomena without exception are the essence of the teaching.
From beginning to end, the assembly and physical forms described in this sutra total two hundred and twenty-eight.
The various classes of beings who follow [the Buddha] adorn the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), each with distinct forms.
The purpose of their gathering all serves as a symbolic representation. In the first chapter, there are forty-seven assemblies; their intended meanings are as follows.
Chapter One: The Sublime Array of the Lord of the World.
All the celestial kings, the eight classes of beings, and the assembly of bodhisattvas who guide and benefit sentient beings are all lords of the world.

When the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment, they all came to offer congratulations and praise, each accompanied by a retinue as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, or bringing [offerings] beyond measure.

The *Liangbu* (Section on Measurement) proceeds from the shared adornment of the ocean-like assembly; because the primary and the attendant interpenetrate to manifest the same dharma-image, it is called "Sublime Adornment" (*Miaoyan*).

This sutra is the true self of the wisdom of the dharma-realm; it reveals the true Buddha of the wisdom of the dharma-realm, hears the true discourse of the wisdom of the dharma-realm, and enters the true principle of the wisdom of the dharma-realm.
It must be that Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra have spiritually penetrated this true source.
This is that which is transmitted and upheld by those whose wisdom is equal to the ocean; it is not something that can be attained by those of the three vehicles.

As for "at one time": the Dharma-realm has no time; this is the time when the Buddha preaches the Dharma. Magadha is translated here as "Universal Wisdom," a country so named because its people possess much wisdom.
Āraṇya-dharma is translated here as "the place of supreme tranquility"; it is the very center of Jambudvīpa.
Therefore, all Buddhas attain enlightenment at this very place. A "field" (*kṣetra*) is a location selected for its purity; the Bodhimanda symbolizes the subduing of delusions.

It clearly demonstrates that attaining Buddhahood is the subduing of the delusions of sentient beings. Regarding "initially attaining perfect enlightenment": the exhaustion of all worldly sentiments throughout past and present is "initial";
the mind having no dependence is "perfect"; and the correspondence between principle and wisdom is "enlightenment. To obtain such a Dharma is called "attainment."
Furthermore, that ground is composed of vajra. Regarding the ten kinds of jewel adornments upon the ground: these are the causes for the Dharmakāya;

having attained the vajra-ground as a result of retribution, one adorns the ground with the ten pāramitās as its jewel ornaments. Regarding the rows of jewel trees and the ten kinds of adornments upon those trees:

these are the causes for providing shade and shelter for sentient beings through their conduct; having attained the jewel trees as a result of retribution, one [adorns them] with the practice of wisdom.
Because their characteristics penetrate one another, the reflections of all adornments appear within the trees. Because they dispel darkness through skillful means (*upāya*), the trees emit radiance.
Because they give rise to wisdom through vows, jewels rain down from within the light. Because cause and effect penetrate one another, Bodhisattvas appear like clouds from within the jewels.
As for the palaces and towers filling the ten directions, these are also the ten kinds of adornments; they contain great compassion.
He nurtures them to form his palace; great wisdom gives birth to life to form his hall.
Taking the illumination of wisdom as the towers, and knowing the faculties to establish the teachings as the pavilions, his great vows pervade everywhere, thus filling the ten directions.

Through the ten *pāramitās* arising in accordance with great compassion, he further establishes ten kinds of secondary environments (*upabhoga*), where boundless bodhisattvas all assemble. This is his teacher.
As for the statement that "the seat of the Son is high, broad, and exquisite, also adorned with ten kinds": because he attains fearlessness amidst the great assembly, he is called a lion.
Because he takes the dharma-realm as the cause of his seat, it is immeasurable. Because wisdom accords with the myriad practices, the seat is fully adorned with ten kinds of ornaments.
Because the Dharma-cloud of the ten stages of the causal rank provides moisture, the seat emits sounds that preach the Buddha-dharma.
The spheres [of experience] delight sentient beings. Such adornments are all obtained as spontaneous retributions through the Tathāgata’s great wisdom and great vows.

It is like clouds arising when a dragon moves through them, or wind being generated when a tiger roars; the response of retribution is thus natural, not something that can be produced by external objects.

Regarding "wisdom enters the three periods of time and is entirely equal": wisdom is able to accord with worldly conventions, hence it is said to "enter the three periods. The essence of the conventional is fundamentally...

It is true; therefore, it is called "equality. This is because the meaning of the six characteristics—totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration—is fully encompassed therein:
in being total, it is entirely particular; in being particular, it is entirely total; in being the same, it is simultaneously different; in being different, it is simultaneously the same;

in being formed, it is simultaneously disintegrating; and in being disintegrating, it is simultaneously forming. None of these are the marks of birth and extinction, such as oneness and difference or existence and non-existence, as conceived by the intellect.
It can be seen by illuminating it with the great wisdom of the power of non-conceptualization within one's own essence.

From the passage "His body fills all worlds" onwards, this section generally clarifies that the Tathāgata’s three activities of body, speech, and mind—both the primary and secondary, as well as their functions—are sovereign.
Surrounded by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, the presiding Bodhisattva named Samantabhadra acts in perfect accord with principle to benefit sentient beings.
"Pervasive" (*pǔ*) means to be universal in all respects. "Virtuous" (*xián*) means to accomplish virtue in accordance with conditions.

Regarding the fact that the first characters of the names of the nine bodhisattvas are all the same, "Pǔ," this clarifies that the meaning of these ten "universals" (*pǔ*) constitutes the universality of a single person; that is, each and every bodhisattva possesses the ten universals.

As for the subsequent clarification of their distinctions, it clarifies that because each and every Samantabhadra is able to pervade the distinct [realms], the meaning of "universal" is thereby fully established.

These ten universals are the practices shared by all Buddhas of the ten directions; there is nothing therein that is either old or new, like a king’s main highway—what can be done if one does not travel it?
These ten universal Bodhisattvas are the fruit of the Buddha’s own Samantabhadra-practices. The Tathāgata is the fruit of perfect enlightenment.
The Flower Treasury Pure Land where the Tathāgata dwells is the environmental fruit obtained as retribution for the Buddha’s merit. One.
All sentient beings, by means of their own faculties and natures, contemplate the threefold causes and effects of the Buddha.
Furthermore, they give rise to faith through the gateway of Samantabhadra himself. If it were not for this, from what could faith arise?
Therefore, the Tathāgata causes sentient beings to believe, delight in, and practice these threefold causes and effects. The Bodhisattva Sāgaraprabha-mahāprabha proceeds directly to the Great Self...
In the Heaven of the Kings, there are forty assemblies in total. Each assembly consists of ten leaders and attendants, totaling four hundred people.

This represents the four hundred gates of *pāramitā* within the Buddha’s own practice of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*).
Within these four stages, there are forty gates of *pāramitā*, and each individual gate of *pāramitā* inherently possesses ten [sub-gates].

...pāramitās. Thus, they constitute four hundred gates of pāramitā. The aforementioned assembly of Samantabhadra consists of ten individuals, each of whom is endowed with the virtue of the ten universals (*daśa-samanta*).
These ten individuals mutually interpenetrate, thereby naturally embodying ten assemblies;

since ten individuals equal one hundred, this further symbolizes the one hundred gates of pāramitā of the Buddha’s own stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Therefore, although there are forty-one assemblies, they in turn...
The assembly of fifty represents the five stages of the Buddha himself and his five hundred attendants, symbolizing the five hundred gates of the *pāramitās*.
From the Bodhisattva Sāgaraprabha-mahāprabha up to the Great Sovereign Heavenly King, there are forty assemblies;
these include the single assembly of Samantabhadra, as well as the assembly of those with radiating light within the Bodhi tree and the assembly within the Tathāgata’s palace. The Tathāgata...

The assembly within the seat, the assembly of bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions, the assembly from the pores of the bodhisattvas, and the assembly from within the ūrṇā-hair between the eyebrows of the Tathāgata—these constitute forty-seven assemblies in total.
The assembly within the Bodhi tree and the assembly in the palaces have already been explained previously.

The assembly within the seat consists of those who clarify that this is the Tathāgata’s own practice in the past; they are the assembly that manifests the fruit through causes identical to those of antiquity.

The assembly of those who have come from afar is the assembly that offers worship. The assembly of light rays from the pores is the inconceivable assembly of inexhaustible great compassion, which is the unimpeded arising of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, wherein unity and multiplicity, identity and difference, are sovereignly interpenetrating. The assembly within the ūrṇā-hair between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows is the assembly that reveals...
"Resulting in the cause, giving rise to faith, and benefiting sentient beings"— this refers to the assembly of the Dharma-gate that, after attaining Buddhahood,
encompasses the stages from the ten levels of faith through the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten bhūmis, and equal enlightenment, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
By citing this as the cause and result of his own cultivation, he causes students to emulate it.

The ten bodhisattvas, such as Sāgaraprabhāmahārciṣmatī, constitute the assembly that enters into the mundane world to benefit sentient beings through the practices of Samantabhadra within the stage of Buddhahood.
Because their practices differ, their names also differ; it is only through this universal differentiation that the meaning of "universal" (samanta) is established.
This clarifies that the initial mind of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) is a sudden vehicle (*tong-sheng*) according to the ancient method;

it does not deviate from the old traces, being like the great royal road where the new and the old travel together. By means of this, the deluded masses are enlightened and led back to study the ancients, so that they may become one with the Dharma itself.

Therefore, it is assigned to the position of the "Initial Resolve" (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*) to symbolize the ten *pāramitās*—both primary and secondary—within the *dāna-pāramitā* practiced during the first stage.
Pāramitā. The Bodhisattva Ocean-Light Moon-Great-Brightness (Sāgaraprabhācandramahāprabha) represents the Dānapāramitā.
Taking the Dānapāramitā as the primary element, the names of the other nine Bodhisattvas serve as its companions. Extensive salvation through the gift of Dharma constitutes the "ocean";

causing others to attain coolness constitutes the "moonlight"; and universally illuminating both self and others constitutes the "great brightness. Thus, it represents Dāna. [The Bodhisattva] Cloud-Sound Ocean-Light...
The Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha represents the Pāramitā of Śīla. His nature-precepts and great compassion universally rain down the sound of the Dharma as the "Cloud-Sound.
His nature-precepts are like the ocean; it does not harbor corpses, yet because all phenomena are universally pure, it constitutes the ocean. This is the Light of the Stainless Treasury.
Thus, this represents the precepts (*śīla*). As for the Bodhisattva Guṇaratna-śikhara-jñānasaṃbhava representing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*):
a topknot (*śikhā*) is an ornament for the head; since patience is the foremost [virtue], he adorns his crown with jewels. Because he is able to endure, he is "Born of Wisdom" (*Jñānasaṃbhava*).
As for the Bodhisattva Guṇasvayaṃbhū-rāja-mahāprabha representing the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*): he is untiring in benefiting sentient beings. For himself—
He is like a king because he universally causes all to be enlightened; thus, he is the "Great Radiance. The Bodhisattva Lotus-Crest of Skillful Valor represents the perfection of dhyāna (meditation).

This clarifies that from the stage of an ordinary person, one gives rise to faith and enters the path of realization. In a single thought-moment, free from discursive thinking, one suddenly transcends all conceptualizations.
True wisdom is darkly united [with reality]; this is the meaning of "valor. Because the essence of dhyāna abides in the world as the truth itself, it is unstained by tranquility.
The "Chaos" [character] forms the Lotus Topknot. The Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom Cloud-Sun Banner represents the Prajñāpāramitā:
he takes the rain of Dharma through wisdom as his cloud; the light of wisdom that destroys darkness as his sun; and the crushing of the heterodox to manifest the orthodox as his banner.
The Bodhisattva Mahāvīryavajrasama represents the seventh perfection, that of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).

His great compassion is firm and steadfast; entering into the mundane world without weariness is called "Great Diligence" (*mahāvīrya*). Destroying the stubborn defilements of others is called "Vajra.

Because he abides at the midpoint between wisdom and compassion, he is called "Equal" (*sama*); this "equality" refers to the center of the body. The Bodhisattva Gandhavyūhaprabhāketu represents the eighth [perfection], that of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Regarding the *pāramitās*: the great vows, vast and fragrant, constitute the incense; wisdom that follows these vows to shatter delusions constitutes the light;

entering into the heterodox to break through obstructions constitutes the banner—this is exemplified by the eighth stage’s spiritual friend, the seer Vimukta, who manifests as a non-Buddhist practitioner to act in concert with the heterodox in order to destroy the paths of heterodox teachers and the like. The Bodhisattva Mahāprabhāśrī-gambhīrasvaravyāhāra represents the ninth [stage].
The *Bala-pāramitā* (Perfection of Power) is so named because the Dharma-master’s rank excellently expounds the Dharma.
As for the Bodhisattva Mahāpuṇyaprabhājñānasaṃbhava, this clarifies that it is the *Jñāna-pāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom).

These names of the ten bodhisattvas clarify that within the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one utilizes these ten dharmas to govern defilement and purity, thereby accomplishing the gates of compassion and wisdom within the *Dharmakāya*. One should calculate [the practice] according to this cultivation and purification.

The Dharma is unified as a single Dharma. Now, it is explained that while the various pāramitās are each distinct, they clarify how one Dharma is cultivated, refined, and made increasingly luminous through ten dharmas, thereby perfecting that one.

This Dharma does not depart from its original practice, nor does its time shift from its original time, because time has no intrinsic nature and the three periods of time have no coming or going. It is simply that within this single Dharma, all [qualities] are fully present.

The essence and function of the ten dharma-practice gates consist simply of the stages of cultivation—whether immature or mature—within a single dharma, which are divided into the first and second dwellings (*vihāra*).
It is simply that within a single dharma, the convergence of compassion, wisdom, vows, and practice differs in terms of maturity and depth;

according to these differences, the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmi*) are established. This can be understood through the perfect interpenetration of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*); it is not that the dharmas themselves are different.
Furthermore, among these various divine kings and celestial hosts below, each takes one as the principal and the remaining nine as companions;
the names and meanings of each are assigned according to their respective positions.
The ten Vajrapāṇi deities, such as Suvarṇavarṇa and Nārāyaṇa, represent the Dharma-gate of the second stage, the Stage of Refining the Ground (*bhūmi*).

They preside over the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Taking the protection of ethical discipline as their "grasping" (*ādāna*), and the indestructibility of the essence of discipline as their "vajra," they are equal in nature to all Buddhas and identical in wisdom to ultimate truth. Following the conduct of Samantabhadra, they abide in the world to provide protection and sustenance. From [here]...
When the mind accords with principle, its wisdom becomes spontaneously divine. To penetrate all phenomena without thinking or acting is called "divine" (*śen*);
it is not the divinity of ghosts and spirits. The wondrous form of the Nārāyaṇa deity represents the gate of *dāna-pāramitā* within the *śīla-pāramitā*.
By means of natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*), one perfects *dāna* and thereby evokes a wondrous form. "Nārāyaṇa" signifies indestructibility; through natural morality...
By destroying delusions, one attains the indestructible body. Regarding the Sun-Disk Swift Banner Deity (*Sūryamaṇḍala-āśu-ketu-deva*) who represents the precept within precepts:

the light of the precepts being without deficiency is called the "Sun-Disk" (*sūryamaṇḍala*); those who perceive it are true ones (*arhat*), hence it is called "Swift" (*āśu*). The exhaustion of the delusions of self and others constitutes the "Banner" (*ketu*);

the mind being free from divergent thoughts constitutes "Grasping" (*dhara*); its nature being indestructible constitutes "Vajra"; and being sovereign in accordance with reality, it is named "Deity" (*deva*). One must...

The deity Mīhuāguāng (Flower-Light) represents the practice of patience within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Taking the excellence of the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) as Mount Sumeru, adorning one's conduct with patience so that all who see it are delighted constitutes the "flower.
For those who observe, the destruction of pride constitutes the "light. The meanings of the remaining seven deities are to be understood by applying them in sequence accordingly.
This is the second stage, the Dwelling of the Purified Ground (*viśuddhabhūmi*), consisting of the ten principal and attendant perfections (*pāramitā*) of the ten stages.
The ten classes of body-deities, such as those adorned with flower-crests (*puṣpa-keśa*), represent the third stage of cultivation, the "Abiding in the Dharma Gate.

They preside over the ten *pāramitās* within the *kṣānti-pāramitā*. As stated in the "Praise of Virtues" (*Guṇaparyāya-stava*): "All have in the past served and made offerings to all Buddhas. [One might ask:
"Since they have already become Buddhas, why do they require offerings? This clarifies that they manifest through numerous clouds of bodies and numerous adornments.
Equipped with these, at all times he makes offerings to all sentient beings, causing them to attain Buddhahood.

Because his own body and that of the Buddhas are non-dual, this is the meaning of "harmonious patience" (*kṣānti*), for it is the meaning of the "multitude of bodies. Thus, the deity Flower-Tuft Adornment (*Puṣpamaulī-vyūha*) represents *dāna* (generosity) within patience;
by means of the most supreme retribution of patience, he obtains the crown ornament. The deity Light-Illuminating the Ten Directions (*Daśadig-prabhāsa*) represents [patience] within patience...
Regarding the precepts: taking patience as the essence of the precepts, the light of the Dharma-patience precept causes all beings to rejoice; this is what is meant by "light-illumination.

The deity Haiyin-tiaofu (Ocean-Sound-Subduer) represents the "patience within patience" among the various forms of patience. Hearing various reports of good and evil, or of slander and praise, he remains as unmoved as the sound of the ocean tide, giving rise to neither sorrow nor joy.
Furthermore, he uses his voice like the tide to teach and transform others so that they do not miss their proper timing; this is the meaning of "subduing patience."
The meanings of the remaining seven deities are to be understood by assigning them in sequence.
The ten "feet-walking" deities (*pādagāminī*), such as Ratnamudrāhasta and the others, represent the Dharma-gate of the fourth stage, the Dwelling of Noble Birth.
They preside over the ten *pāramitās* within the *vīrya-pāramitā*. Because they fulfill all practices through wisdom that accords with diligence, they are called "feet-walking" deities.

The deity Ratnamudrāhasta (Jewel-Seal Hand) represents the perfection of diligence within the perfection of generosity (*dāna*); it clarifies that one draws in and guides sentient beings by practicing the diligence of the wisdom-seal of the Dharma-jewels.
The deity Padmaprabha (Lotus-Light) represents the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*) within the perfection of diligence;

dwelling in the ocean of birth and death like a lotus, unstained by it, those who see [this deity] arouse the aspiration for awakening—this is called "light. The deity Viśuddhakusumajaṭā (Pure Flower Topknot).

One attains purity through the stainlessness of *dharmakṣānti* (patience regarding phenomena). Furthermore, one obtains a crown ornament; since "patience" (*kṣānti*) carries the meaning of a "flower garland," it symbolizes patience.

The deity Sarvadarśanasaṃgrahaṇī symbolizes the most excellent diligence within diligence: by constantly restraining the sense faculties so that views do not arise, there is no unwholesome view—this is diligence.
The meanings of the remaining six deities are to be understood by applying them in sequence accordingly.

The ten shrine deities (maṇḍala-devatās), such as Viśuddhālaṃkāradhvaja and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the fifth stage, the Stage of Complete Skillful Means (*upāyaparikarman*), which has the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) as its essence.
A "shrine" (*maṇḍala*) signifies the meaning of removing the impurities of the aggregates (*skandha*);

since meditation can treat the aggregates, it is like a worldly threshing floor. This is to clarify that meditative concentration purifies the defiled grasping of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, thereby manifesting prajñā.

It opens the wondrous wisdom that discerns the fundamental reality of the essence of principle and wisdom; thus, *dhyāna* (meditation) serves as the field and substance, while *prajñā* (wisdom) serves as human effort.

With the myriad practices of Samantabhadra serving as the vehicle for transport, one reaches the Great Capital of Universal Radiance within the *dharmadhātu*, the treasury of all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Within this, there are ten spirits, each spirit representing one *pāramitā*, which brings benefit to oneself and others.
Their meanings correspond in sequence as follows:
the ten city-ruling goddesses, such as Ratnakūṭaprabhā and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the sixth stage, the Stage of Right Mindfulness (samyakcittatā-vihāra).
Taking Prajñā as its essence, it takes the sovereign protection of the city of the mind through the wisdom of emptiness as its tutelary deity.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, in the chapter on the "Stage of Right Mind" (*samyakcitta-vihāra*), states: "This Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of dharmas and his mind remains steadfast and unmoving.
This clarifies the meaning of the "City. When Sudhana visits the spiritual friend of the sixth stage, the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, he sees him sitting upright in silent stillness.
The exhaustion of inhalation and exhalation signifies the realization of this city. Regarding the deity Jewel-Peak Radiance (*Ratnaśikhara-prabhāsa*):

the "Jewel-Peak" refers to reaching the limit where all marks are exhausted through the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*). "Radiance" refers to the universal bestowal upon all sentient beings through the wondrous wisdom of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-prajñā*).
The remaining nine deities are to be explained in sequence accordingly; one should understand these principles briefly, as in the case of the deities of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The presiding deities of cities, lands, and so forth are always goddesses. This is to clarify their compassion;
however, in terms of their actual substance, they are neither male nor female, appearing in accordance with the needs of sentient beings.
The ten Earth-Ruling Goddesses, such as Samantaguṇaviśuddhikusumatala, represent the ten pāramitās within the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya*).

With the pāramitā of skillful means (*upāya*) as their essence, they give birth to all phenomena through great compassion; because their nature is without retrogression or movement, they serve as the Earth-Ruling Goddesses.

The ten mountain deities, such as Ratnaśikhara-kusumita and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the eighth stage, the Abode of Youthful Truth (kumārabhūmi), which is the perfection of vows (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
Here, the immovable, effortless wisdom (anābhoga-jñāna) constitutes the mountains, while the sovereign mastery of the arhats constitutes the deities.

The ten forest-deity lords, beginning with "Scattering Flowers Like Clouds," represent the ninth stage, the Abode of the Dharma Prince. Their primary power is the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*).
This clarifies that preaching the Dharma is like a forest, providing vast and abundant shade; therefore, this is the rank of the Dharma Master.
The ten principal medicinal goddesses, such as Śrī and others, clarify the tenth stage, the Abode of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), which presides over the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

Within this, the ten goddesses preside over the ten perfections within the Perfection of Wisdom; by means of wisdom, they know the faculties [of beings] and act as deities who provide the medicine of the Dharma.
These aforementioned ten groups of one hundred [deities] share the same divine rank, symbolizing the Buddha’s own practice of the ten abodes and one hundred [perfections].
This is a gate of pāramitā.
The ten presiding deities of crops, such as Mṛdusvararasa (Gentle Superior Flavor), symbolize the ten pāramitās within the first joyful practice of dāna-pāramitā.
Just as worldly grain serves as sustenance to nourish the physical body, so too does the Buddha-dharma [serve as sustenance for the spiritual body].

The practice of the ten pāramitās serves as the provision (*saṃbhāra*), nourishing the *dharmakāya* and causing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) to gradually diminish. Through the cultivation of supramundane compassion and wisdom, these habitual tendencies become fully perfected.

In the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are designated as the provisions prior to the Path.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), because it is at the first stage that one first perceives the Path.
This is not yet clear. In this sutra, within the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one has full faith that one’s own mind is no different from the Buddha.

At the initial mind of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), one perceives the Path through the *upāya-samādhi*. From the first abiding upward, all the abidings collectively constitute the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

The ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) collectively constitute the stage of Preparatory Application (*prayoga*) and collectively constitute the stage of Provisions (*saṃbhāra*). As for the provisions and the preparatory application...
The Buddha’s cause and fruit advance together; thus, the practices of Samantabhadra are employed to support the fulfillment of compassionate vows.
By employing the fruit of the nature of the dharma-body and its principle-wisdom as perceived at the initial stage of abiding, one supports the practices of Samantabhadra.

Because these do not belong to the conditioned states of humans or devas, the cultivation of the five stages—the fruit of the nature of the dharma-body and its principle-wisdom along with the practices of Samantabhadra—interpenetrate within the single true dharma-realm.

They serve as the provisions for enlightenment; if one is abandoned, the other two cannot be established. By means of wisdom and principle, one adorns the Buddha-fruit with practice, and by means of practice, one adorns the fruit.
It is like the flower and fruit of a melon growing together: the flower and fruit mutually support one another, which is called the "Flower Adornment of the Buddha" (Buddhāvataṃsaka).
The ten river-governing deities, such as Samantānupravr̥ttā, represent the ten pāramitās within the second pāramitā of the precept of beneficial conduct (anugrahacaryā).
Sudhana’s spiritual friend for beneficial conduct, the youth Śakradevendra, gathers sand on a riverbank;

by taking the welfare of others as his practice, he clarifies the essence of the precepts. Here, the river deity serves as the essence of the precepts, illustrating the correspondence between the preceding and succeeding stages.
It is as follows: the "Universal Emission of Swift Currents" (Pufaxunliu) clearly corresponds to the seed of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The "Universal Purification of Springs and Streams" (Puqiejuanjian) takes the deities of the rivers and streams as its presiding spirits, corresponding to the wholesome dharmas of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) and those of humans and devas, serving as the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*). This is the meaning of "universal purification. If it were not thus, [the analogy would fail].
The practices are not yet fulfilled.

There appear ten sovereign ocean-deity kings, such as Ratnārcis (Jewel Light) and others, representing the ten pāramitās within the third stage of the practice of patience that is free from opposition.
Taking the great compassion of the *dharmatā* as the essence of patience, it is like the ocean which, situated at the lowest point, is able to contain all.
The stream of all ignorance, pride, and birth-and-death—all these become the flow of the Dharma without obstruction.

This constitutes the practice of non-opposition and the practice of universal exertion within the tenth stage, "Cloud Banner," among the ten water-governing deities. This represents the fourth stage, the practice of being unyielding and the practice of diligent application.
Regarding the ten pāramitās: through the water of the dharma-nature, one constantly exerts diligent effort; knowing the faculties [of beings], one benefits them without ever wearying the mind.
This is like water containing moisture that benefits things according to their nature; each receives what it needs without being disturbed.

The ten fire-governing deities, such as Samantaprabhā-jvālā-kośa and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the fifth stage, the Bodhisattva practice of *dhyāna-pāramitā* (meditative concentration) characterized by non-delusion and non-confusion.
Because it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, and because phenomena are identical with principle, compassion and wisdom function in illumination without obstruction;
thus, the fire deity represents the essence of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). In the celestial realm, fire is the sun; in humans, it is the mind; in the directions, it is [the element of] fire.
It is the South; it is the deity of Li. In the Dharma, it is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); it is the Middle Way; it is the Correct; it is wisdom that illuminates all phenomena.
Sudhana’s journey to the South is like this.

The ten sovereign wind deities, such as Unobstructed Radiance (*Anāvaraṇaprabha*), represent the ten *pāramitās* within the sixth stage, the Good Manifestation (*Sādhumatī*), which practices the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Wind corresponds to the direction between the hours of Chén and Sì, the deity of *Xùn*, representing speech and command.

When *Xùn* (wind) is above and *Kūn* (earth) is below, it forms the hexagram *Guān*. It is said: "Wind blowing over the earth can be observed," serving as a symbol for a great man establishing government and instruction.
Thus the world follows it. This clarifies that the merit of the sixth pāramitā, wisdom (*prajñā*), has been perfected. Subhūti’s teachings transform and edify sentient beings.

Furthermore, above, it coincides with the lunar mansion *Jyeṣṭhā* (the Horn), which serves as the Gate of Heaven and presides over the rules for the collective observance of precepts by monks and nuns.

An elephant uses its mouth as the Gate of Heaven to inhale and exhale the vital breaths; thus, it disseminates instruction and brings about transformation. Therefore, wisdom is taken as the Wind Deity. As for "square" (*fang*):...
This is the Dharma. The Great Elephant has no fixed direction; one merely takes its Dharma.

The ten presiding space-deities, such as Pure Light Shining Universally, represent the ten *pāramitās* within the seventh *pāramitā*, the *upāya-pāramitā* (the perfection of skillful means) of the stage of Non-attachment.
The emptiness of all phenomena can give rise to great compassion and skillful means, thereby gathering and transforming sentient beings.
Being without attachment, the presiding deity of space symbolizes skillful means (*upāya*).
The ten presiding deities of the directions, such as the one who dwells everywhere and so forth, symbolize the ten *pāramitās* within the eighth stage, the practice that is difficult to attain.

With the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) as the primary factor, wisdom functions without effort. Because such effortless accomplishment is difficult to achieve, one employs aspiration to guard it.
Recalling one's original vow, one draws forth wisdom to initiate practice, causing that practice to be all-pervasive—neither abiding in nirvāṇa nor abiding in saṃsāra.
Through the eighth stage, effortless wisdom is perfected, fully encompassing the dharmas of the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.
The ten night goddesses, such as Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the ninth stage, the Stage of Good Dharma (Sādhumatī).
With the pāramitā of power (*bala*) as the primary one, they signify that the power of the Dharma has been perfected and the work of the Dharma King is accomplished.
They constantly dwell within the long night of birth and death, illuminating the world with the light of the Dharma.

The manifestation of the ten Palace-Dwelling Day-Governing Deities (*divā-vihāra-devatā*) represents the ten *pāramitās* within the tenth *pāramitā* of wisdom—the wisdom practiced in the stage of true conduct.
Wisdom is the sun that is eternally luminous, thus constituting "day"; wisdom is unconditioned yet responds to all phenomena, thus constituting the "deity.

The deity manifesting the palace represents the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) within wisdom: through the palace of compassion and the hall of wisdom, one brings sentient beings to fulfillment.

The palace of compassion, wisdom, and emptiness mutually benefits one another. The aforementioned ten assemblies of one hundred beings represent the Buddha’s ten practices and one hundred gates of *pāramitā*.
Rāhu and the other ten asura kings represent the first [practice]: rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining detached from the notion of sentient beings.
These are dedicated toward the ten pāramitās within the dāna-pāramitā. The asuras are called "non-gods" (asura);

although they are included within the celestial realm (*deva-gati*), because they are full of deceit and guile, they lack the sublime bliss of the gods. Furthermore, though they dwell in the great ocean, they are not submerged by its waters.
In this way, the bodhisattva’s great compassion and skillful means are like their deceit and guile: although he enters into saṃsāra, he is not [submerged] by it.
Although he possesses the pleasures of the five celestial desires, he does not have the bliss of nirvāṇa or the peace of cessation found in the supramundane.
Because he dwells neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa, yet attains mastery over both, he is called a "King. Rāhu means "obscuring light" in this language;
his hands are able to obstruct the brilliance of the sun and moon. Vemacitra means "high resonance"; it refers to his battle with the Lord of Devas (Śakra).
At that time, he raised his voice and cried out so loudly that it could shake the mountains and peaks; this was to establish his name.

This asura manifested the precepts within *dāna* (generosity), clarifying that through the sound of great compassion and great vows, he vowed to deliver those in the three realms and six paths of existence. Thus, compassion and vows constitute the essence of his precepts.
The ten *garuḍa* kings, such as Mahāśīghravala and others, represent the ten *pāramitās* within the second *akṣaya-pariṇāmanā* (imperishable dedication) of the *śīla-pāramitā*.

A *garuḍa* is the golden-winged bird (*suparṇin*). With its two wings spanning three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*, it gazes with its pure eyes upon the dragons whose lives are ending over the great ocean, and fans [them] with its wings.
Just as one opens the waters at both sides to seize [a corpse], the Bodhisattva constantly dwells upon the great ocean of birth and death;

with the eye of wisdom that is pure through the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), he observes sentient beings whose roots of virtue have matured, and with the two wings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, he seizes them and places them on the shore of self-nature pure *nirvāṇa*.
This illustrates that just as the sea does not harbor a corpse, the nature of great compassion, great wisdom, and natural morality does not harbor [afflictions].

The corpses of the two views—defiled and pure—of humans, devas, and the three vehicles are like the ocean; just as the golden-winged bird (garuḍa) seizes the nāgas before the waves have closed together, it is due to its power of extreme swiftness.

The ten Kinnara kings, such as Sunetra-prabhāsa (善慧光明天), represent the ten pāramitās within the third stage, the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), of all Buddhas.
"Kinnara" is translated here as "doubt-god" (*yi-shen*); they resemble humans but have horns on their heads and mouths like oxen.
When people see them, they doubt their identity. By the power of the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), they are born into the six realms of existence.

They practice for the benefit of sentient beings; their wisdom is like that of a Buddha while they appear as ordinary beings, and their conduct is like that of ordinary beings while they resemble sages.

Thus, they are manifested as the "Mysterious Spirits" (Guhyakas). The ten Mahoraga kings, such as Suprajña and others, represent the fourth dedication, "Dedication Reaching All Places," characterized by diligence.
Among the *pāramitās*, there are ten *pāramitās*. The *mahoraga*—here translated as "great python" (*dà mǎng*) and also as "one who crawls on chest and belly"—is a guardian deity of the *ārāma*.

The elephant represents diligence; entering everywhere throughout the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, crawling to benefit others, and abandoning arrogance to practice humility and respect—these are the deeds of a bodhisattva.
The ten yakṣa kings, such as Vaiśravaṇa and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the fifth dedication, the inexhaustible treasury of merit, which is the dhyāna-pāramitā.
"Yakṣa" is translated here as "one who lives in hardship" (kǔhuó) and also as "one who investigates" (sìchá).
King Vaiśravaṇa leads the host of yakṣas on the northern face of Mount Sumeru; he employs the yakṣas of meditative concentration (dhyāna) for the purpose of investigation.
To guard the mind that seeks to alleviate the suffering of all sentient beings so that it does not arise falsely is to attain the treasury of great merit.
The ten dragon kings, such as Virūpākṣa and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the sixth "Firmly Adhering" dedication (*anulomika-dṛḍha-pariṇāmanā*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The celestial king Virūpākṣa leads the host of dragons and dwells on Mount Sumeru.
West: Virūpākṣa, which means "Various Eyes. This elephant symbolizes the adornment of all views with the various wisdoms of emptiness through *prajñā*, causing all seeing to be free from attachment.

Just as a dragon soars through the sky, appearing and disappearing at will while raining down to nourish all things, this represents the sovereign mastery over existence and non-existence within the wisdom of emptiness, raining down the Dharma to benefit living beings. There are five kinds of dragons; the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita is the foremost among them all.
The Nāga King who is the lord of those with elephant forms is Nanda; he is the lord of all serpent-form nāgas.
The Nāga King Anavatapta is the lord of all horse-form nāgas. The Nāga King Varuṇa is the lord of all fish-form nāgas.
