The Nāga King Mānasa is the lord of all frog-form nāgas. All nāgas are able to transform their shapes, except for those that have just been born.
At times of sleep, anger, or sexual desire, they are unable to transform their forms.

All nāgas are subject to the fear of the garuḍa, the fear of hot sand falling upon their heads, and the suffering of their bodies being exposed when their precious garments are blown away by the wind.

Only the Nāgarāja Anavatapta does not engage in sexual desire in his serpent form, nor does he suffer from these three aforementioned afflictions; for this reason, he is so named. This is explained according to the Three Vehicles.
It is said: "Now, this Dragon King within the One Vehicle possesses virtues that are entirely those of a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Buddha-fruit of the inconceivable vehicle.

To transform sentient beings, he manifests his body universally throughout all realms of existence. He has come to this assembly to celebrate the appearance of the Buddha, fulfilling his original karmic conditions.
His stationing here serves to symbolize the Dharma; 'Sāgara' (Sāgarakumāra) means 'Ocean' in this world, symbolizing Great Compassion."
Entering the ocean of birth and death. Takṣaka—here translated as "The Able Harmer"—is so called because when he is enraged, his venomous gaze brings both humans and animals to their deaths.
He is also called "Many-Tongued," signifying that Prajñā skillfully expounds many teachings and destroys all afflictions.
The ten Kumbhāṇḍa kings, such as Virūḍhaka and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the seventh dedication that accords with all sentient beings.
Kumbhāṇḍas are spirits that consume vital energy; they are also called "Winter Melon" (Dōga) spirits because their scrotum is as large as a winter melon.
When walking, they carry it upon their shoulders; when sitting, they squat upon it. [This refers to] Virūḍhaka.

The king’s retinue dwells on the southern side of Mount Sumeru; because they greedily seek and devour [food], this represents the Bodhisattva’s complete renunciation of all greedy seeking and its subsequent cessation.
The ten *gandharva* kings, such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others, represent the ten *pāramitās* within the dedication vow of the eighth *tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pāramitā*.
*Gandharva* is translated here as "seeking fragrance"; they seek their sustenance by finding pleasure wherever there is a scent of fragrance.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra leads them and dwells on the eastern side of Mount Sumeru. The elephant represents the *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā*.
The fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body, free from defilement, constantly aspires to bring joy to sentient beings and cause them to cherish it.

The Moon Deity represents the ninth power of dedication—the liberation of being unbound and unattached—which, through the power of the wisdom of intrinsic emptiness, illuminates sentient beings, purifies the heat of their afflictions, and causes them to attain coolness; therefore, it takes the moon as its symbolic representation.
The ten months are not assigned according to their sequential order.
The Sun Deity represents the tenth dharma-realm, the Sovereign of Immeasurable Dedication, and the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Just as the sun dwells in the sky, illuminating all phenomena, its position is above while its merit benefits those below; this symbolizes that the wisdom of this stage is exceedingly lofty.
Their conduct reaches down to all levels; humans, devas, spirits, ghosts, those of external paths and heterodox practices, animals, and those in the hells all share in their conduct.
It is like the sun and moon: though their forms are above, their efficacy is below, illuminating both the good and the evil.
The Ten Sun Deities correspond in sequence to the ten *pāramitās* within wisdom. The *Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra* states: "Above the Moon there is a city, square and one [yojana] in extent."
It is nineteen hundred and sixty *li* in circumference. It is composed of two parts of celestial gold and one part of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).

From a distance, it appears circular. The lifespan of its devas is five hundred years; their descendants succeed one another for an entire *kalpa*. When the sun and moon draw near to each other, their light and shadows reflect upon one another, resulting in waning and waxing.
The sun is fifty *yojana* in breadth. Its city is square, measuring two thousand and forty *li*, and is made entirely of pure gold.
They are formed; their lifespans and descendants are identical in month. Because they are sustained by wind, they revolve around Mount Sumeru.
All are governed by the Four Heavenly Kings. The above ten assemblies represent the Buddha’s own practice of the ten dedications and one hundred gates of *pāramitā*.
The ten kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, such as Śakrendra and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the dāna-pāramitā of the first stage, the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
"Trāyastriṃśa" means "thirty-three. This heaven is located at the summit of Mount Sumeru;
on its four peaks there are eight attendant deities each, and together with the Lord of Devas, Śakra, they constitute the thirty-three. The height of the bodies of these deities is...
One yojana [in height]; their garments are twice that length and weigh six *zhū*. Their lifespan is one thousand years.
One day and night there is equivalent to one hundred years in the human world. Thirty days constitute a month; twelve months constitute a year.
Śakra is also named Śakradevendra, also named Kauśika, and also named Śakrendra. This heaven is located where the mountain peaks meet.
This stage clarifies that when one ascends to this first bhūmi from the conditioned habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the preceding stages, a portion of those tendencies is exhausted;

therefore, it is metaphorically represented by this deva. Just as the ten abidings and ten practices are metaphorically represented by the *ṛṣis*, and the ten transferences by kings, these ten bhūmis are represented by devas.
This clarifies that through progressive cultivation, one gradually becomes habituated to increasingly sublime states. [This is explained] by means of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*).
The Ten Mysterious Gates encompass this; it is all the identity and difference within a single kṣaṇa, and must not be grasped through conceptual calculation.
The ten [deities] such as the Good Time (Kāla) and the others are the Suyāma Heaven Kings, representing the second stage, the Stainless (Vimalā).

"Suyāma" here means "Time" (Kāla). Because they dwell relying upon space, there are no sun or moon; their own radiance illuminates one another, so that night and day are not distinguished. However, [the text continues:]
The opening and closing of the lotuses indicate the divisions of day and night. The bodies of the devas are two yojanas in height;
their garments are four yojanas long and weigh three *zhu*. Their lifespan is two thousand years. The calculation of days, months, and years is double that of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

These ten classes of devas represent the ten *pāramitās* within the precepts. By means of these superior and most excellent ten wholesome precepts, they counteract the coarse afflictions and habitual tendencies currently active in the desire realm.

Regarding the *vāyu* (wind/energy): by practicing the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) on the third bhūmi, one is finally free from the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, is born into the family of the Tathāgata, and shares the nature (*dhātu*) of the Tathāgata.
One becomes equal to the ten Tuṣita Heaven kings, such as Saṃtuṣita, representing the ten pāramitās within the patience (*kṣānti*) of the third bhūmi, the Radiant (*Prabhākari*).
Tuṣita (Mìdōushù) is translated here as "Contentment. Its inhabitants are four *yojana* in height and wear garments eight *yojana* long;
their lifespan is four thousand years. The measurement of days, months, and years is double that of the Yāma heaven. Bodhisattvas in their final birth receive instruction here;

by cultivating the nine successive meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), they transcend the three realms. This is illustrated by the analogy of refined gold, which does not lose even a *zhū* or two of its weight.

The nine successive attainments are refined by the Dharma-eye and observed through practice; added thereto, they do not diminish the fundamental dharma, but rather become increasingly bright and pure.
The ten transformations, such as those of the Good Transformation [Heaven], represent the ten pāramitās of the fourth stage, the Flaming Wisdom (Arciṣmatī) Bhūmi. By means of these—

Its essence is diligence. This deity constantly delights in himself through transformations. This stage is characterized by the adornment of the wisdom-karma with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
It counteracts the obstacles of false views within the three realms, refining and polishing the ground of the mind to make it even more luminous and pure.
Using the transformation of sentient beings as his own joy, he is thus called "Blazing Wisdom" (*Arciṣmatī*).
The ten Heavens of the Lord of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), beginning with those who have attained mastery, represent the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjaya).

These gods take the emanations produced by others as their own pleasure. They reside at the summit of the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) in the abode of Māra. This indicates that for a Bodhisattva, the realm of desire is difficult to transcend until the fifth stage;
prior to this, the five sensory desires are not yet fully mastered, and one merely practices the various pāramitās through contemplative observation.

By the power of cultivation, one does not sink into them; yet, because one has not yet attained the effortless mastery of the flow of non-action characteristic of the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), one takes meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) as the essence [of practice].

One cultivates the contemplation of the ten truths (*daśa-tattva-vipaśyanā*) to remedy the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) regarding the defiled and pure states of the three realms.

By attaining the gateway of the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-vidyā*), one teaches and transforms sentient beings, making the attainment of happiness by others one’s own happiness. If one does not act thus, one is a māra.
As for their retinue, the bodies of these devas are sixteen yojanas in height, and their garments are thirty-two yojanas in length.
Their lifespan, measured in days, months, and years, is all double that of the previous [deva realm].
The ten great Brahmā kings, such as Śikhin and others, represent the ten *pāramitās* within the *prajñā* of the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
"Brahmā" is so named because of his speech and voice. King Śikhin utters the Great Brahmā-sound, and each member of the Brahmā assembly thinks to themselves, "He is speaking only to me.
He is most sovereign throughout the great trichiliocosm; his countenance is like that of a youth, and his body...
They are white-silver in color, half a yojana in height, and their robes are golden. They have no male or female form;

they take the joy of dhyāna as food and live for one kalpa, delighting in the cultivation of meditative stillness. This stage is illustrated by the metaphor of polishing pure gold with lapis lazuli to make it even more brilliant and pure;
it shows that this bodhisattva employs the ten types of contemplation on the twelve links of dependent origination and the ten emptiness samādhis as [the means of purification].
Vaiḍūrya is used to polish wisdom, making it increasingly bright and pure. Clearly contemplating ignorance results in the formation of fundamental wisdom, which becomes even more bright and pure.
The ten light-sound heavenly kings, such as Priyadarśana-prabha and others, represent the skillful means within the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi.
The ten pāramitās: the Light-Sound (Ābhāsvara) is the second dhyāna. Having already extinguished sorrow and suffering, light arises from the mouth when speech is uttered.

This signifies that the bodhisattva of the seventh stage has perfected the practice of great compassion; by enduring his own suffering and impermanence to deliver others from suffering, he teaches through light to shatter darkness.
The ten Śuddhāvāsakāyika kings, such as Viśuddhakīrti and others, represent the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā) of the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā).

These deities of the third dhyāna heaven are moved by the joy of meditative rapture (dhyāna-prīti), and thus the calamity of wind still reaches them; this represents that the effortful application (prayoga) of the eighth stage has reached its conclusion, and non-effortful wisdom (anābhoga-jñāna) has manifested.
Although the wisdom of the bliss of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-sukha-jñāna) is pure, the residual habitual tendencies (vāsanā) still remain. Thus, the Buddhas...
Furthermore, they are exhorted to recollect their original vows, whereby they subsequently act in accordance with wisdom to extensively benefit sentient beings.

The ten *Mahāphala* Heaven Kings, such as Priyadharman (愛樂法) and Dharmāvabhāsaketu (法光明幢), represent the ten *pāramitās* within the power of the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*) on the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
These deities of the fourth dhyāna heaven are without inhalation or exhalation, and the three calamities do not reach them; they possess form (*rūpa*).
Although the resultant mental consciousness still exists, the mental consciousness of the desire realm is already absent.
In this stage, one teaches various dharmas without mind or mental consciousness, acting as a great Dharma Master who possesses all-encompassing wisdom and the illumination of the Dharma.

The ten great sovereign celestial kings, such as Sublime Flame-Ocean (Sudharmasāgara), represent the ten *pāramitās* within the wisdom *pāramitā* of the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha-bhūmi*).
This entire host of deities diligently observes the phenomena of ignorance; they signify the perfection of the signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) of the tenth stage.
Having taken the true Dharma as their object, their internal and external habitual tendencies are extinguished. The Great Sovereign Heaven (Maheśvara) dwells in the fourth dhyāna.
The "Peak Color" (Kūṭāgāra-varṇa) within the Heaven of Ultimate Perfection (Akaniṣṭha) symbolizes the pinnacle of mastery over the wisdom and compassion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

This is an expedient means of introduction that relies upon phenomena to manifest the Dharma; thus, the spheres of conversion and transformation gradually increase in excellence. To speak according to reality, in the single-vehicle Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), principle and phenomena are interpenetrated:
within a single atom, the Buddha-lands and the realms of humans and devas coexist, their bodies and atoms being non-dual.

The pores [of the Buddha's body] are like reflections, entering one another; they encompass the ten gates of mystery (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*) and cannot be described according to the marks of manifested transformation.
The ten assemblies mentioned above are provisionally assigned to the rank of the devas, symbolizing the Buddha’s own practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the hundred gates of *pāramitā*.
Thus, the Bodhisattvas, the divine kings, and the various devas collectively clarify the gate of causal practice through the five stages of the Tathāgata’s own conduct.
Because wisdom is like space—formless and colorless yet its great function is all-pervasive;

it moves swiftly without going, it arrives without coming, it acts without effort, and it achieves results by responding to things—it is termed "divine" (*śiva*). This is due to the nature of non-active wisdom.
In a single thought-moment, one universally knows the similarities and differences throughout the ten directions; being sovereign and unimpeded regarding all objects, one is called a King.
With a body pure and stainless, not obstructed by material substance, yet appearing and disappearing with mastery, one is called a Deva.

Therefore, while he temporarily assumes a station identical to that of a deity, a celestial being, or a human—indeed, sharing these same conditions with all ordinary beings throughout the ten directions—he is nonetheless a spirit who is neither a celestial being, nor a human, nor a ghost or spirit.
Just as the Buddha is in reality not a king of oxen, a king of dragons, or a king of elephants.

However, by relying on phenomena to express the Dharma, it is made easy to understand. Hereafter, from the Great Lord Maheśvara King down to the Bodhisattva Samudrareṇuprabhāsa, forty-one assemblies each set forth the gates of liberation they have attained and each speak ten verses.
In the first verse of each, there is pure praise of the Buddha; in the subsequent nine verses, three lines of each verse praise the Buddha, while one line [praises the Dharma].
Rejoicing that what they had attained was identical to that of the Buddha, the assembly of Sāgaraprabha alone praised the Buddha’s virtues as being similar to the Dharma they themselves had entered.
Thus, they provided a general introduction to four hundred and twenty gates of liberation. Among the forty-one assemblies of leaders and their retinues, there were four hundred and ten individuals;
however, because the single person Samantabhadra himself had personally attained ten gates of liberation, nine [of these] were universal bodhisattvas.
Sakyamuni, with his pure virtues and wondrous light, personally [manifested] as ten people; thus he attained four hundred and twenty gates of liberation.

This clarifies that they equally attained the liberation of the Buddha and equally entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It clarifies that those who have not yet awakened are ordinary beings, while those who awaken are identical to the Buddha.
This was done to serve as a model for future students, so that they might emulate it.
From Maheśvara, King of the Heaven of Great Sovereignty, to Śakra, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven— these ten lords of the assembly and their retinues, numbering one hundred kings,
attained a hundred gates of liberation and praised the Buddha’s practice and fruition of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

From the Sun Deity (*Sūrya-devaputra*) to the ten assemblies of a hundred *asura* kings, they attained a hundred gates of liberation and praised the Buddha’s practice and fruit of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
From the Lord of Day deities to the Lord of Crops deities, ten assemblies of a hundred deities attained a hundred gates of liberation and praised the Buddha’s ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).
The fruit thereof.
The principal medicinal deity and the ten assemblies of one hundred bodhisattvas, beginning with Sāgaramati-prabhāsa-mahāvyūha,
attained one hundred gates of liberation and praised the Buddha’s fruit of the ten stages of practice.
Samantabhadra alone enters the ten gates of liberation to clarify the ten dharmas within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
One is all; one and many are sovereign; extension and contraction are free; this is the meaning of total integration.

Among the assembly of Samantabhadras, nine persons plus the person Pure Virtue Wondrous Light (*Viśuddhaguṇa-prabhā*) make ten, who attain the ten gates of liberation. Pure Virtue Wondrous Light is...

Mañjuśrī is a specific epithet [for the Buddha] that clarifies how, within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), cause and effect, wisdom and prajñā, and the myriad practices are perfectly integrated.
At that time, from every single article of adornment upon the Tathāgata’s lion throne, there emerged Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of Buddha-fields.
Each of these leaders raised clouds of offerings and spoke verses in praise of the Buddha, each according to their respective direction.

Regarding "sitting upon a transformed seat": this clarifies that the Dharma-body is the substance of the seat, the myriad practices of Samantabhadra are the adornments upon the seat, and non-conceptual wisdom is the Buddha seated upon it.
That Bodhisattvas emerge from the seat signifies that these are the ancient practices of former Buddhas;

it clarifies that the present Buddha accords with ancient practice and ancient practice accords with the present Buddha. Thus, the ancient and the present are non-dual, which also clarifies the non-duality of cause and effect. Therefore, within...
Within the fruits obtained as the retribution for one's fundamental practice, there emerge again the multitudes who were originally the causes for their own practice.

Furthermore, the assembly of Samantabhadra outside the seat represents the Buddha’s practice of benefiting others, while those within the seat represent the assembly of Samantabhadra realized through the Buddha’s own practice.

This great assembly—the path of all Buddhas of the past and present is one and not two—when sentient beings ride upon it, it is called "riding the Tathāgata-vehicle" to reach the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). For all dharmas are the site of enlightenment.
At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the earth shook in six ways and eighteen aspects. This clarifies the assembly of those who constantly follow the Buddha;

the assembly of various heavenly deities and kings; the assembly of all Buddhas of the past and present within the seats; the assembly within the trees whose light flows forth; the assembly of the ten types of compassion within the palaces;
and the assembly of those who have gathered from their own respective groups to receive benefit, rejoice in the Buddha, and experience joy in their hearts.

It moves; thus the earth moves along with it. This clarifies that from the initial gathering of the great assembly, light is emitted from the face-gate and universally gathers those from other lands who also arrive.

This clarifies that within the non-duality of self and other, there is no "other" apart from the "self. The ritual of transformation—of the principal and the retinue—is like the movement of dragons and the response of clouds;

such is the natural harmony of the Dharma-activity. Because the true *dharmatā* universally pervades all lands throughout the dust-motes of the universe, the three periods of time are co-extensive within a single *kṣaṇa*.

This is further encompassed by the gate of the mutual inclusion of the one and the many. Thus, the emission of light and the gathering of the assembly are intended to make known that the characteristics of the Buddha’s realm interpenetrate without duality.
The above constitutes the first section: the manifestation of the five stages of practice, which completes the cause and fruit.
Chapter Two: The Tathāgata Manifests His Signs.

Regarding the Tathāgata manifesting his signs: because all the bodhisattvas and the lords of the world harbored thirty-seven doubts concerning the Buddha-ground, the Buddha-realm, and so forth, they remained silent while recollecting [the Buddha].
Thereupon, from among the ritual offerings, a voice emerged to speak verses and pose questions; and thus, the Tathāgata...
Upon their arrival, the mind immediately perceived that the assembly was in doubt regarding the emission of light from between the Buddha’s teeth.

That light pervaded the ten directions and produced sounds that recited verses as the ocean-like multitudes from the ten directions gathered like clouds. This is the manifestation of the sovereign marks of a Buddha’s realm. The offerings were accompanied by the recitation of verses.
This clarifies that the mind and its objects are non-dual, for all phenomena are the inconceivable essence of the *dharmadhātu*.
The Tathāgata, knowing the doubts of the assembly, employs the mind of the *dharmadhātu* which is identical to the minds of sentient beings. He manifests the sign of the light from his teeth;

since the mouth and teeth are the locus from which speech and sound are emitted, this signifies his command for the assembly to gather. Thus, the worlds of the ten directions are illumined by the Buddha’s light.

It is clearly stated that Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields, come from their respective Buddhas' abodes, all raising clouds of offerings as numerous as the atoms within oceans of worlds;
these are the multitudes coming from other lands, who are "others" within the context of neither self nor other.
By means of these perfected rites of transformation, the principal and its retinue manifest ten clouds of offerings, which represent the ten *pāramitā* practices.
From every single pore of the bodies of these bodhisattvas, there appear rays of light as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.

Within each ray of light, there appear bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds. Each of these bodhisattvas enters everywhere throughout the *dharmadhātu* and establishes [the teachings].
Within every single atom of all the oceans, there are as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in a buddha-field;
in each and every field, there are the Buddhas of the three periods of time. May all those bodhisattvas be able to go to each of them, act in concert with them, and benefit sentient beings.

This clarifies the inconceivable essence of the dharma-realm, wherein the realms of body and mind are unimpeded between self and other, capable of both identity and difference, like the realm of Indra’s net, with layers upon layers of mutual reflection.

As for the light emitted from the ūrṇā-kośa (the tuft of hair) between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, named "Universally Illuminating the Treasury of the Ten Directions," this clarifies that it is the light of the wisdom, the middle path, and the practice of the ten stages of Bodhisattvas who have perfected their realization. This light...

The foremost among the assembly who emerged was named Sarvadharmavijayasvara (Victorious Sound of All Dharmas). This represents the practice of the fruit of the Middle Way, perfected through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Taking this dharma-gate of the Middle Way—wherein awakening, conduct, compassion, and wisdom are fully realized within the *dharmadhātu*, and which is a non-obstructive dharma across oceans of lands as numerous as atoms—he answered the thirty-seven questions of the previous assembly, so as to inspire faith in those of the present and the future.
Because this Dharma-gate of the cause and fruit of the ten stages of the Dharma-realm fulfills practice and causes all throughout the ten directions to obtain benefit, the Sūtra says:
"Desiring to enable the entire great assembly to attain the Tathāgata’s boundless realm and supernormal powers, he emits light from between his eyebrows.
As for that light returning and entering beneath the Buddha’s feet: the space beneath the feet is the juncture where initial faith gives rise to practice. This is because [he wishes to...]
This causes the great assembly to believe in and practice that which is the Dharma of the inseparable essence and function of the ocean-like wisdom and principle of the Buddha-fruit.

As for the primary figure sitting upon the lotus pedestal with his retinue sitting on the filaments, this symbolizes the principal and attendant aspects of the myriad practices, similar to the assembly produced from the light rays flowing from the pores of the Bodhisattvas mentioned previously; it clarifies the perfection within the wisdom and principle of the *dharmadhātu*.
The conduct of mastery is such that there is no substance to obstruct it.
○ Chapter Three: The Samādhi of Samantabhadra.
Regarding the entry of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra into the Tathāgata Vairocana’s Treasury-Body Samādhi: *Vairocana* here translates as...
*Vairocana* means "variously illuminating all. The Tathāgata is the essence-body of *dharmatā*, while the *saṃbhogakāya* is the wisdom that encompasses all phenomena.

"Luminous" (*prabhāsvara*) refers to the benefit bestowed according to the faculties [of beings] through the integration of principle and wisdom, as well as teaching and practice. Thirdly, it is called "correct" (*samyak*):

just as the third month of the lunar year, when the three yang energies arise, is designated the first month (*zhengyue*), so too does "one-pointed stillness" constitute correctness; by stilling the one mind, its Way becomes naturally correct. [Otherwise, one would be] obscured.

It is said that "concentration" (*samādhi*) means that when the five aggregates and the mental consciousness are dark and inactive, true wisdom manifests before one; therefore, *samādhi* is right concentration.
As for "entering Samantabhadra," the *Samantabhadra-samādhi* is eternally free from both fixed concentration and distraction. This is as described in the "Ten Concentrations" chapter:
when the consecrated Bodhisattva gives rise to various thoughts in search of Samantabhadra, Samantabhadra is already constantly within *samādhi*, whether in a state of concentration or distraction.

Both are true. However, because Samantabhadra succeeds to the family of the great wisdom of the Buddha’s Dharma-realm, and serves as the eldest son who brings the Buddha’s myriad practices to universal completion, he must enter meditative absorption to establish the ritual protocols for discussing the ocean of the Buddha’s fruition and the ocean of sentient beings’ karmic retribution.
When Samantabhadra enters this samādhi, the entire Dharma-realm and empty space...
Within every single atom of all lands throughout the realms, there are Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds.

Within each of those fields, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds. Before each and every Buddha, there are Samantabhadras as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, all of whom have likewise entered this samādhi.
Within each and every Samantabhadra, the manifestations of the objects of the ten directions appear.

Regarding "touching the crown of the head" and "bestowing wisdom": this clarifies that the conduct of Samantabhadra pervades the entire Dharma-realm, like the interlacing light and shadows of Indra’s net, infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
To bring the wisdom of differentiation into accord with fundamental wisdom is the manifestation of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
to have these two wisdoms reach one another is the touching of the crown of the head; and to be mutually sealed and approved is the bestowing of wisdom. [The Bodhisattva] then arises from samādhi.
This is because, intending to lift up both the ocean of the Buddha-fruit and the ocean of sentient beings, one gives rise to the activity of practice from the essence of the fruit.
Chapter Four: The Accomplishment of Worlds.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva describes the various forms and various bases of the oceans of worlds, as well as their various sufferings and joys.
Purity and defilement are both produced according to the karma of sentient beings themselves. When the karma of sentient beings transforms, the ocean of lands transforms;
when the karma of sentient beings forms and disintegrates, the ocean of lands forms and disintegrates; when the karma of sentient beings is defiled or pure, the ocean of lands is defiled or pure.
Because the mental activities of sentient beings are boundless, the oceans of lands are likewise without limit.
Within such oceans of lands, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas achieve pure adornment through their great vows, great compassion, great practices, and the power of inconceivable transformations.
Because the ocean of sentient beings' karma is inexhaustible, the vast bodies, speech, and [minds] of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
The ocean of the fruits of wise conduct is likewise inexhaustible. To clarify the ocean of the practices of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Samantabhadra:
all arise from the ocean of the karmic actions of sentient beings. This causes those who practice and study to know that the realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of the Buddha.

The mental realm of sentient beings is equal to the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space; like light and shadow, they interpenetrate one another in infinite layers without obstruction. This is not for those ordinary people.
This concludes the section on the various deviant views concerning heaven, power, existence and non-existence, unity and difference, purity and impurity, self and other, and coming and going.
Chapter Five: The Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng Shìjiè Pǐn*).

Regarding the Flower Treasury World: it is the fruit of adornment obtained through the retribution of the practices and deeds of the five stages of Buddhahood, as expounded by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

The Ocean. It opens up and expands the vision and knowledge of sentient beings. Because this vast land of fruition is supported by a lotus flower that contains all worlds within it, it is named "Flower Treasury" (Kusuma-garbha).
Beneath this Flower Treasury World, there are ten kinds of wind-circles that support and sustain it;
these are the fruits of the ten perfections accomplished within the perfection of great vows. By means of...
The Dharma-body is without intrinsic nature. If there were no aspiration, then all practices would be unable to be accomplished, like a rudderless boat drifting and turning with the waves.
Therefore, the wheel of great aspirational wisdom sustains all myriad practices, just as the wind-circle produced by karmic retribution sustains all worlds.
These worlds reside within the Lotus Treasury; this is the retributive wisdom of the Dharma-body’s unattached and non-reliant conduct that accords with practice.
The flowers named *Vicitra-kesara-gandha-dhvaja* (Various Stamen-Fragrance Banners) are the retribution for the wisdom of differentiation that is never swayed or deluded.
The ocean of fragrant water is the retribution for immeasurable and boundless great compassion. The river of fragrant water is the retribution for unremitting progress in cultivation.

The diamond ground is the retribution for firm practice in the nature of equality. The Cakravāḍa mountains are the retribution for the protective observance of precepts through great kindness. The assembly...

The exquisite jewel-flowers are the retribution for the blossoming of the myriad practices; the jewel-trees are the retribution for the practice of providing shelter and protection for sentient beings.

Indeed, retribution is never obtained in vain; therefore, it is said that all these are adorned and purified by the countless great vows cultivated by Vairocana Tathāgata in the past at the abodes of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds. As for the world-systems:
A number of three thousand great thousandfold world systems equaling one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) constitutes one world-ocean.
A number of such ocean worlds equaling one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* constitutes one world-nature. A number of such world-natures equaling one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* constitutes one world-lineage.
Within this Flower Treasury [World], there are worlds numbering as many as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields.

Within this world-system of the central fragrant water-ocean, there are twenty tiers of worlds, each separated from the one above or below by a number of worlds equal to the atoms within a buddha-field. This Sahā world is located in the thirteenth tier.
In the very first tier at the bottom, it is surrounded by a number of worlds equal to the atoms within a buddha-field; this number increases successively up to the highest tier.
It is surrounded by twenty layers of worlds as numerous as the atoms in twenty buddha-fields.
Outside this world-system, there are ten world-systems arrayed in the ten directions, each also consisting of twenty layers.
Their vertical distances and their surrounding perimeters increase progressively, all being identical to those of the central world-system. Outside these ten world-systems...
There are one hundred world-systems surrounding [this central system]. Within these one hundred world-systems, there are ten world-systems closest to the Cakravāḍa Mountains.
To briefly illustrate, four tiers are enumerated from top to bottom; although the number of tiers is small, their total height is equal to that of twenty world-systems.
As for the remaining ninety world-systems, their tiered arrangement is not mentioned here, but they are included in the total count.
One hundred and eleven world-systems are distributed and abide like the net of Indra.
Within them, the successive worlds—like the sun, moon, and stars—are sustained by wind and situated in space.
By what cause do these world-systems exist? The single world-system at the center is the fundamental, immovable realm of the Buddha.
This is the retribution of wisdom. The ten world-systems outside of that are the retribution of one cause and one fruit for each of the five stages of the Buddha-dharma.
Each of these contains twenty layers, which are the retribution of one cause and one fruit for each of the ten *pāramitās*.
All the Buddhas within each layer are the fruits of further advancement (*viśeṣa-gati*). Next, the hundred world-systems outside of those are the five stages.
Within this, the fifty *pāramitās* constitute the retributive fruits produced by one cause and one effect.

Among them, the ten world-systems (*lokadhātu-vīja*) consist of only four layers, which are the retributive fruits of benefiting sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Since the four means of integration are themselves the practice of the ten *pāramitās*, they correspond in height to the twenty layers [of the Flower Treasury World]. Within this Flower Treasury World...
Regarding the various distinctions within the manifold world systems: these are the realms formed as the retributive fruits of the respective karmas of the sentient beings contained therein.
Because of the differences in the individual karma of sentient beings, even though they occupy the same location, their environments differ.
These lands are sustained by the wind of the deluded karma of sentient beings, whereas those sustained by the wind of the great vows and wisdom of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the true [lands].

Regarding the land of retribution: fundamentally, it is a single land. Because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas traverse the realm of sentient beings, their lands of retribution likewise naturally pervade that realm of sentient beings.

It is only because of the differences in the karma and conduct of sentient beings that they themselves are unable to see them—just as worldly spirits, ghosts, and deities coexist with humans, yet humans cannot perceive them. This Flower Treasury World is perfectly round.
Regarding the subsumption of the three periods of time: the three periods are identical to a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is identical to non-thought.

Within this state of non-thought, one does not destroy various thoughts; within the absence of time, one does not abandon various times. Therefore, the karmic actions, retributions, and objective realms of the Buddhas and sentient beings throughout the three periods of time all manifest within it in mutual interpenetration.
It is like hundreds of thousands of mirrors suspended on four sides, wherein the reflections of the past and future appear simultaneously.

The characteristics of the elephant and the [other] signs interpenetrate one another. This Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu), which manifests and conceals with sovereign freedom, is such that when following the Dharma-body, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously quiescent;
when following the function of wisdom, the myriad phenomena are all produced; when following great compassion, it constantly dwells within birth and death;

and when following the principle of wisdom, birth and death are eternally true. Therefore, although there are myriad modes of concealment and manifestation, the pure and the mixed are without obstruction. Indeed...

The Buddha-land is fundamentally empty; yet this Flower Treasury World is so vast and expansive because there are those of the Two Vehicles who stagnate in quiescence and abandon practice, those of the provisional teachings who delight in being born in other lands, and sentient beings who fear emptiness, who remain bound to their environments and their karma, and are thus unable to attain liberation.
Therefore, this vast realm of merit, wisdom, vows, and practice is manifested, so that it may be known that the Buddha-land is neither born nor extinguished,
but dwells eternally therein by the power of his original vows solely for the benefit of sentient beings.
Chapter Six: Vairocana. Regarding the arrival of this chapter:

having presented the present fruit of Buddhahood of Vairocana in the preceding five chapters, there may be doubt in the minds of later students as to whether there were ancient precedents in the past, wondering, "From where does he now come?
Therefore, this chapter cites the appearance in the world of the Buddhas of antiquity to clarify the path.
The traces [of the teaching] remain; the dharma-marks of the present Vairocana’s appearance in the world have been transmitted without change.

By citing the past, he establishes faith in the present; furthermore, this chapter is titled after the name of the present Buddha. It was originally preached by Samantabhadra, yet as the preceding text was insufficient, this chapter lacks a concluding colophon.
The six chapters above contain the meaning of the three dharmas and the six universal pervasions. Vairo...
Vairocana Tathāgata is the formless Dharmakāya; Mañjuśrī is Great Wisdom; Samantabhadra is Great Conduct. These three dharmas constitute the essence of the five stages of progressive cultivation.
In the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of World Rulers," it is clarified that the Buddha’s body of wisdom is all-pervasive.

In the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata," the light from his teeth shines throughout the ten directions to inform the assembly, clarifying that the Buddha’s vocal activity and voice are all-pervasive.

The "Universal" [Chapter] clarifies the pervasiveness of the Buddha’s essence, function, and practice-gate within the Samantabhadra Samādhi Chapter; the "World-Formation" Chapter clarifies the pervasiveness of the Buddha’s bodily activities;
the "Flower Treasury World" Chapter clarifies the pervasiveness of the Buddha’s land of fruition, wherein the myriad practices of wisdom and compassion are perfected;
and this chapter clarifies the pervasiveness of the Buddha’s timeless wisdom-essence throughout the three periods of time. Students should embody these three dharmas.
Sixth is the meaning of universal pervasion. By believing in the rules and models practiced by the Buddha, one establishes one’s own faith;

only then does one realize the Buddha’s knowledge and vision without error. The above has explained the defiled and pure karmic retributions of Bodhisattvas and sentient beings, as well as the Buddha’s land of reward.
This answers the doubts of the former World-Ruler regarding the ocean of Buddhas, the ocean of the Buddhas’ spheres of activity, and the ocean of Bodhisattva practices and *pāramitās*.
The "Sea of Honey" and the "Sea of Sentient Beings" are posed as silent questions.

*The Compendium of the Essential Points of the Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Volume Two.
Compiled by Li Tongxuan, the Elder of Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty;
edited by the Bhikṣu Fangze of Mingxi. Chapter Seven:
The Names and Epithets of the Buddhas.
In the first assembly above, the ocean of the Buddha-fruit was presented to cause all scholars to believe in the Dharma attained by all Buddhas.

At the beginning of this second assembly, the inherently unmoving wisdom—the primordially existing Dharma of sentient beings—is presented, so that all scholars may have confidence that their own minds are themselves the Buddha, no different from all Buddhas. From here until the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter:
This briefly presents the methods for practicing the five stages of application; it is the standard for the practitioner’s own mind to achieve Buddhahood.

Regarding the name of the Buddha: one must have faith that the fundamental wisdom-seal (*mūla-jñāna-mudrā*) of one’s own *dharmadhātu* universally seals all phenomena and all names and terms, such that they are all devoid of intrinsic nature and are all identical to the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. All Buddhas [attain their state] by means of this...

When the Dharma-nature, which is free from [duality], attains Buddhahood, then all phenomena and all names and expressions are entirely the aspect of perfect enlightenment within the nature of one's own Dharma-realm.

This is like the ten Buddhas beginning with Immovable Wisdom (Acalamati), as well as the ten Moon Buddhas in the Ten Abodes, the ten Eye Buddhas in the Ten Practices, and the ten Banner Buddhas in the Ten Transferences; all of these are one's own.
These are names established according to the practice of the fundamental wisdom of the essence.

Furthermore, within the realm of sentient beings, appearing as Buddhas, devas, spirits, kings, humans, or immortals—these bodies that transform sentient beings everywhere are all names for the form-body manifested in accordance with the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*. By means of such meanings of these Buddha-names, [he causes] all...

Sentient beings, from this very moment, should have confidence in themselves as Buddhas. They should not delight in provisional teachings concerning other pure lands, nor should they be hindered by the Small Vehicle’s notion of attaining Buddhahood only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. To reiterate:
the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-koṭi*) is the reward-dwelling of the Dharma-realm.
The two bodies of Dharma and Reward are identical in their essential nature and characteristics; they are one in truth, with no difference between the root and the branches.

Because it pervades all places without shifting from its original locus, this is recounted again. The vows of the various Bodhisattvas and the four kinds of Buddha-fields revealed by the Buddha, as well as the thirty-two points of doubt regarding the Ten Abodes, the Ten Practices, and so forth, are similar to the doubts of the World Rulers in the first assembly; however, this assembly...
One must believe that one's own mind is the Buddha; within the phenomena of one's own mind, one should inquire further. Regarding the four kinds of Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*):
the fundamental locus is the place where both sages and ordinary beings dwell together, and is called the "Buddha-abiding Buddha-field.

Among the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*), the methods of progressive cultivation that adorn the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body are called the "adorned Buddha-field of the Buddha-nature. [It] demonstrates the attainment of perfect enlightenment and the turning of the wheel of Dharma...
The Buddha-field named Pure Dharma-Wheel is the field of the Buddhas who preach the Dharma;
the Buddha-field named Essential Nature of Manifesting Spiritual Powers According to Capacities through Appearing in the World is the field of the Buddhas of Majestic Virtue.

The World-Honored One knows the thoughts of all beings and accordingly manifests spiritual powers for each according to their kind, appearing under various names in all lands and among all sentient beings, as described below in the case of Mañjuśrī.
This refers to the proclamation of the names of the Buddhas and the names of the fruits manifested according to each of the five stages.
Thereupon, beyond ten Buddha-land-microdust worlds in each of the ten directions, in the ten worlds such as Golden and others, at the abodes of the ten Buddhas such as Immovable Wisdom and others,
there were ten Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī and others, each accompanied by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the dust motes of ten Buddha-lands.
They came to where the Buddha was, each manifesting a Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne in the direction from which they had come and sitting upon it in the full lotus posture.
Their karma, which transcends the ten afflictions (*kleśa*) and is beyond the reach of comprehension, is called "Transcending Worlds as Numerous as the Dust-Motes of Ten Buddha-fields.
They are named for their faith in their own *dharmakāya*—its purity and freedom from defilement—as well as the dharmas that accompany the *dharmakāya*.

The ten material worlds, such as Gold and so forth, which are the fruits resulting from faith in one’s own fundamental wisdom and the wisdom-body that accords with it, are called the Ten Wisdom Buddhas, beginning with Acala (Akṣobhya).

Mañjuśrī—here translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode)—is the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) within one’s own fundamental wisdom, along with the wisdom that accords with the dharma and practices in various ways; these are called the Ten Great Bodhisattvas, beginning with Mañjuśrī. By means of...

The wisdom-body is all-pervasive, and its primary and attendant manifestations are inexhaustible; this is what is meant by "each being accompanied by a multitude as numerous as the atoms of ten Buddha-fields.
Boundless Buddha-lands do not exceed a single atom or a single pore. Fundamentally, there is no distinction between internal and external, near and far, or coming and going.

It is only because of past delusion that they were separated; now, through awakening, they come to the presence of the Buddha. That all phenomena do not depart from the fundamental Dharma is what is meant by [this term].
In each of the directions from which they came, that which is unstained is called a lotus; that which is fearless is called a lion.
Containing all dharmas while remaining unstained, and dwelling in the world to benefit others while remaining fearless, it is named the "Transformed Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne.
Ten thousand gathered become one without restriction; one dispersed becomes ten thousand without confusion; this is named the *paryaṅka* (full-lotus) posture.
This is the seat. In the Eastern World of Golden Color, there is a Bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, belonging to the Buddha Akṣobhyajñāna. The East is the first illumination;

it signifies vibration and the springtime birth. Its golden essence is white in substance yet yellow in color, representing the inner seal of the stainless, pure Dharma (anāsrava-dharma), while externally manifesting the harmonious yellow appearance of a realized sage (arhat). Although the position of gold is in the West, it is here called the "Gold of the East."

Regarding form (*rūpa*): it is conceived in the womb of gold during the Tiger month (*yīn*), enters the fetal stage in the Rabbit month (*mǎo*), takes shape in the Dragon month (*chén*), is born in the Snake month (*sì*), is nurtured in the Horse month (*wǔ*), attains the rank of *guāndài* in the Sheep month (*wèi*), manifests its characteristics in the Monkey month (*shēn*), and reaches its peak (*wàng*) in the Cock month (*yǒu*).

Taking the aspiration for faith as the holy fetus, one is only then born into the Buddha-family upon reaching the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). Therefore, the East is of golden color. Because it remains unmoved amidst all movement, the Buddha is titled "The Immovable" (*Akṣobhya*).
The Wisdom of Movement. All sublime practices arise from wisdom; therefore, Mañjuśrī is the mother of all Buddhas.
From the Buddha Unobstructed Wisdom in the world of Sublime Color in the south—the direction of wisdom—a bodhisattva named Chief of Enlightenment [Bodhiśiras] resides there.
The south represents emptiness, fire, the sun, the eye, and literary expression. When one realizes the emptiness of phenomena, the phenomena themselves become sublime. Therefore...

He is named Wondrous Form (*Rūpa*). Since the fundamental nature of phenomena is empty and luminous, inherently free from obstruction or stagnation, the Buddha is titled Unobstructed Wisdom (*Anāvaraṇajñāna*).

Having realized the nature of all phenomena and transcending them with sublime nobility, he is named Chief of Enlightenment (*Bodhiśiras*). In the western world-realm of Lotus Color (*Padmavarṇa*), where the Buddha Extinction-of-Darkness Wisdom (*Tamo-nirvāṇajñāna*) resides, there is a bodhisattva named Chief of Wealth (*Dhanaśiras*).
The west corresponds to the White Tiger; it is associated with punishment and execution, and with darkness and obscurity. Regarding this... [text continues]
Abiding in a state of excellence without being defiled is called "Lotus Color" (Padmavarṇa). Not being obscured even in places of darkness is called "Wisdom that Extinguishes Darkness.

Since one is not personally obscured, one destroys the darkness of others; possessing the principle of benefiting beings through the wealth of the Dharma, one is named "Foremost in Wealth" (Dhanapati).
As for the Bodhisattva named Ratnamati (Jewel Forehead) in the world of Campaka-flower Color in the northern direction, under the Buddha Vidyā-vinaya-jñāna (Wisdom of Dignified Conduct):
The north is associated with Xuánwǔ (the Dark Warrior) and the *kǎn* trigram of water. *Kǎn* signifies entrapment and peril. Water is dark on the outside and bright within;

it serves as a metaphor for a ruler who applies punishments and governance through the manifestation of brilliant virtue. It descends to the lowly to moisten all things; it serves as a metaphor for a teacher who establishes instruction for the ignorant and naive.
The *champaka* is a yellow flower; yellow is the color of auspiciousness and celebration. At a time when people are foolish, deceitful, and estranged from one another—

He transforms through the virtue of wisdom and thus achieves auspicious merit; his name, Candraprabha (Campaka-flower-colored), signifies this. He guides ordinary people by means of various rules and regulations;
his name, Īśvaraprajña (Wisdom of Dignified Conduct), signifies this. He honors the precious Dharma and universally responds to the needs of all seekers;

his name, Ratnaśrī (Jewel-Crest), signifies this. As for the Bodhisattva named Guṇaśrī (Virtue-Crest) in the northeast: the northeast corresponds to the trigram Gen, to mountains, to stillness, and to the youngest son; it is symbolized by the elephant.
This is to inspire the ignorant and the young through the virtue of dignified steadfastness. Regarding the names of the Bodhisattvas in the southeast:

the southeast corresponds to the trigram Xun, which represents wind and transformation; it nurtures and grows all things, symbolizing the use of the eye of wisdom to observe the faculties [of beings] and thereby bring them to spiritual accomplishment through teaching.
Regarding the Bodhisattva in the southwest named Qinsou (Dharmakṣema): the southwest corresponds to Kun, the earth.
They serve to inspire faith and compliance; they serve to bring peace and stability; they serve to give birth and nurture; and they serve to carry burdens.

Like great compassion, they are ever compliant with the virtue of loving life, bearing the heavy responsibility of benefiting sentient beings without weariness. The Bodhisattva in the northwest is named Dharmottara (法首).

The northwest is the realm of Qian, the Metal element. It represents strength and vigor, the sovereign, and the father. Its imagery symbolizes how one presides over all sentient beings with the virtue of lofty brilliance and strength, nurturing and sustaining them.
As for the Bodhisattva named Zhishou (Wisdom-Head) in the lower direction: the lower direction is the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). The wind is exceedingly firm and dense;
its imagery symbolizes the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), which skillfully expounds all dharmas without being subject to defeat or destruction.
Regarding the Bodhisattva named Worthy Leader (Bhadramukha) in the zenith: in the zenith, the sun, moon, and stars dwell in space to illuminate all things.
Because his elephant-like wisdom (*gajñāna*) and *pāramitā* illuminate sentient beings as most worthy and most supreme, he is named Worthy Leader. Such is the meaning of the ten directions:

though they exist within the directions, they are not fixed directions; one merely takes up their phenomena. Since there is no fixed phenomenon, there is no fixed direction—this applies to each and every one.
Method: This involves mutual inclusion and perfect integration. As it is said: "Everywhere is the Golden World;
everywhere is the Buddha Immovable Wisdom; everywhere is Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva"—this is not a fixed direction within the mundane world.

That all worlds are called "form" (rūpa) means that, for the time being, believing in one's own Buddha-mind is still the mind of form and consciousness subject to arising and ceasing; one has not yet been born into the family of Buddhas.
This is not a matter of actual realization. To cite the names of ten billion kinds of Buddhas in each of the ten directions so that all sentient beings may individually know and see them:
because the names of the Buddhas pervade all phenomena and pervade all names, they are equal and pure, beyond grasping or rejecting;
they are, in essence, the nature of all dharmas within the dharma-realm, free from [the concept of] "Buddha-name," and are intended to cause all to awaken.

Entering one’s own dharma-realm through the self-realized knowledge and vision of a Buddha, one thereby perfects the stage of faith; thus it was spoken by the Youth Mañjuśrī. Chapter Eight: The Four Noble Truths.
Regarding the "Four Noble Truths" (*catur-āryasatya*):
*satya* has the meaning of "reality. This means that the four dharmas of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path all possess the meaning of reality. That is to say:
These sages, because they are able to penetrate the true nature of suffering, understand that the origin of suffering is like an illusion, and abide in accordance with the Dharma;

they cultivate the path in accordance with the Dharma without weariness or attachment, without longing or grasping. They are one with the *dharmadhātu*, having no nature of coming or going, and no nature of abiding.
This is not like the *śrāvakas*, who loathe suffering, sever its origin, aspire for cessation, and cultivate the path, thereby realizing a *nirvāṇa* characterized by attainment. Thus...
These—the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—are collectively the Noble Truths of the One Vehicle.

To cite the ten directions of the world and state that the four noble truths each have hundreds of billions of millions of names, which according to the minds of sentient beings cause them all to be tamed, clarifies that the Buddha’s verbal activity in preaching the Dharma is all-pervasive.
This is because all worldly realms do not depart from suffering and its origin, and all supramundane realms do not depart from [their cessation and the path].
Cessation and the Path. Because these are able to comprehensively encompass many dharmas and enter into the Dharma-realm, only the Four Noble Truths are taught.
○ Chapter Nine: Awakening through Radiance.
Regarding "Awakening through Radiance": the Buddha uses radiance to awaken sentient beings to the luminous nature of their own minds, causing it to be unimpeded.
Light issued from beneath the wheels on the two feet of the World-Honored One, first illuminating one world in each of the ten directions.

This light proceeded in succession, expanding until it reached the tenth stage of expansion, universally illuminating ten billion worlds in each of the ten directions, throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
In each and every world of the ten directions, there was a great bodhisattva accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.
They all came together to the place where the Buddha was. The great bodhisattvas were Mañjuśrī and others;
the lands from which they had come were Suvarṇavarṇa and others; and the Buddhas whom they had originally served were Acalajñāna and others.

In every instance, Mañjuśrī expanded the light tenfold, and ten times he spoke verses to praise the Buddha’s virtues. When the light from beneath his feet first appeared at the assembly, it returned to enter between his eyebrows.
The light beneath your feet manifests the cause of the initial practice of what is believed; it is entirely the fruit of the Middle Way.

This light shines forth in succession, illuminating the entirety of the realm of empty space, thereby enabling later students to understand that the vast realm of their own minds is unimpeded and inexhaustible.
One should contemplate each [aspect] pervasively with the light of the mind, and further observe that the observing mind itself has neither interior nor exterior.
Thereafter, one seals this with the samādhi-mudrā of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Entering the initial mind of the Ten Abodes, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

Because one is able to open up and expand the realm of wisdom, having self-confidence in one's own mind, and because the body of wisdom and the body of practice are all-pervasive and inexhaustible, it is said:
"Everywhere is the Golden World; everywhere is the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom; everywhere is Mañjuśrī."
Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattvas’ Questions on Clarifying Wisdom.

Regarding "Questions on Clarifying Wisdom": since the preceding chapter has already opened up vast faith and understanding, Mañjuśrī and the other ten bodhisattvas now engage in mutual inquiry by means of the dharmas corresponding to their respective names.
Each answers with verses explaining the dharmas of their own practice, thereby causing [others] to...
The various scholars eliminate their doubts and set forth in practice. Ten Bodhisattvas elucidate the practices of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*).
Mañjuśrī first asks: "If the nature of the mind is one, why do retributions differ? Vajramati answers that this is due to the creation of karma through delusion regarding the Truth;

yet, since all karma is itself the Truth, when one realizes the Truth, karma ceases. This is the awakening at the beginning of the stage of faith. Second, he asks: "Since the substance of karma is already the Truth..."
"Why rely on various transformations according to the times? Vaiśravaṇa answered that the realm of karma is fundamentally empty and that these transformations are likewise provisional.
To practice such giving is the wealth of the Dharma. He asked three times about the equal Dharma-realm. Why are beauty and ugliness, suffering and pleasure, not the same?

The Dharma is noble. The fourth question concerns how the Dharma, which possesses but a single flavor, can be described through immeasurable dharma-gates.

In the twenty-first chapter, "The Ten Practices" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*), Bodhisattva Guṇakara enters the Samādhi of Excellent Contemplation (*suvicintita-samādhi*). From the ten directions, they each pass through worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-fields.

In this realm, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-fields, all sharing the same name, Guṇakānanarāja (Forest of Merit), who are currently present before him and touch his crown with their hands.
Because he has abandoned both mental sinking and agitation, he observes with discernment and establishes the Dharma-gate named "Excellent Contemplation" (*suvicintita*).

Having thoroughly realized the source of the mind and the practice of inexhaustible wisdom, he shares in the inexhaustible merit and wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions; thus, they are said to bear the same name.

The Buddha comes and bestows the empowerment of touching the crown of the head upon Wisdom (Jñāna). Regarding the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*): first, because one brings joy to oneself and others through the practice of giving (*dāna*), it is called the "Practice of Joy" (*pramuditā-caryā*).

*Pudgala*—here translated as "one who repeatedly takes up existence"—and *māṇava*—here translated as "youth," also called "scholar-child"—are mentioned to show that there is no discrimination between good and evil, or old and young, thereby clarifying the equality of the practice of giving. Second, by means of natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*)... [benefit]...
1. The person named Beneficial Conduct (*Upakāra-caryā*). 2. Third, that which accords with the practice of patience is called the Practice Without Contradiction (*Anupaghāta-caryā*). 3.

Fourth, that which is characterized by diligent self-exertion is called the Practice Without Deflection (*Anavalīna-caryā*). 4. Fifth, that which is characterized by the constant clarity of the essence of dhyāna is called the Practice Free from Delusion and Confusion (*Amūḍha-vikṣepa-caryā*).

5. Sixth, that which spreads forth through sublime wisdom is called the Practice of Excellent Manifestation (*Sudarśana-caryā*). 6. Seventh, that which benefits sentient beings through skillful means without attachment is called the Practice Without... [The text ends here].

If one practices: eighth, by means of non-effortful wisdom manifesting [the teachings], it is called the practice of what is difficult to attain; ninth, by means of skillfully expounding the Dharma, it is called the practice of wholesome dharmas;
tenth, by means of practicing with wisdom that is sincere, truthful, and free from error, it is called the practice of reality.

These ten practices, taken together, constitute the sequential order within the state of no sequence, wherein all are simultaneous and of a single wisdom. In each of the ten directions, there are one million Buddhas.

"Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, all named Guṇakānanā (Forest of Merit), come to bear witness. Regarding the phrase "those in the worlds of the ten directions also all go to bear witness":
the essence of wisdom and practice interpenetrates and pervades one another; it is the natural law that they are thus identical throughout the ten directions.
The Twentieth Chapter: The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries. Regarding the twenty inexhaustible treasuries:
first is the treasury of faith (*śraddhā-kośa*). To testify to the practice of the Dharma with the power of faith and without cowardice is called the treasury of faith;

this is the faith within the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), not the faith of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) of Mañjuśrī, Bodhiruci, and the others. Second is the treasury of precepts (*śīla-kośa*).
They achieve the precept of universal benefit; the precept of non-acceptance; the precept of non-abiding; the precept of freedom from regret; the precept of freedom from contention;
the precept of non-harming; the precept of freedom from impurity; the precept of freedom from greedy seeking; the precept of freedom from fault; and the precept of freedom from transgression.

Third is the treasury of shame (*hrī-kośa*), which is to look up with shame before all Buddhas. Fourth is the treasury of remorse (*apatrāpya-kośa*), which is to feel remorse for the evils of past lives.

Fifth is the treasury of learning (*śruta-kośa*), which is to benefit sentient beings by preaching the Dharma through the wisdom of extensive learning. Sixth is the treasury of giving (*dāna-kośa*), which refers to:

partial giving, exhaustive giving, internal giving, external giving, internal-and-external giving, universal giving, giving in the past, giving in the future, giving in the present, and ultimate giving.

1. The Treasury of Giving (*dāna-kośa*). 2. The Treasury of Precepts (*śīla-kośa*). 3. The Treasury of Patience (*kṣānti-kośa*). 4. The Treasury of Effort (*vīrya-kośa*). 5. The Treasury of Meditation (*dhyāna-kośa*). 6. The Treasury of Wisdom (*prajñā-kośa*). 7. The Treasury of Wisdom (*prajñā-kośa*):

though there is nothing whatsoever in either the mundane or supramundane realms, one universally awakens all sentient beings. 8. The Treasury of Mindfulness (*smṛti-kośa*): through right mindfulness, one perceives that all phenomena are free from faults.

9. The Treasury of Retention (*dhāraṇī-kośa*): one upholds the treasury of the Buddha’s teachings, never neglecting or forgetting them. 10. The Treasury of Eloquence (*pratibhāna-kośa*): these ten dharmas collectively encompass the inexhaustible teachings; this is called [the Treasury of Names].
The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries (daśākṣayā nidhayaḥ) fulfill the practices of the preceding Ten Practices (daśa-caryā), ensuring they are never exhausted;
they initiate the subsequent Ten Dedications (daśa-pariṇāmanā-dharma), causing further advancement and ensuring that the gates of practice for all scholars do not become obstructed.

Regarding these four preceding chapters, the Ten Practices, the Forest of Merit (Guṇakānanā) serves as the presiding lord of the Dharma; it clarifies how the myriad practices benefit sentient beings, and thus it is a forest of merit.
Chapter Twenty-three: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. The Fifth Assembly:
The Dharma Gate of the Ten Dedications. Regarding "Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven": this heaven is among the five heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

It is free from the lower states of Yāma and Trāyastriṃśa, and free from the attachment to pleasure; it is free from the negligence found in the higher states of Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
Regarding the practice: there are six heavens in the Desire Realm. Since the Heaven of the Four Kings is governed by the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they are referred to as the "Five Heavens.

With Tuṣita at their center, this represents the gate of the Great Compassion practice of the Ten Stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), wherein wisdom and means are equally integrated and pervasive.
It is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas in their final existence; it signifies that although they abide amidst the five desires, they remain unstained by and unattached to the objects of desire.
Thus, the World-Honored One ascended to this realm without departing from the site of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), the summit of Mount Sumeru, or the Yāma Heaven.
The essence of clear wisdom is without dependence or fabrication, yet it pervades the ten directions, manifesting in response to conditions.

"Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar" signifies proceeding from the Ten Practices toward the Ten Dedications. "Spreading out a seat and inviting the Buddha" signifies the Great Compassion responding to the mundane world to bring forth and develop all manner of goodness.
That "all the adornments number in the hundreds of millions of billions" signifies that the gateways of Great Compassion's practice are limitless.
It is a measure. There are one hundred and eighty-four million billion kinds of ornaments that adorn the jeweled thrones, the jeweled grounds, and fill all of space.
The teaching of the pure dharmas serves as the golden net; wondrous conduct that protects living beings serves as the flower canopy;
noble and honorable acts of wisdom cover the beings as a jeweled parasol; and patience serves as the floral garland. With...

Precepts are the incense; the various practices within the precepts serve as the powdered incense. Contemplative insight is the pavilion; compassion is the palace; wisdom is the hall, with the wisdom of differentiation serving as its upper chambers.
The myriad practices extending downward constitute the necklaces; the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) acting as lower adornments form necklaces that hang down on all four sides.
Guiding those who are mired in suffering constitutes the silk ribbons; the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) serves as the seat; and the sound of the Dharma...
Harmony and joy serve as the bells. The blossoming of the practice of the Path serves as the flowers. The unmoving mind in meditative concentration serves as the banner (*dhvaja*).
Unimpeded turning and revolving serve as the pennants (*patākā*). Bringing delight to sentient beings serves as the music. *Bimbapaṭa*: this means "shadow-image.
This canopy is named for its luminous clarity, which manifests images in accordance with objects. *Ratnastika*: this refers to the mark of excellence on the Buddha’s chest; this means...
There is joy; it is said that only when there is the joy of the Buddha do these signs appear. The *deva-mudrā* is the celestial drum.
Because his merit, wisdom, and great compassion pervade the realm of sentient beings, all manner of adornments fill the void of space.

Furthermore, there are one hundred and eight million billion types of colors, classes, and clans, some of whom join their palms in reverent salutation, some who hold banners and scatter offerings, or [some who are] Bodhisattvas...
Within the assembly of Bodhisattvas, devas and gods are interspersed; or within the assembly of devas, the eight classes of beings are mixed.
That they do not follow a fixed order clarifies that this stage involves following wisdom with compassion to form a great ocean of compassion.

Through limitless and all-pervading conduct throughout the Dharma-realm, one simultaneously and equally transforms beings within the six destinies of humans and devas, bestowing the Dharma according to their faculties—whether by sequential or skipping methods, or through faith.
Some abide [in this state], some rank among the ten stages (bhūmi), and others belong to the various vehicles of humans and devas; there is no fixed order.

They follow the various devas of the desire and form realms but do not include those of the formless realm, because the concentration of the formless realm is sunken and incapable of responding to transformation through emanation (nirmāṇa).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "there are another ten hundred-thousand million [offerings] produced from the cultivation of roots of goodness," this clarifies that such adornments are all accomplished through the activities of the mind;

they do not arrive by chance. Among these, the Bodhisattvas who previously resided in the Tuṣita Heaven represent the "original residents," while those who have come as a result of their preparatory practices represent the "newcomers. These various offering implements proceed from the wisdom of the Dharmakāya.
It arises from the knowledge and vision of liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). It is for the purpose of transcending all devas.

That each and every one perceives the Buddha as if facing them before their eyes is the correspondence with fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*). As for the ten Buddhas of antiquity who once entered the hall, they are the same in both the past and the present.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.

The ten Bodhisattvas of the Banner type, such as Vajradhvaja, who came from the ten worlds of Wondrous Jewels and so forth, from the presence of the ten Buddhas of the Banner type, such as Akṣayadhvaja, have, through the practice of great compassion, crushed the afflictions of sentient beings while remaining themselves unmoved.
Therefore, the lower characters of the Bodhisattvas' names are all "dhvaja" (banners), because they benefit sentient beings through sublime conduct.

The upper characters of their world-names are all "praṇīta" (sublime), because within the ocean of birth and death, the fruit of their wisdom remains unshakable. Thus, the lower characters of the Buddhas' titles are likewise all "dhvaja.
As for the dharmas symbolized by the ten Bodhisattvas: first, because their practice of giving is inexhaustible and is both noble and indestructible, it is the "Inexhaustible Banner."

1. From the Buddha World of Wondrous Jewels, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja [came] with the wind of the great compassion of signless precepts (*animitta-śīla*), which completely blew upon the fragrant implements, causing the mind to become equanimous, universally attaining peace and happiness, and remaining unmoved by any sensory objects. 2.

For the sake of the Buddha Wind-Dhvaja of the World of Sublime Joy, the Bodhisattva Sthiradhvaja [came] with the third [wind], which is pure and stainless through the essence of patience (*kṣānti*) and non-attachment, and is characterized by diligent vigor (*vīrya*).

He does not cease [his efforts]. As the Bodhisattva Courageous Banner in the Buddha World of Sublime Silver of the Buddha Liberation Banner, he serves as a model for the world through his practice of diligence and does not fail in the True Principle, radiating the light of great wisdom.
As the Bodhisattva Radiant Banner in the Buddha World of Sublime Gold of the Buddha Dignity Banner, he initiates the clear wisdom that benefits sentient beings through the gates of dhyāna. And...

1. Their own essence is stainless, never failing their fundamental wisdom; for the sake of the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu in the world of Buddha Prabhāketu, the Wondrous Maṇi, they are noble because they destroy delusion through ever-burning wisdom. 2.

For the sake of the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu in the world of Buddha Nityaketu, the Wondrous Vajra, they are noble because they dwell amidst the dust of the world through skillful means without being defiled, always acting in concert with others.

8. The Bodhisattva Vīryadhvaja from the world-system Padmottara of the Buddha Varadhvaja, who benefits sentient beings with mastery through wisdom that accords with his vows, remaining untainted and stainless; 9.

The Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja from the world-system Mahānīlotpala of the Buddha Īśvaradhvaja, who purifies others through the power of the Dharma, causing them to enter pure precepts and perfecting their distinctions.
The Bodhisattva Vidyutprabha became the Bodhisattva Jyotiṣketu in the world of Divyācandanā of the Buddha Brahmaketu;
he universally observes the ten directions with non-reliant, wondrous wisdom, seeing that their intrinsic nature is non-existent, yet he does not destroy the various established dharmas.

The Bodhisattva Dharmadhvaja in the world of Sugandhā of the Buddha Avalokanaketu [became] the Bodhisattva Gajamati; by means of fragrance, which is formless, he universally perfumes all. Gajamati... [the rest of the text follows].
Furthermore, each of these ten bodhisattvas manifested a lion throne made of exquisite jewel-treasuries and sat upon it.

That their bodies all emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light signifies that they abide fearlessly in the world by means of the Dharma-jewels, and that the light of their wisdom shines universally.
Regarding the World-Honored One emitting light from his knees: the knee is the place where one rises and sits, turns and revolves, and bends and extends with ease.
This symbolizes that the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) consist of being constantly in nirvāṇa while within saṃsāra, and being constantly in saṃsāra while within nirvāṇa—sovereign and unimpeded.
