He manifests as a Māra king to afflict and delude practitioners, intending to make their resolve firm; even when he practices non-ways, there is nothing that does not benefit sentient beings.
This is like his acts as King Ajātaśatru, such as the murder of his father, which were intended to make them know that once one attains the Way, karma is eliminated.
Regarding those who understand or do not understand the wisdom of the world, he may cause some to recognize him as a sage, or he may cause others not to recognize him as such.

The "sage" is the ordinary person. This Bodhisattva, in a single moment of thought, is able to fully receive the great Dharma-illumination, the great Dharma-radiance, and the great Dharma-rain from the Buddhas of the ten directions.
That which is produced throughout the worlds of the ten directions—the Dharma that is not not fully known and fully understood—is called the "great Dharma-illumination.
That which perceives every faculty, karma, and disposition of all sentient beings, whether good or evil, without exception, is called the "great Dharma-radiance."
According to the faculties of sentient beings, they simultaneously rain down the equal Dharma-rain as a great Dharma-rain.

Because their wisdom is equal to that of a Buddha, they are able to receive it all within a single thought-moment. As for this Bodhisattva’s mastery over the power of mental recollection, supernormal powers, and virtuous functions, it is like the realms of karmic retribution of all sentient beings in the six paths of humans and devas, which are all created in reliance upon the mind. This Bodhi...

By the power of the great wisdom of the Dharma-body of non-conditioned action, there is nothing that the mind does not perceive throughout the ten directions simultaneously and with sovereign mastery.

Because the essence of universal luminosity wisdom—which accords with the nature of reality, is without dependence, and is equal in measure to space—pervades the ten directions, the great function of the wisdom of non-substantiality follows every thought. By means of the wisdom of non-forgetfulness, everything is perceived in accordance with every recollection.
It is accomplished. By means of the wisdom that discerns the general and the particular, as well as their similarities and differences, one performs both creation and destruction.

By means of the sovereign wisdom of breadth and narrowness, or largeness and smallness, transformations proceed unimpededly. By means of the wisdom that shares the same essence as all sentient beings, one is able to transform the realms of sentient beings entirely into pure benefit.
By means of the wisdom that is unimpeded regarding self and others, one manifests many bodies from a single body, and [many bodies from] many bodies...
He manifests a single body. By means of the wisdom that perceives the dharma-realm as free from measure, he can contain vast Buddha-lands within a single pore.
By means of the wisdom that is equal to space—boundless and without direction—he manifests birth in a single thought-moment throughout the ten directions without coming or going.
By means of the wisdom that is like an echo, he responds to all and manifests forms equal to those of sentient beings. This is because he is fully endowed with perfected merit.
Wisdom is able to dwell together with sentient beings while constantly abiding in a wondrous land; yet, unless sustained by the empowerment of a Sage, sentient beings do not perceive it.
Such power of wisdom and spiritual penetrations, though equal to space and devoid of intrinsic nature, is like a *cintāmaṇi* jewel:
although its nature is without subject or object and without fabrication, it assumes the same color as all surrounding objects, unlike empty space.

It is merely vast and without practical application. The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha enters the essential nature of all Buddha-lands through the three branches of practice, constantly abiding within the distinctions of birth and death to benefit sentient beings.

This is explained through seventy alternative names, collectively clarifying the stages from the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh bhūmis up to the stage of Buddhahood, while never abandoning the practices prior to the seventh bhūmi.
Emptiness is the skillful means of the seven factors of enlightenment. When Samantabhadra Bodhisattva entered the Lion’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi,

and the Universal Eye Bodhisattva entered samādhi three times in longing to seek him out, yet could not see the body of Samantabhadra, it was because Samantabhadra, by means of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body,
had purely perfected the gateways of practice for the differentiated great wisdom that abides within birth and death, and thus constantly dwelt therein.
The ocean of wisdom of Great Practice arises simultaneously with the boundless thoughts of all sentient beings for their universal benefit.
It is like a lion’s majestic display, when every hair on its body vibrates all at once; this is called the Ocean of Samādhi of Great Function.

It cannot be sought by means of entering or emerging from samādhi. Although the Universal Eye has ascended to the stage of the Dharma-Cloud and received consecration, he remains within the tenth bhūmi.

The previously mentioned practices of Samantabhadra, which primarily benefit oneself and others, are not yet the practices of Samantabhadra’s great function within birth and death that occur after the eleventh stage;

therefore, they cannot be seen. When the Buddha said, "Samantabhadra appears sitting near me, never moving from his original place," he clarified that the great function exists without departing from fundamental wisdom. Upon receiving this instruction, Universal Eye (Puyan) immediately...
Through immeasurable perceptions, one beholds Samantabhadra seated upon a lotus throne before the Buddha;
or, as one who has come in succession from other worlds, the body of Samantabhadra’s practice is like space—without fabrication, without coming or going, and without arising or ceasing.
It is like an echo: there is only the sound that responds to objects, yet it has no location, being like a magical illusion.
Regarding the syllables: if one seeks their essential nature, it is utterly unobtainable; yet the substance of the mental conception is likewise nowhere to be found.
The entire body is the body of Samantabhadra; therefore, the moment a mental conception arises, it is the very moment the body of Samantabhadra manifests.

When the Buddha himself speaks of the names of the ten concentrations (*samādhi*), and Samantabhadra speaks of the functions of the ten concentrations, the Buddha represents the fundamental concentration, while Samantabhadra represents...
This is the function of the wisdom of differentiation. Regarding the "Ten Samādhis," the first is named the Universal Radiance Great Samādhi (*Samantaprabhā-mahāsamādhi*).

This means that correct wisdom is all-pervasive, illuminating delusion and destroying afflictions. It is said that one takes the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system as a single lotus flower and manifests a body sitting upon this flower.
Within that body, there further appear three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-systems, each containing ten billion sets of four continents. One...

Manifesting ten billion bodies throughout the four continents, with each body entering ten billion times ten billion trichiliocosms, clarifies the principle that the Dharma-body is without marks (*animitta*).
The manifested realms of worldly retribution and worldly phenomena are all like reflections, layered upon one another without obstruction.
It is said that the body of Rāhu, the Asura King, is seven thousand [yojanas] long.
2. Regarding the *yojana*: he manifests a transformed body sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojanas* tall, with half his body emerging from the great ocean level with Mount Sumeru.
As for the statement that he does not destroy his original physical form, it means:

if even an asura can do this, how much more so a bodhisattva who realizes the mind is like an illusion and realizes the world is like a dream—how could such a one fail to manifest the sovereign spiritual powers of the fundamental dharma-realm? 2.
That which is called the Samādhi of Wondrous Radiance takes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as its essence and illusion-like wisdom (*māyopama-jñāna*) as its function.

Because it is fundamental, many enter into one; because it is illusion-like, one manifests many objects. The mastery over the one and the many, wherein self and other interpenetrate, constitutes "wondrous radiance.
The analogy of the sun’s reflection in the seven golden mountains for this samādhi refers to the seven golden mountains as being the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
As listed at the end of this chapter, with the exception of the Snowy Mountains, the Fragrant Mountains, and Mount Sumeru, these appear as successive reflections.

This serves as a metaphor for the mutual interpenetration of the bodies and lands of the Indra’s Net, wherein they neither abide nor depart from one another. If they were to abide [statically], they could not interpenetrate;

if they were to depart [separately], there would be no form to interpenetrate. If one were to abide within the mundane world, the body could not encompass the world; if one were to abide within the world...
Externally, it would otherwise be unable to penetrate the world universally. Regarding the "world of light and color":

the sun, moon, and stars are transformations produced by the collective karma (*saṃbhāra-karma*) of emperors, ministers, and the masses of people; because there are celestial beings dwelling within them, they are called "worlds.

As for the third [stage], "the meditative concentration that successively goes everywhere to the lands of all Buddhas": this refers to the spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) whereby the essence of wisdom functions pervasively throughout all things.
It is pervasive and all-encompassing; like an echo in a valley responding to a strike, it produces sound while being inherently devoid of agent or object, and free from volitional construction.

Fourth is the meditative concentration of the practice of the pure profound mind: one makes offerings with immeasurable requisites to immeasurable Buddhas, yet understands that the arising and passing away of these Buddhas is as ungraspable as a flame or a phantom. Although they are like flames and phantoms, one nonetheless beholds them.

Upon hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, he retains it all in memory without forgetting, and thus universally expounds such teachings for the sake of sentient beings. Fifth is the samādhi called "Knowing the Treasury of Adornments of the Past.
In a single thought-moment, he enters into the sequence of the lands and adornments of the Buddhas who appeared throughout unspeakable numbers of past kalpas;
this is also the possession of the wisdom of particulars within the fundamental wisdom. It is as follows:

it serves as a metaphor for extreme swiftness. Sixth is the Samādhi of the Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom (*jñānālokagarbha-samādhi*), which is able to know all events, such as the appearance of Buddhas throughout all future kalpas, and contains all lands within a single thought-instant as its treasury. From the Anavatapta Lake at the summit of the mountain flow four rivers: the one in the east is named Sītā, which enters China and reaches the eastern ocean;

The western river is the Sindhu, which reaches the western ocean. The northern river is the Vakṣu, which reaches the northern ocean.
The pond represents the bodhicitta. The four rivers entering the sea symbolizes the four wisdom-rivers entering the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.
The ten unimpeded wheels of samādhi clarify that compassion, wisdom, vows, practice, spiritual powers, and the power of the Way fill the realms of sentient beings without ceasing;
they do not depart from a single thought-moment, universally enter the three periods of time, and pervade the ten directions without leaving a single pore. Thus it is said: "I..."
The elephant king Rāvaṇa, dwelling in a cave on Mount Kāñcanapārśva, perceived the intention of Śakra. He immediately vanished from the cave and appeared in the heavens.
There, he manifested various musical instruments upon his body and carried King Śakra to the pleasure gardens for sightseeing.
He then transformed his own body so that it resembled the appearance of the other devas, and they enjoyed themselves together. When Śakra wished to return, [Rāvaṇa] again...

He transformed himself into the body of an elephant and carried [the Buddha] back to the palace. As for those who dwell in the cave, it is called Erāvaṇa, which in this language means "Fragrant Leaves" (Gandhaparṇa).
Because there are many trees with fragrant leaves beside the cave, the elephant is so named. The Golden Flank Mountain (Kanakakhaṇḍa) refers to the flank of the first mountain range of gold.
This metaphor illustrates that although a bodhisattva enters the stage of Buddhahood and becomes equal to all Buddhas, they never abandon the bodhisattva practice of delivering sentient beings.
It is like an elephant king who, though able to manifest a body identical to that of the devas, never loses his original form as an elephant king,
remaining the mount for the Śakra-devānām-indra.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Supernatural Powers (Daśābhijñā).

Regarding the ten supernatural powers: arising from the eighteen meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), they consist of ten kinds of inconceivable, effortless, and unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) for the sake of benefiting sentient beings with sovereign mastery.
First, by knowing all minds exhaustively, it is called the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Pervasive. Second, because it exhaustively perceives the ten directions, it is called the supernormal power of the divine eye-knowledge (*divyacakṣur-jñāna-abhijñā*).

"Divine" (*deva*) here refers to the *paramārtha-deva*, the divinity of the All-Knowing One; it is not like the "divine eye" of the three vehicles, such as that of Aniruddha, who merely observes the trichiliocosm as if looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand. Third, because it exhaustively knows the past, it is called the [knowledge of] former abodes (*pūrvanivāsa*).
1. Abiding in the supernormal knowledge of wisdom; 2. The fourth is the supernormal knowledge of wisdom that knows all kalpas to the end of the future; 3.
The fifth is the supernormal knowledge of wisdom of the unimpeded, pure divine ear that exhaustively hears the names [of beings] throughout the ten directions; 4.

The sixth is the supernormal knowledge of wisdom abiding in the absence of intrinsic nature, which pervades the ten directions without moving from its original location; 5. The seventh is named the supernormal knowledge of wisdom that skillfully discriminates all speech and terminology.
Eighth is the supernormal knowledge of manifesting countless form-bodies. Ninth is the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of all phenomena, named for its application of differentiated wisdom.

Tenth is the supernormal knowledge of the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena, named for the fact that while never abandoning the great function of benefiting sentient beings through great wisdom and great compassion, one remains constantly in great meditative concentration, appearing like reflections or shadows.
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Ten Patiences Regarding the "Ten Paticences":

by means of spiritual wisdom and penetrating realization, one accomplishes ten kinds of *dharmakṣānti* (patience regarding phenomena). First, hearing what the Buddha has taught without being startled or terrified is called the patience regarding sounds (*śabdakṣānti*).
Second, deeply comprehending the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in accordance with it is called the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

1. Patience (*kṣānti*). 2. The patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): because all phenomena are entirely quiescent, wisdom shines forth in profound stillness; this is called the patience of non-arising. 3. The patience of illusion (*māyopama-kṣānti*):

because all phenomena arise yet lack the characteristic of arising, it is called the patience of illusion. For example, when a cloth is used as an illusion to manifest a horse: the cloth represents the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which originally is not a horse;
the magical artifice represents karma and afflictions, which have existence [in appearance] but lack substantial reality; and the horse represents the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The appearance exists, yet it is substantially non-existent; therefore, the birth of the horse is precisely non-birth. The horse is identical to the cloth. All phenomenal appearances are entirely the essence of wisdom; for this reason, they are called "illusion-like.

Fifth, because the object is without the characteristic of an object, it is called the "patience like a mirage" (marīci-kṣānti). Sixth, because cognition is without the characteristic of cognition, it is called the "patience like a dream" (svapna-kṣānti).
Seventh, because hearing is without the characteristic of hearing, it is called the "patience like an echo" (pratiśrutkā-kṣānti). Eighth, as for manifestation...

The absence of manifest characteristics is called the "patience like a shadow. Just as the moon in water neither drifts nor sinks, this serves as a metaphor for how a bodhisattva, while participating in the worldly flux, does not drift in saṃsāra, yet by realizing true quiescence, does not sink into nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called "like a shadow.

Ninth, the presence of the characteristic of both existence and non-existence is called the "patience like a transformation. For example, a magically conjured person is neither ordinary nor noble, neither existent nor non-existent.
Because they are neither born of the world nor subject to its extinction, and so forth, they are called "like an illusion.
Through the patience of being like an illusion, one realizes that the characteristics of all phenomena are entirely like an illusion.

Tenth, because the bodhisattva’s wisdom-practice is without dependence or abiding, unobstructed, indestructible, and immeasurable, it is called the "patience like space. These ten concentrations, ten supernormal powers, and ten patiences are all universal.

The "Venerable Proclaimer" explains that these three dharmas are the functional efficacy of the single virtue of Great Compassion—the skillful means for entering the ocean of birth and death—within the stage of equal enlightenment across the eleven grounds.
They are also the dharma-gate cultivated in common by Bodhisattvas of the five stages, which is without sequence and without end; therefore, they belong to Samantabhadra.
Chapter 30: On the Incalculable (*Asaṃkhyeya*).
This chapter on the incalculable follows the ten concentrations, the ten supernormal powers, and the ten patiences because these have already fulfilled the practices of the eleventh stage.
From the chapter on the incalculable to the chapter on the appearance of the Tathāgata, there are eight chapters in total.
This chapter generally elucidates the dharma of the vast mastery of the three karmas within the state of Buddhahood.
These dharmas of vast number, along with the dharmas of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) and their radiance, constitute two types of ignorance regarding the fruit of Buddhahood.

That the Buddha himself explains them is to clarify that even if one has entered the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), if one cannot perceive these dharmas of vast number and the quantity of the merits of the secondary marks with the eye of wisdom, [one has not yet attained full Buddhahood].

As for their measure, they still possess these two obstacles; therefore, they are called the "two delusions. Only the Buddha’s discerning wisdom (*viveka-jñāna*) being perfected can thoroughly comprehend them;
thus, the Buddha himself declared that this teaching on the vast number of dharmas is a Dharma-gate of the sovereign mastery of the Buddha’s mind-activity.

Therefore, it was asked by Citta-rāja Bodhisattva. *Lakṣa* here means "hundred million" (*koṭi*), and *koṭi* here means "billion" (*zhào*). In this land [of China], [the numbers] were established by the Yellow Emperor...

The algorithmic units range from one up to ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, hundred-thousand, million, ten-million, hundred-million, billion, ten-billion, hundred-billion, trillion, ten-trillion, hundred-trillion, quadrillion, ten-quadrillion, hundred-quadrillion, quintillion, ten-quintillion, hundred-quintillion, sextillion, ten-sextillion, and septillion—totaling twenty-three units.
Beyond the unit *rāṅ* (壤), there are three methods of calculation: the lower method multiplies by ten at each step;

the middle method multiplies by ten thousand at each step; and the superior method multiplies by one hundred million at each step. This chapter employs the superior method of calculation; therefore, it is said:
Ten *koṭi* make one *ayuta*, and so on, up to the *anabhilāpyānabhilāpya-parivarta*. These one hundred and twenty numerical units constitute a single cycle;
the prose portion describes the vastness of the numbers that can be counted, while the verse portion reveals the inexhaustibility of the virtues being counted.
This collectively clarifies that the fruit of Buddhahood and the practices and vows of Samantabhadra are as infinite as space.
Measure: It cannot be compared to the dust motes of kalpas; it is vast and limitless, beyond the reach of worldly calculation.
○ Chapter Thirty-one: The Lifespan of the Tathāgata.
This chapter sets forth the sovereign power of the Buddha’s lifespan. That it is spoken by Citta-rāja Bodhisattva is because the Buddha is the Sovereign King of the Mind (*citta-rāja*).
Life-span follows the faculties in its extension or brevity, acting with sovereign freedom according to the capacities of beings.

Just as fundamental wisdom is without birth or extinction, length or shortness, coming or going, so too the Buddha’s life-span is without birth or extinction, length or shortness, coming or going; yet it appears long or short in accordance with beings.
Chapter Thirty-Two: The Abodes of Bodhisattvas.

This chapter enumerates the abodes of bodhisattvas and is spoken by the Mind-King (Cittarāja). It clarifies that the Buddha, through the bodhisattvas, sustains the world’s conduct and dwells in various places.
Although these abodes have their bases, the transformative activities are not restricted to any one place; they reach everywhere without limit.
Because it dwells in sovereign mastery, it belongs to the Mind-King (*cittarāja*). "Zhendan" (震旦) is sometimes called "Zhandan" (真丹) and also "Zhina" (支那);
this means "contemplation," as the people of this country engage in much contemplation. It refers to the interior lands described in the *Yugong* (禹貢). "Kāśmīra" is the kingdom of Jibin (罽賓).
Mount Qingliang, where Mañjuśrī dwells together with ten thousand bodhisattvas, is Mount Wutai. [End of] excerpt.
In the various places within the ocean of Jambudvīpa, and likewise in the other three continents, the scriptural text is incomplete.
○ Chapter Thirty-Three: The Inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha. Regarding the "inconceivable dharma":
it is called "inconceivable" because it is beyond the reach of thought and mind; it is called "incomparable" because it is beyond the reach of names and words. This clarifies—

The Buddha’s three karmas of body, speech, and mind are vast and sovereign; they pervade all according to their nature, responding without deliberate effort, beyond the reach of intellectual speculation or discursive debate.
In this chapter, the great assembly contemplates these ten kinds of inconceivable dharmas of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, knowing their thoughts, then raised up the Buddha’s land, body, eyes, ears, and nose.
Regarding the announcement to the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha of these thirty-two kinds of universally pervasive Dharma-gates: blue is the foremost of the five colors;

because fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is perfectly luminous and untainted, it is called the "Blue Lotus Treasury" (*Nīlotpalagarbha*). Because discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is entirely untainted, it is called the "Lotus Treasury" (*Padmagarbha*).
Because the vast function of the Buddha’s three karmas—whereby a single karma unfolds into ten—is manifested, [it is so named].
Thirty. By taking these thirty and accumulating them so as not to be separate from the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, they become thirty-two.
Using these thirty-two kinds, each is further elaborated tenfold, forming three hundred and twenty types of Indra’s Net interpenetrating dharma-gates.

This clarifies that the great functions of the Buddha’s three karmas—the three dharmas of the ultimate and conventional truths—reach fulfillment here in numbers from hundreds of thousands of millions up to the unspeakable;

therefore, the Buddha is titled the Honored One Among Those with Two Feet (*dvipadottama*). The Blue Lotus Treasury (*nīlotpalagarbha*) symbolizes ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*), while the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*) symbolizes conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*);
thus, these two individuals discourse on their own inconceivable and vast Dharma-gates according to their respective characteristics.
There are three hundred and twenty types in total. The Piśācas belong to the realm of hungry ghosts; this is translated as "those who devour vital essence.
The thirty-fourth chapter, "The Ocean of Marks and Signs of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata":
Regarding the ocean of marks and signs of the ten bodies, the thirty-two marks pertain to the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha when speaking in terms of physical form and color. There are eighty-four thousand...
The thousand marks belong to the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) Buddha. In terms of meditative concentration and wisdom, these inexhaustible oceans of marks belong to the Ten Bodies.

Because this is the Buddha’s vast and great benefit for sentient beings—the all-pervasive, perfect, and inexhaustible Great Practice of Samantabhadra—he has obtained through reward the body of adorned merit-marks as numerous as the atoms within ten Flower Treasury worlds; therefore, it is called the "Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies. This, too, is Samantabhadra.
This is the explanation of the Sage. First, regarding the presentation of the thirty-two kinds of jewel-adorned marks of a Great Man upon the crown of the head:
the ocean of myriad roots of goodness has the three karmas and two wisdoms as its essence; therefore, these are manifested as the foremost of the retributive marks to adorn the Buddha’s crown.
Regarding the brief enumeration of ninety-seven kinds of marks of a Great Man, extending from the crown to the body, they are able to purify the three...
Regarding the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) within the realms: upon each of these nine grades of afflictions, one respectively accomplishes an ocean-like practice of the ten *pāramitās*.

Consequently, one gives rise to the retributive marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) in ninety varieties. By means of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) as skillful means for the path, these together constitute the ninety-seven varieties of the marks of a Great Man.
As for the nine grades of afflictions: there is one grade in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and four grades in each of the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Chapter: The Four Grades of the Formless Realm and the Four Dhyānas; these constitute the nine. ○ Chapter Thirty-Five:
The Merit of the Light of the *Anuvyañjana*. Regarding the "light of the *anuvyañjana*":
*anu* has the meaning of being without dependence (*an-āśrita*). This is the Buddha’s own fruit—the great wisdom that is independent and pure.
The radiance of the marks and secondary characteristics (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana), which are produced by pure merit, culminates in the category of incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) causes;

because these secondary characteristics represent the ultimate fruit, the Buddha himself spoke of them all. Furthermore, since even the secondary characteristics—which are inferior to the primary marks—possess such inconceivable functions, the functions of the primary marks themselves must be even more inconceivable.
Fearing that sentient beings might not believe this, it was likewise necessary for him to speak of them himself. He used jewels as a metaphor for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Because the light of the nature of wondrous wisdom draws in and receives sentient beings, he addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi.
When [the Buddha] was a bodhisattva, he was known as King Paripūrṇa, the mark of excellence beneath his feet; he constantly emitted forty kinds of light. Among them was one light named "Pure Virtue.
Sentient beings in the Avīci Hell who encountered this light had their suffering stilled and were reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where they heard the celestial drum.
He uttered various words of exhortation and taught various forms of true repentance, whereby his mind was immediately liberated.
One who has attained the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) possesses the thirty-two marks of a Buddha’s transformation body along with eighty minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).

Now, the marks of the Buddha [of this text] are as numerous as the atoms within ten Flower Treasury worlds (*daśa-kusumagarbha-lokadhātu*), and thus his minor characteristics are even more abundant. Therefore, he briefly cites but one characteristic; yet even that single characteristic— [The text continues: ...is merely... (Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly here).
To speak of its inferiority, [the sūtra] mentions the soles of the feet. On each sole there is one auspicious mark, which in turn emits many rays of light.
These forty kinds of light represent the light of the wisdom-practices (*jñāna-caryā*) of the four stages: faith, abiding, practice, and direction.

Since the ten *bhūmis* merely fulfill the function of these four stages and do not possess distinct dharmas of their own, they cannot compare to it. Furthermore, the resultant light of the Buddha is ineffable; therefore, [the sūtra] mentions the Bodhisattva.

Regarding "light": although there is much light within the cause, only one is mentioned. Because it is accomplished through the seal of stainless, non-reliant wisdom, it shines universally with mastery as the King of Perfection and constitutes pure merit.

As for the sentient beings in the hells, because they previously drew near to virtuous friends and cultivated the ten kinds of faith, yet failed to cultivate them exclusively and instead reverted to committing evil deeds, they follow [the karmic force] into the hells of extreme suffering.
Because the seeds of their past faith remain indestructible, the light reaches their bodies; through the power of that light, their suffering is stilled and they are reborn in heaven.
If they lack the seeds of faith, even if the light were to shine upon them, they would not perceive it.

Furthermore, by the power of their faith and the force of the effortless, sovereign, and wondrous wisdom within the Samādhi of the Bodhisattva Vairocana, they are able to hear the formless celestial drum and its effortless resonance.

Through the various exhortations and admonitions of the Sublime Sound, and by means of the Dharma-gate of Repentance according to the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one instantly extinguishes karmic obstructions and ascends to the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*): within each of the ten fundamental afflictions, they mutually interpenetrate to form ten variations each, thus constituting one hundred afflictions.
Furthermore, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and the mind-organ constitute the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Each of these one hundred afflictions...
Possessing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they constitute five hundred afflictions. Form, sound, odor, taste, and touch are the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
The five aggregates take these five objects as their conditions, acting as mutual primary and secondary factors to form one thousand afflictions.

All of these are created through the causal interaction between the manas-consciousness and the six consciousnesses, thus forming seven thousand. Through the causal flow across the three periods of time, these seven times three become fourteen thousand.

There are twenty-one thousand for those whose conduct is dominated by greed; twenty-one thousand for those whose conduct is dominated by anger; twenty-one thousand for those whose conduct is dominated by delusion;
and twenty-one thousand for those whose conduct consists of an equal portion of greed, anger, and delusion. These constitute the eighty-four thousand [dharmas].

Since they are accomplished in a single thought-moment, they are all accomplished throughout the three periods of time. Since a single affliction is accomplished, the eighty-four thousand [afflictions] are accomplished.

The thousand afflictions were accordingly pacified. The sons of heaven, receiving the instruction from the celestial drum, recognized their debt of gratitude and repaid it by holding various fragrant flowers as offerings to the Bodhisattva Vairocana.

Sentient beings who encountered these fragrances also attained the eradication of eighty-four thousand afflictions and achieved the sovereign radiance of the Fragrant Banner Cloud. Even those who merely beheld its canopy planted the seed of gold.
The net of the wheel-turning king possesses roots of goodness as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Abiding in this station of a wheel-turning king, he emits a great radiance such that all sentient beings who encounter this light attain the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*). This clarifies the vast mastery in benefiting sentient beings through the various lights of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
First, the sons of the gods heard the Dharma preached by the celestial drum and attained the fruit of the tenth stage; second, they beheld his flower-canopy.

They attain the rank of a Golden Net Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) and transform sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* Buddha-fields;
this is also the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). Thirdly, sentient beings who encounter the light emitted by this Universal Monarch also attain the tenth stage.
These three types of the tenth stage are equal in their Dharma-gate, each simultaneously [attaining it] for many classes of beings as numerous as atoms.
This is the power of a single ray of light from among the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). The power and capacity of all the other marks and rays are even more abundant than this.
Although supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are not discussed here, this radiance possesses such mastery over supernormal faculties.

However, when great wisdom manifests before one, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that great compassion and great vows should result in the attainment of supernatural powers and transformations as skillful means for benefiting sentient beings.
Just as a person who practices the ten wholesome paths of action is born in heaven and likewise attains supernatural transformations therein, how much more so must this be true for a Bodhisattva?

Chapter Thirty-Six: The Conduct of Samantabhadra The practitioner of Samantabhadra’s conduct is such that a single practice pervades all practices without ever becoming confused with them; yet all practices are this single practice, never differing from it.
It is like a brocade formed by many threads: though each thread has a different color, every thread is the brocade. It is not...
This is the thread outside the brocade; yet, there is no brocade existing separately outside the thread.

This chapter, which follows upon the light of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), implies that where there is the light of the wisdom-nature of the ultimate fruit, there must necessarily be conduct that abides in the mundane world.

When the principle and the practice are thoroughly realized, one then achieves the gate of non-dual mastery. Therefore, it was spoken by Samantabhadra. Regarding how a bodhisattva gives rise [to thoughts] toward other bodhisattvas...
"A single thought of anger immediately brings about one million obstacles" means that anger is utterly contrary to the cultivation of the Way;
thus, it causes all Bodhisattvas to be cautious and guard against it. To briefly cite one hundred types of obstacles:

regarding "obstacles created by malevolent deities and ghosts," because they gain the power to assist them through even a fraction of the practitioner's resolve for the Way, they follow after [the practitioner] among the evil deities and ghosts.
Anger is irresistible. One who knows the mental activities of sentient beings is said to possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Because one is personally without a [discursive] mind, and because the obstructions between self and other are severed, one's own mind and that of sentient beings are non-dual.

By means of this, one can know the minds of others, even the subtle principles of all Buddhas, through the realization of non-mind. Without the distinction of self and other, or near and far, wisdom thus pervades the ten directions.
Being square [in its nature], it is without coming or going; it immediately manifests physical bodies to teach the Dharma in accordance with the faculties of sentient beings.
Thus, one body and many bodies interpenetrate with sovereign mastery. Therefore, it is said that with little effort, one swiftly achieves perfect enlightenment.

Beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields who share the same name, Samantabhadra.
"Each of you has come here from the presence of the Buddha Universal Banner Sovereign in the world Universal Victory to bear witness.
That all those in every world throughout the ten directions have likewise gone to bear witness means that the inexhaustible and non-dual conduct of Samantabhadra has now reached full completion."

Therefore, those of the same name Samantabhadra come here to bear witness, filling the ten directions. Abiding in the Way with humility and harmony, they constitute the world of Universal Excellence (Pushe-sheng).
Capable of destroying the arrogance of self and others as well as all afflictions, they are called Universal Banner (Puchuang). Although they dwell within birth and death, [they remain thus].

Not being accompanied by defilement is called "mastery. Since the principles of Samantabhadra’s great practices are entirely identical [to these], it is said that he "expounds this Dharma in all places.
The verse states: "The Buddha speaks, sentient beings speak, and lands speak; thus they speak throughout the three periods of time.
All such various [utterances] are fully understood. This clarifies that the practice of Samantabhadra exhausts the three limits of time and pervades the ten directions.
Square. Whether concerning oneself or others, whether ordinary beings or sages, each and every thing is proclaimed and clarified without concealment.
○ Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Appearance of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the appearance of the Tathāgata: Mañjuśrī is the gateway to the fundamental wisdom of the wondrous principle of the Dharmakāya. Universally...
The Worthy One (Bhadrapāla) is the gateway for the practice of great compassion through discerning wisdom. Without Samantabhadra, the wisdom of principle would stagnate in empty quiescence;
without Mañjuśrī, all practices would fall into impermanence. Only when these two gateways are thoroughly integrated can one be called a Buddha.
Upon reaching this stage of cultivation in the five positions, the two dharmas are perfected. Since the appearance of the Buddha, it has been like Sudhana’s pilgrimage.
The youth Guṇākara and the maiden Guṇavatī represent the fulfillment of wisdom, compassion, and conduct; thus, they behold Maitreya Tathāgata. This is also the same meaning:

therefore, the Tathāgata emits from the space between his eyebrows the light of the fruit of the Middle Way, which enters the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra of the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava*, causing him to inquire about the Dharma-gate of the ultimate summit of one’s own Buddhahood. Furthermore, he emits from his mouth the light of the teaching to empower Samantabhadra.

The "Worthy Mouth" (賢口) refers to the teaching of the Dharma in which the wisdom and compassion of the myriad practices of one’s own Buddha-fruit—extremely differentiated and perfectly fulfilled—are brought to mind.

"Nature-Surpassing Sublime Virtue" (性超妙德) is a specific epithet for Mañjuśrī. Since the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one has always traversed the two dharmas of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra;
however, it is only upon reaching this point that they are fully integrated and matured. Yet, within the *dharmadhātu*, time does not move and wisdom does not move.

Their practice is immovable, for the Dharma-assembly is eternally thus. Therefore, from the time of expounding the Ten Faiths onward, whether ascending to the heavens to manifest the Dharma or manifesting bodies throughout the ten directions, they never depart for even a single kṣaṇa from the essence of fundamental wisdom within the Hall of Universal Radiance.
Furthermore, this chapter concludes with the teaching on the dharma of the "completed fruit," which was originally expounded within the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantāloka-maṇḍala*).
This is analogous to how Sudhana, after visiting Maitreya Buddha, returns to see his first spiritual friend, Mañjuśrī, and subsequently enters into the body of Samantabhadra.
Regarding the ten immeasurable dharmas of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, the first concerns the ten kinds of causes and conditions for such appearance. First:

1. The formation of the great trichiliocosm is a metaphor for the appearance of a Buddha, which is accomplished through a multitude of conditions. 2. A great deluge covering the great trichiliocosm is a metaphor for the vastness of the Dharma-gates manifested by a Buddha’s appearance, which are difficult to comprehend.
3. Clouds and rain having no point of origin is a metaphor for how the manifestation occurs through the resonance of responsive capacity (*gotra*), appearing without coming from anywhere.
4. The difficulty of knowing the great rain is a metaphor for how it cannot be known unless one possesses a great capacity. 5. By means of the great... [text ends]

1. Rain brings about both success and failure; this is a metaphor for the destruction of afflictions and the accomplishment of virtues. 2. A single rain follows different [conditions]; this is a metaphor for the Dharma of one flavor, which varies according to the differences among vessels.
3. Superior places are established first; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s superior conditions providing salvation first. 4. The distinction between matters arises from their causes.
The excellence of the Buddha’s virtues arises from wisdom. Ninth, by means of the mutual dependence of the four wheels, it is illustrated that the Buddha’s compassion bears all like the earth;
his skillful means adapt to the capacities of beings like water; his ten powers can sustain all like wind; and his state of being without support and without obstruction is like the wheel of space.
Tenth, by means of the benefit of the great trichiliocosm, it is illustrated that while the Buddha’s virtues for benefiting sentient beings are distinct, they are universally received by all.
Second, regarding the ten kinds of bodies: first, by means of the pervasiveness of space, it is illustrated that the Dharma-body pervades the ten directions; the Dharma-body is bodiless.

There is nowhere to which it goes; because there is no going, there is nowhere to which it does not reach. Second, by means of emptiness and non-discrimination, it is unimpeded by manifest color (*varṇa*);
this is a metaphor for the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) being without attachment or obstruction, and thus unimpeded in benefiting sentient beings.

Third, by means of the sun’s light providing benefit, it is a metaphor for the majestic power-body (*vibhūtikāya*) whereby all, according to their capacity whether great or small, receive the benefits of the Dharma. Fourth, by means of the sun’s light shining equally, even low places are illuminated.
"Slow. This is a metaphor for the Bodhi-body, which is equal and responds according to capacity; yet for those of inferior faculties, the benefit received is always slow.
It is like the sun of the body when first attaining perfect enlightenment, which first illuminates the mountain-kings of the bodhisattvas—this is the meaning of the Bodhi-body.

Fifth, the daily benefiting of those born blind is a metaphor for the Adornment-body, which secretly benefits everywhere. For example, although one born blind does not see the sun, they still engage in their daily activities, eat, and so forth.
Respite still depends upon the sunlight; this is a metaphor for how the Buddha’s compassion secretly reaches even the most extreme states of suffering.
Just as the light from the *anuvyañjana* (secondary marks) pacifies the sufferings of hell, this is the meaning of the "adorned body.

Sixth, just as the moonlight outshines the stars, waxes and wanes according to the seasons, and appears in all pure waters before the eyes of every person—metaphorically representing the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body) abiding in perfect symmetry—and just as the Buddha appears when the mind is serene, there is no... [end of fragment].

Seventh, the manifestation of the Universal Monarch (Brahmā) is used as a metaphor for the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), which responds universally to all without conscious effort.

Eighth, the life-prolonging of the King of Physicians is used as a metaphor for the sustaining power of the [recompense] body, which endures until the limits of the future. Ninth, the mani-jewel benefiting sentient beings is used as a metaphor for the merit body, which adorns the lands and benefits living beings.

Raining down jewels to benefit the poor is the meaning of adorning the buddha-field. Tenth, by using the king of wish-fulfilling jewels to eliminate calamities and fulfill aspirations, it serves as a metaphor for the vow-body (*praṇidhāna-kāya*);
sentient beings who behold it have their wishes fulfilled. This is precisely the ten bodies within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), though the order is merely different.

Regarding the third [category], there are ten kinds of sounds: 1. **The Sound that Follows the Species**: This is because it is heard simultaneously by all ten thousand classes of beings, such as humans and devas, despite their differences.
It is illustrated by the analogy of wind, clouds, thunder, lightning, and rain, whose forms and sounds each vary according to the distinctions of the world. 2. **The Sound that Follows Preferences**:

This is illustrated by the analogy of falling rain that nourishes different things according to their specific needs. 3. **The Sound that Follows Faculties and Understanding**: This is illustrated by the exquisite [voice of] a celestial maiden...

1. It is called the "Sound of Metaphors," illustrated by the analogy of an echo following conditions. 2. It is called the "Sound of Transformation that Does Not Miss its Time," for when the faculties are mature, one will certainly hear it;

this is named the "Sound According to the Time," illustrated by the Brahma-voice and various metaphors; "various" here refers to the meaning of the faculties being mature. 3. It is called the "Sound of Non-arising," illustrated by the analogy of an echo following conditions. 4.
It is called the "Sound Without a Master," illustrated by the analogy of the sound of the proclamation at the end of an eon (*kalpa*). 5. It is called the "Profound Sound," illustrated by...
The ninth is named "Inconceivable Rainfall," which is illustrated by the analogy of the single flavor of all waters.

The tenth is named "Uninterrupted Sound," which is illustrated by the celestial drum awakening beings; it signifies that the Buddha pervades the Dharma-realm and his transformations are without cessation.

The eleventh is named "Unchanging Sound," which is illustrated by the provisional containing the real, like clouds containing rain; thus, it is compared to how [rain] gradually falls to bring beings to maturity, even though the Buddha—

He speaks according to what is appropriate, yet his ultimate wisdom remains unchanging. These ten are a harmonious fusion into a single flavor; this is the "perfect voice. Regarding the fourth [section], there are ten kinds of mind (*citta*):
"mind" is a designation for knowing, just as "water" is a designation for moisture. Because there is no wisdom outside of suchness (*tathatā*), the Buddha’s knowing is entirely suchness;

because there is nothing other than suchness, the Buddha’s knowing is entirely wisdom. First, using the metaphor of space being without support, he illustrates the non-reliant wisdom that accomplishes tasks (*anāśrita-kṛtya-anuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Second...

1. Using the profound stillness of the *dharmadhātu* as a metaphor for the wisdom that the essence neither increases nor decreases; 2. Using the ocean’s hidden nourishment as a metaphor for the wisdom that equally benefits all living beings through its essence; 3.

Using the great jewels within the palace of the Sūkke Dragon King that can produce all the jewels within the sea as a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom that manifests activity while its essence remains subtle and secret; 4.
Using the four jewels, such as the Sun-Treasury (*sūryagarbha*), which transform and evaporate the waters of the sea as a metaphor for the Buddha’s extinction of delusions.
The Wisdom of Accomplished Virtue: The secular classics state that the "Wojiao Stone" (the Water-Consuming Stone) can dissolve the waters of the ocean.

This is either known through conjecture, or it is because one sees a treasure but fails to distinguish it, taking it for a stone. Furthermore, they say it pours into the abyss of the Weilu; this is merely naming it after its power to dissolve based on what is observed.
Sixth, the metaphor of space containing all things illustrates the unimpeded wisdom of support and maintenance. As it is said: "It embraces the six directions within..."
Within the breast, spiritual illumination abounds; within the square inch of the heart, the myriad phenomena are reflected. Its spirit is eternally empty—this is precisely this meaning.

Seventh, by the metaphor of the growth of the Medicine King, it refers to the wisdom that brings benefit and joy throughout kalpas. Eighth, by the metaphor of the kalpa-fire burning everything to exhaustion, it refers to the wisdom that knows all things without exception.
Ninth, by the metaphor of the kalpa-wind sustaining destruction, it refers to the skillful wisdom that allows for the retention of afflictions. Tenth, by the dust...

The "Sūtra on Containing the Metaphor of the Scroll" refers to the nature that pervades the Wisdom of Equality; it means that there is nothing that does not possess the Buddha’s wisdom, virtues, marks, and so forth.

These ten [aspects] are perfectly integrated and briefly manifest the characteristics of wisdom, serving as a provisional manifestation of the Buddha-mind. However, they do not exhaust even a hair’s breadth of the Buddha-mind;
therefore, one should further understand the Buddha-mind through immeasurable and unobstructed knowledge. Fifth, regarding the ten kinds of spheres, as mentioned above—
The clarity refers to the wisdom that is capable of knowing; the present discussion concerns the mirror of the objects of cognition (*ālambana*). Both are immeasurable, like a box and its lid.

These are: the realm of all worlds, the realm of all three periods of time, the realm of all lands (*kṣetra*), the realm of all phenomena (*dharma*), the realm of all sentient beings, the realm of the non-differentiation of *tathatā*, and the unimpeded realm of the *dharmadhātu*.
The spheres of experience: the sphere of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) which is boundless; the sphere of empty space which is immeasurable; and the sphere that is itself without a sphere.
These ten spheres are infinite, and the sphere of the Tathāgata is likewise infinite. Regarding the sixth [section], there are ten kinds of practice.
Previously, the boundlessness of the realm of wisdom was made clear; now, the inexhaustibility of its application is revealed. First, one accomplishes practice by conforming to suchness (*tathatā*).

First, practicing according to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Second, practicing according to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) by means of the extinction of emotional attachments. Third, using the empty space through which birds fly as a metaphor for the practice of non-measurement:
the more the mind is void, the more expansive the practice becomes; though one practices all day long, one has never actually practiced. From the fourth to the tenth [sections], the text is explicit.

The analogy of the golden-winged bird (garuḍa) cleaving the ocean represents wisdom’s compassion. The analogy of the sun and moon being without thought represents compassion not losing sight of wisdom.
Regarding the seventh [section], there are ten kinds of attaining perfect enlightenment: first, wisdom merges with principle, enabling one to practice non-duality;
second, the seal manifests for all capacities, which is the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi); third, the nature and characteristics are profoundly deep, beyond the reach of words.
The fourth refers to attaining the three treatises that are equal in measure to the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Since all phenomena and principles are precisely what I have realized, and since even those [realms] are identical to me, how could they be difficult to master? Therefore, the Sage is empty and formless; there is nothing that is not the self.
He unifies the myriad things and takes them as his own self. This is what is called the measure of sentient beings, as well as all lands, all dharmas, and all the three [times].

The measure of the world (*loka-pramāṇa*) and so forth is the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*). The measure of true thusness (*tathatā-pramāṇa*) and the measure of the dharma-realm and so forth is the noumenal dharma-realm.

The measure of the unobstructed realm is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomenon and noumenon. The measure of all vows and the measure of all practices is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.
These are called the four dharma-realms. The fifth refers to the identity of Buddhas and sentient beings within the same non-...

Because their nature is thus, they all attain perfect enlightenment. The nature of delusion is fundamentally empty; its source is originally the Buddha. True nature cannot be grasped, for it was not newly established this morning.

Because sentient beings do not know this, they require the transformation of the Buddha. Sixth, it means that whether one attains Buddhahood or not, the Dharma-realm remains eternally as it is, just as the world undergoes formation and destruction while space neither increases nor decreases. Seventh, it means that attaining Buddhahood is like a magical transformation.

That a human being, through the transformation of mind, manifests as a Tathāgata is inconceivable. Eighth, it refers to manifesting a single vast body, wherein each and every part of that body is likewise vast and so forth.
Ninth, it refers to the hair-pores containing the Dharma-realm; they contain it according to principle and pervade it according to principle, such that there is nothing that is not the Buddha-body.
Tenth, it refers to the realization that, just as one’s own mind attains Buddhahood in every thought-moment, so too does the mind of all sentient beings.
It is also accomplished in every thought-moment, for the attainment of Buddhahood by all Buddhas is precisely this mind. The eighth [section] concerns the ten kinds of turning the wheel of Dharma:
namely, the mind that turns, the Dharma that is turned, the fruit attained, the teaching that expresses it, and the principle revealed.
These five are quiescent in their essential nature; though spoken of all day long, they have never been spoken. The sixth refers to contact with words.
All are wheels. The seventh means that while functioning, they are quiescent. The eighth means that the one is many yet has no master. The ninth means that horizontally there is nothing left out.

The tenth means that vertically there is no end. Because they function while remaining eternally quiescent, they are likened to written characters that universally enter into all matters and all speech, yet abide nowhere.
Regarding the ninth [wheel], there are ten kinds of *parinirvāṇa*; *pari* means "to enter."

The meaning [of *nirvāṇa*]: *Nirvāṇa* has the meaning of perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*). Its significance fills the Dharma-realm; its virtues are as complete as the sands of the Ganges, which is called "perfect" (*pari*). Its essence exhausts true nature;

it is wondrously detached from the burdens of phenomenal characteristics, which is "quiescence" (*nir*). Since the cycle of transformation is complete, it dwells securely in secrecy. To manifest extinction for the sake of sentient beings—this is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.

First, it means that its essential nature is inherently eternal. Second, it means that its virtuous functions are perfectly complete. Third, it means that its appearance and disappearance are constant.

"Zhan" (Profound/Still). Fourth, its essence is said to be non-transmigratory; it is like the sun appearing in water: when the water is turbid, the reflection vanishes. Fifth, it means that while manifesting extinction, it wondrously persists.

Sixth, it means arising and ceasing in accordance with conditions. Seventh, it means existence and non-existence appear alternately, as if sustained by the power of illusion for kalpas, or sometimes withdrawing once its task is finished.
Eighth, it means its great function is boundless; because it is quiescent and motionless, there is nothing it does not move.
They constantly perform Buddha-works throughout the limits of the future. Ninth, the essence is free from the two extremes: if the body were real, it could not cease;
if the body were empty, how could it arise and cease? If it had a fixed location, it would exist here while being absent there.

Because it is not real, its arising and ceasing are not constant; because it is not empty, it can manifest anywhere without exception. Because it has no fixed location, it takes form wherever it is invoked.

The tenth refers to returning to the non-abiding. It means not dwelling in saṃsāra while yet not abandoning sentient beings. Regarding the tenth [stage], there are ten kinds of seeing, hearing, and associating with [the Buddha].
These ten roots of goodness do not transcend the three virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and grace (*anugraha*).

Taking a small amount of *vajra* is a metaphor for the virtue of wisdom. A small fire burning much is a metaphor for the virtue of abandonment. The medicinal king benefiting all is a metaphor for grace.

The merit of these six roots of virtue benefits all; even if one’s final actions are heavy with transgression such that sentient beings do not believe upon seeing or hearing them, it nevertheless plants seeds for distant benefit—just as reviling medicine makes it more potent, or reviling incense makes it more fragrant. To revile the Buddha is still superior to revering other heterodox teachers;

as in the case of Bhadrapāla and others who reviled the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, they suffered the retribution of sin for a thousand kalpas, yet once their sins were exhausted, they encountered the transformative guidance of Never-Disparaging. Reviling...

If even this [mere hearing] brings ultimate benefit, how much more so for those who possess deep faith, understanding, practice, awakening, and realization? How could one possibly express the extent of such rejoicing?
This Dharma-gate does not fall into the hands of other sentient beings, except for the true sons of the Dharma King who are born into the family of the Tathāgata.
If there were no true sons, this Dharma-gate would soon perish and vanish, like a wheel-turning monarch who has no legitimate crown prince; after the king’s death, the kingdom...
The fact that these seven treasures naturally dissipate and vanish within seven days clarifies that those of the Three Vehicles lack the compassionate wisdom that benefits sentient beings;

they are all termed "remaining sentient beings. If ordinary people without the Great Mind do not believe, rejoice in, and enter into this teaching, then the realm of sentient beings and the seeds of Buddhahood would be severed, and the Dharma would not circulate.
Therefore, it was not entrusted to the great Bodhisattvas; rather, its circulation relies upon [the Great Mind].
He is a great-hearted being. All those in the assembly attained the prediction of attaining Buddhahood in one lifetime (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

This clarifies that once he himself had attained the fruit, the beings he transformed likewise transcended the view of the three periods of time and perceived the reality of phenomena as they truly are;

sharing a single essential nature, they obtained the prediction of attaining Buddhahood in one lifetime. This sutra has three conclusions regarding cause and effect: the first assembly concerns the Buddha’s own five stages of development.

The first cycle of cause and effect concludes here. From the second assembly through the eighth assembly, this section represents the cycle of cause and effect for the cultivation and advancement through the five stages of faith for those who study the Buddha;

thus, it is one completion of the cause and effect of the five stages. The tenth assembly, the "Dharmadhātu" chapter, represents the cycle of cause and effect of the five stages for Sudhana’s cultivation and realization as a model for the world;
this constitutes the third completion. As follows, the ninth assembly is the "Detachment from the World."

This chapter concerns the inexhaustible conduct of Samantabhadra, which constantly benefits the world after the attainment of Buddhahood; therefore, the "Chapter on Manifestation" (Avatamsaka) concludes with its entrustment for circulation.
○ Chapter Thirty-Eight: "Leaving the World" (Lokottara-parivarta).
Regarding the ninth assembly, in which the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) was preached again in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsa-kuṭāgāra*):

Universal Wisdom (*Samantamati*) posed two hundred questions concerning the dharmas of the five stages, to which Universal Virtue (*Samantabhadra*) responded with two thousand dharma-gates. These constitute the constant practice of Samantabhadra after attaining Buddhahood, solely for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings;
thus, their functional efficacy is similar to that of the Buddha’s own practice of Samantabhadra in the first assembly. Therefore, at the beginning—
Within this assembly, Samantabhadra likewise serves as the Lord of Dharma. When Sudhana has completed his studies and travels, he re-enters the body of Samantabhadra;
this too is the realization and entry into this very dharma-gate. Indeed, within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), neither Buddhahood nor non-Buddhahood can be apprehended.
However, as long as the Dharma-realm, the realm of empty space, and the realm of sentient beings are inexhaustible, the practices of Samantabhadra will likewise never come to an end.
This Great Practice is the single path shared equally by all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions.
Within it, the manifestation of practicing the path, attaining Buddhahood, and even entering Nirvana—all are the conduct of Samantabhadra within the Wisdom of Universal Radiance.

Therefore, it is taught once again in the Hall of Universal Radiance; for the attainment of Buddhahood occurs in a single thought-moment, and the teaching of the Dharma is likewise proclaimed in a single thought-moment. In the human realm...
In the heavens, it is stamped all at once; therefore, in all the assemblies for ascending to heaven, it is said that they do not leave the Hall of Universal Radiance.
Yet this chapter returns to the time of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment. There are two meanings of "leaving the world":

the emptiness of the nature of the world is "leaving by nature," and the accomplishment of practice without defilement is "leaving by fact. Because compassion is inseparable from wisdom, there is no world that is not [left].
Detachment. It is ever-present within the world and never fails to emerge from it; its wisdom is never without compassion.

Therefore, there is no detachment that is not worldly, yet it constantly transcends the world while never failing to roam within it—this is the meaning of "detachment from the world. Regarding the two hundred questions: the first twenty phrases inquire about the practice of the ten faiths;
the next twenty phrases inquire about the practice of the ten abodes; the subsequent thirty phrases inquire about the practice of the ten conducts.

Finally, fifty-one phrases inquire about the practice of the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of fruits. This chapter concerns the constant conduct for benefiting sentient beings after attaining Buddhahood;
yet, such questions are posed because it is a gateway where a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) suddenly seals all [thoughts], and a single thought encompasses all thoughts. One...

I reflect deeply: every thought-moment has the same essence. For this reason, the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) and the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), as well as their identity and difference, are mutually free.
Within this sutra, there are four turnings across six stages: the first assembly concerns the stage of faith; the second through eighth assemblies concern the stage of understanding;

this [ninth] assembly concerns the stage of practice; and the "Dharmadhātu" chapter concerns the stage of realization. These constitute the four divisions, yet all four divisions are the dharma of the six stages.

Compiled by Li Tongxuan, the Elder of Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Fangze of Zhulin. Chapter Thirty-nine:
Entering the Dharma Realm (*Dharmadhātupraveśa*). Regarding "entering the dharma realm":
it refers to the initial attainment of realization after a period of delusion; thus, it is termed "entry. The realms of body and mind are, by their very nature, without dependence.

That which is termed "Dharma" is that wherein the one and the many are mutually penetrating, and where the barriers of true and false, right and wrong, have vanished; this is termed a "Dhātu" (Realm).
Furthermore, when it is purely coextensive with wisdom (*jñāna*) and is not an object of emotional consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is termed the "Dharmadhātu.

Moreover, when one penetrates the seeds of ignorance and consciousness so that they function purely as the activity of wisdom, no longer being subsumed under delusion, this is the sphere of non-reliant wisdom; it is termed the Dharmadhātu. Furthermore, by means of the essence of wisdom...

Without dependence, without direction, and all-pervading, it universally perceives both the ultimate and conventional truths as collectively inconceivable. Within a single pore or a mote of dust, the myriad phenomena are interlaced;
boundless realms and Buddha-fields are layered upon one another. Wisdom and ordinary beings share the same essence, and objective realms and their reflections mutually penetrate one another;

this is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, with a single wondrous voice, it is heard throughout the ocean of lands; with a single fine hair-tip, its measure equals the infinite directions.

Views of large and small vanish; things and self are of one substance. Consciousness ceases and emotions are extinguished; wisdom penetrates without obstruction. This is called "entering the Dharma-realm.
This is the eternal fruition, without beginning or end, of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. All progress and cultivation throughout the preceding five stages take this as their essence.
Upon reaching this stage, habitual practice is perfected; one acts spontaneously through wisdom, returning to the original source and the ancient Dharma, which fundamentally never undergoes change.
Furthermore, regarding the World-Honored One being in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park: Śrāvastī is also called Śrāvastī;
this means "Good Road," as it was named after the people of the country who were fond of the Way. The Jeta Grove was planted by Prince Jeta;
it is also called the Jeta Grove because it was named after many people going there to visit where the Buddha resided. Anāthapiṇḍika...
The "Orphaned Garden" (Gulyuan) was established by the elder Sudatta; it derived its name from the elder’s compassionate relief of the orphaned and the elderly.

A garden is what we here call a monastery (*vihāra*). While all previous assemblies were said to take place nowhere other than the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-bhavana*) at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and three times [the Buddha] was specifically in the Universal Radiance Hall, this Dharma-realm assembly is stated directly to be in the Jeta Grove (*Jetavana*) in the human realm.
This garden clarifies that the preceding six stages do not depart from the essence of bodhi while they engage in cultivation;
they do not shift from the fundamental, universal radiance wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*), nor do they migrate from the momentary instant (*kṣaṇa*) as they constitute the realm of wisdom.

Once this progression through the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is complete and the fruit of Buddhahood is fulfilled, it is like the hundred rivers entering the ocean, where all lose their original names, existing only through non-effort (*anabhoga*).
By practicing through spontaneous engagement (*anābhoga*) for the benefit of sentient beings, the human realm is thus the garden of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
Furthermore, because the nature of sentient beings is identical to the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, the world of sentient beings is itself the world of perfect enlightenment.

Regarding the enumeration of one hundred and forty bodhisattvas, yet the general statement that they were "accompanied by five hundred bodhisattvas," this refers to the ten *dhvaja* (banner) bodhisattvas, which represent the ten...
The ten Bodhisattvas of Wisdom Abiding in the Middle [Stages] destroy the afflictions by means of the wisdom of those ten abidings;
reaching this stage of the fruit of the Dharma-realm, they are designated as "Banners. The ten Bodhisattvas of Majestic Power are the ten Forest Bodhisattvas within the ten practices.
By the power of various virtuous practices, one is able to accomplish the fruit-practice of the *dharmadhātu*; this is termed "sovereign power" (*vibhūti*).
The ten "Treasury" (*kośa*) Bodhisattvas are the ten "Banner" (*dhvaja*) Bodhisattvas within the ten stages of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Because they destroy biased views and harmoniously integrate principle and wisdom with compassion and vows, they are able to accomplish all virtues; upon reaching this fruit of the *dharmadhātu*, they are designated as "Treasury. The ten "Eye" (*cakṣus*) Bodhisattvas...
"Sā" refers to the thirty-seven treasury Bodhisattvas within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Because they contain and store manifold virtues, their Dharma-eye is clear and they universally perceive the Dharma-realm; for this reason, they are called "Eyes.
Each of these forty Bodhisattvas possesses the ten *pāramitās*, which constitutes four hundred. Next are the one hundred Bodhisattvas beginning with Tianguan (Heaven-Crown) and others. This is...
Within the *dharmadhātu*, the practice of the ten *pāramitās* upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is characterized by the mutual, perfect interpenetration of their essences:
within one are contained ten, and within ten are contained a hundred; thus it is said that "five hundred people are together.

All these bodhisattvas take the fundamental wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s *dharmakāya* as their essence and the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra as their function. By means of these two dharmas, [they] collectively...
These five ranks, along with the causes and fruits of the Dharma-realm, comprehensively encompass all phenomena—whether general or specific, identical or different, forming or decaying.
Therefore, Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī serve as the leaders. The *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"Immeasurable bodhisattvas manifest in the forms of śrāvakas, their names being Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and so forth. Furthermore, in the subsequent text, Śāriputra [instructs] the ocean...
The passage beginning with "The awakened bhikṣu contemplated Mañjuśrī... and so forth clarifies that [the bodhisattvas] are able to follow the Buddha’s practice and enter the dharma-realm;

they are not actual śrāvakas. Therefore, it says: "Together with five hundred śrāvaka assemblies and immeasurable world-protectors, all were born into the Buddha's family and did not sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
The World-Honored One, knowing that the great assembly simultaneously thought of and requested the realm of the Tathāgata himself...
As stated at length [in the scriptures], "entering the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*" (the lion’s yawn samādhi) is explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as follows:

the lion’s yawn has eleven aspects, which serve as metaphors for the Buddha’s *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*, which likewise possesses eleven aspects. First, because it crushes and destroys the deceptive lion-like armies of Māra;
second, because it demonstrates the Buddha’s supernormal powers through his ten powers (*daśabala*); third, because it demonstrates the dwelling place, the pure realm of the *dharmadhātu*.

1. Therefore, it causes ordinary beings with wrong views—who are like wild beasts—to know where to seek refuge. 2. It strikes terror into their factions. 3. It awakens sentient beings who are asleep in ignorance. 4.
It causes those wild beasts who practice unwholesome dharmas to abandon negligence. 5.

It causes the bodhisattvas—who are like wild beasts—to know how to seek refuge and submit. 6. It subdues the fragrant elephants of the non-Buddhists and the two vehicles, rendering them as if deaf and blind.
Because they have abandoned arrogance; tenth, because they cause all the bodhisattva-sons to realize [the truth] instantaneously;

eleventh, because they adorn right view so that the fourfold assembly increases in majesty and is not terrified by the factions of the heterodox. Frequent stretching of the limbs signifies being at ease and free from fatigue.
Upon entering this samādhi, all worlds are universally purified and adorned. The palatial towers where they dwell are vast and boundless. And...

There are those who possess various complete adornments, who clarify that the realm of the *dharmadhātu* is equal to the realm of empty space, and whose individual gates of practice (*caryāmukha*) fully embody the ten thousand practices, pervading the ocean of lands. This is precisely the third dwelling place of the Buddhas:
the pure land of the *dharmadhātu*. In the worlds of the ten directions, there are bodhisattvas who all come together with retinues as numerous as atoms to assemble and manifest [their presence].

Regarding "all those who offer worship": this refers to the vast and flourishing array of the primary and secondary factors of the ocean of the *prajñāpāramitā*. It is also the eighth matter mentioned above concerning taking refuge.
This Jeta Grove is adorned with such wondrous jewels that each and every ornament reflects and penetrates the others, their interpenetrating essences being multilayered, sovereign, and unimpeded.
Yet, although Śāriputra and the others were within this grove, they were as if deaf and mute.
"Those who are blind and cannot see or hear. Śāriputra—this is called "Son of the Śāris.
He received this name because his mother’s eyes were as clear and sharp as those of a śāri bird. Maudgalyāyana—this is called "Bean-clan. He was a descendant of the Sage Māṣa.
Kāśyapa—this is called "Drinker of Light. Revata—this is called "Offering. Subhūti—this is called "Good Appearance. Aniruddha—this...
Aniruddha means "Non-extinction. Nanda means "Joy" in this [language]. Kapphiṇa means "Yellow"; he is a descendant of the Yellow-headed Rishi.
Kātyāyana is the clan name of one lineage; "yana" means progeny, and "kātya" refers to his disorder. Pūrṇa means "Full Compassion.
Since these śrāvakas have all been born into the family of the Buddha, they are equal to the bodhisattvas and the world-protectors.
Although they are able to remember and request [the teaching], regarding this profound realm of the Dharma, they are like those who are deaf and blind. There are two interpretations:

first, in terms of the fundamental and the manifested (honji and kechi), they are able to remember it from the perspective of the fundamental, yet they remain deluded regarding the manifested; second, considering only the manifested aspect, there is no separation between the principle and its locus, and thus they share the same doubt.
Because they have not yet accumulated a great resolve, they do not hear or see it—just as when Ye Gong loved dragons, the true dragon was difficult to behold. It is not otherwise.

This is a demonstration; it does not reveal the true nature of phenomena. Therefore, the great śrāvakas manifest as being like those of the Hīnayāna, appearing neither to see nor hear the inconceivable activities of mastery over the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), in order to cause actual śrāvakas to turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna.
It is through various Dharma phrases and the recitation of verses that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva reveals this Lion’s Roar Samādhi.

This samādhi is the principle of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and Samantabhadra is the practice of the dharma-realm. Because practice accords with principle, it belongs to the gate of Samantabhadra.
When the World-Honored One desired to cause all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in this great samādhi, he emitted a radiance from between his eyebrows that universally illumined all lands and realms.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, seeing the Buddha’s illumination, entered deeply into the Buddha’s [wisdom].
The Ocean of Merit manifested various clouds of great adornments within their own bodies and all objects in the Jeta Grove, filling the entire Dharma-realm.
