As for Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s proclamation of these matters of adorned supernatural power illuminated by this light through the recitation of verses:
the light is the functional activity of the Dharma-realm, while Mañjuśrī is the principle of the Dharma-realm. By means of...
Because it accords with principle and practice, it belongs to the gate of Mañjuśrī. It clarifies how principle and practice, as primary and secondary elements, interpenetrate and mutually fuse;
this is the great mansion of sovereign entry into the Dharma-realm. At that time, because the Bodhisattvas were illuminated by the light of the Buddha’s samādhi, [they attained this realization].

They attain the gate of immeasurable great compassion. By means of immeasurable clouds of bodies that enter into the bodies of sentient beings, they pervade and fill the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
Through immeasurable gates of skillful means, they teach, transform, and subdue all sentient beings, yet they never depart from the Jeta Grove where the Tathāgata resides.
This clarifies that the principle and practice of the dharma-realm are neither one nor different, and neither conjoined nor separate.
It is not separate; it pervades the ten directions, being without action or movement. This above constitutes the Fundamental Gate of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

From the time Mañjuśrī left his chamber to engage in worldly activities for the benefit of sentient beings, this constitutes the Final Gate of the Dharma-realm. The fundamental is not different from the final; though rolled up, it is always extended.

The final is not different from the fundamental; though extended, it is always rolled up. Since the fundamental and the final are without obstruction, they both enter the same Dharma-realm. Thus, we proceed to the final gate.
There are three assemblies: first, the assembly of six thousand bhikṣus; second, the assembly of followers of various vehicles to the east of Puṇyavardhana City;

third, the assembly in which Sudhana visits fifty-three individuals, progressing through the stages to propagate and disseminate the Great Teaching. Regarding the passage "Mañjuśrī Kumāra emerges from the Well-Situated Pavilion":
this refers to the initial stage of entering secular life to enlighten the ignorant; thus, Mañjuśrī is designated as a "Kumāra" (Youth) based on his fundamental nature.
The fundamental wisdom gives rise to the activity of the differentiated wisdom that benefits sentient beings; thus, it emerges from the pavilion.

Because it is accompanied by the myriad practices as its primary and secondary attendants, it proceeds together with immeasurable bodhisattvas, who serve as its superior retinue and provide protection through their differentiated conduct.
Because he is constantly followed by the various heavenly deities and kings, the Lord Fire God is named "Radiance of Wisdom," and the Lord of Day is named "Illumination of the Buddha-Sun.
As for the assembly of six thousand bhikṣus, they have abandoned the Small Vehicle to turn toward the Great Vehicle;

thus, Śāriputra and the others emerge from their respective abodes and suddenly seal the six stages. Therefore, these six thousand serve as his companions, following the True Teaching to enter the Dharma-realm.
Because he possessed wisdom, he circumambulated the Buddha three times and proceeded to the place where Mañjuśrī was.

Because he benefits sentient beings everywhere by means of the Right Path, he observed that the ground for eight paces to the left and right of Mañjuśrī’s path was level. The site of the *bodhimaṇḍa* constantly followed him throughout the ten directions.
Because his practice of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* was majestic and composed, Mañjuśrī turned to look at the bhikṣus like an elephant king, as they waited upon him.
Because their power of wisdom seizes upon non-existence, views are discarded, and the spheres of contact become perfectly penetrating, the bhikṣus attain the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Eye.

Since they all possess the seeds of faith, they realize the Way at the very moment of these words, without passing through the five stages and without departing from fundamental wisdom, yet they give rise to the myriad differentiated practices and enter the gateway to the fruit of the Dharma-realm; thus, they all remain beneath the feet of Mañjuśrī while their bodies are universally manifest.
The ten directions accomplish the Buddha-dharma. As for "the assembly east of the City of Blessings" (Puṇyavatī): the city is so named because its inhabitants cultivate much merit;

furthermore, because one attains the wisdom of immovability amidst all shifting activities, it is located to the east of the city. *Sūtra* here refers to the "long prose" (*dīrgha-pada*) style of scripture;
because one attains the wisdom of the distinctions of the ten thousand practices by hearing the Mañjuśrī-Dharmadhātu-sūtra, there are ten thousand dragons.

Having generated the bodhicitta, they attain non-retrogression. Because the five hundred gates of the pāramitās are all instantaneously perfected within the stage of faith, five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred boys, and five hundred girls each emerged from the city to go to Mañjuśrī.
As for the youth Sudhana’s propagation and transmission of the Great Dharma, he followed the children and stood among the villagers.

I say that from my youth I established my resolve within the village, taking the seeds of faith in the Dharma-body as my womb. Within this faith, I cultivated the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment;
these served as seven hidden treasures from which sprouted the teeth of the seven jewels. Within this faith, I practiced the ten *pāramitās* for ten months while in the womb.
Furthermore, the five stages and five hundred gates of practice were all suddenly sealed within this faith, becoming five hundred precious vessels.

All things are abundant; this retribution is not without cause. Therefore, Mañjuśrī observed this youth and knew that his entry into the womb and his birth had caused various treasures to appear, whereby he received the name Sudhana.

This was intended to lead him to believe in the purity of self-nature and the fundamental immovable wisdom, which is, from the very outset, without arising or ceasing, and without cultivation or realization, thereby enabling him to attain the Bodhi of the stage of faith. Thus it is said.
Mañjuśrī expounded the various Buddha-dharmas for Sudhana, causing him to resolve upon bodhicitta.

Since bodhicitta is neither to be learned nor cultivated, one merely practices the conduct of a bodhisattva as an antidote to habitual tendencies; thus, bodhicitta will naturally and constantly manifest.

It is like clouds dispersing into the great void; the great void is itself empty, and one does not seek emptiness further. One simply practices the myriad deeds of compassion and wisdom as skillful means to abide securely in Bodhi.

If, among all these practices, there is even a single thing that is not clear, a single thing that is not practiced, or a single thing involving acceptance or rejection, then there is an obstruction. In that case, the bodhicitta is not the perfect dharma. For the practice of a Bodhisattva is...
The bodhicitta. Were it otherwise, it would be a practice of impermanence; it would be the bodhi of the three vehicles.
Therefore, once Sudhana had generated the bodhicitta, he asked Mañjuśrī, "How does one learn the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva?

Yet, regarding the bodhicitta itself, he did not ask further, because [its nature] has already been explained in the previous assemblies through the progression of the five stages from raw to matured.
Regarding the method of advancement: as yet, no ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has been seen to realize and enter [this state].

I wish to cite Sudhana as a model for later students, and to employ the names and residences of various masters, as well as the directions and kingdoms of sages and ordinary beings, gods and kings, monastics and laypeople, non-Buddhists and humans, and men and women, using these as metaphors to represent the Dharma.
Furthermore, the South is taken as the direction of correctness, clarity, and emptiness; when the mind reaches emptiness, clarity, and correctness—

From the perspective of wisdom, all directions are south; from the perspective of one’s back, all directions are north. Therefore, Mañjuśrī directed Sudhana to travel south in search of true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He praised the virtues of the bhikṣu Meghashiri and pointed him toward him for attendance and service. From Meghashiri downward, there were fifty-three successive referrals.
This was intended to urge him forward so that his practice would not be obstructed by old learning; thus, all [the instructions] were...

He suspended a eulogy extolling the virtues of his former masters. Within the *dharmadhātu*, he established Mañjuśrī as the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), Samantabhadra as the wisdom of differentiation (*prabheda-jñāna*), and Maitreya as the unconditioned fruit within the wisdoms of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

These three dharmas constitute a single gateway of the sovereign functioning of the essence and manifestation of the *dharmadhātu*. They pervade and correspond with the fifty spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) designated throughout the five stages.

Because they constitute essence and function, there are fifty-three masters. Since each of the fifty dharma-gates possesses both cause and effect—just as the Ten Abodes, the Ten Practices, and other assemblies all feature ten bodhisattvas and ten buddhas to mark the cause and effect—this constitutes one hundred.
Together with the ten fundamental *pāramitās* within the *dharmadhātu*, one thus traverses one hundred and ten cities.

This is because the three dharmas of Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya serve only as causes and fruits for the various stages of supreme progress (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*), yet they themselves possess no cause or fruit.
They are like a worldly sovereign who possesses no official ranks, but through his majestic power and sovereignty, acts according to the meritorious officials.
These are designated as the "Stages of Practice" (Gakubun) and thus serve as the instructions; therefore, there is nothing else represented beyond the one hundred and ten [deities].
Because Maitreya is the Buddha of the future, he is taken as the fruit of realization rather than Vairocana, so that later students may have something upon which to rely and look forward to.
The fifty-three [deities] are as follows: [The list of deities follows.]
Regarding the first instance where Sudhana ascends Mount Supratiṣṭhita to visit the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī and realizes the stage of *cittotpāda*:

the "cloud" (*megha*) has four meanings. Its universality symbolizes meditative concentration (*samādhi*); its moisture symbolizes merit (*puṇya*); its sheltering canopy symbolizes compassion (*karuṇā*); and its pouring rain symbolizes wisdom (*prajñā*). For these reasons, he is named Meghaśrī.
Because he has extinguished the disputes of the views of existence and non-existence, of right and wrong, and of the extremes of self and phenomena, he is a *bhikṣu*. A *bhikṣu*...
This is called "Cessation of Dispute. When one is as tranquil and still as a mountain through non-thought (*amanasikāra*), the wondrous principle of formlessness (*animitta*) manifests.

By the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one attains entry into the Buddha-abode; thus, one ascends the mountain to the limit where all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are exhausted, observing and seeking throughout the ten directions.

The separate mountain symbolizes entering from the gate of expedient meditation (*upāya-dhyāna*) into the dharma that is fundamentally free from both concentration and distraction. The slow pace symbolizes...
He was not distracted. His walking meditation (caṅkrama) demonstrated that he was not stagnant in meditative concentration (samādhi).

Thus, seeing this bhikṣu on a separate mountain performing walking meditation, it was proven that he had attained the first stage (prathamabhūmi) and was born into the family of the Buddha. He fully perceived all sentient beings as the essence of the Buddha-fruit;
the three realms and six paths were like light and shadows—neither real nor unreal. Their nature is inherently stainless. Without impairing his physical eyes (māṃsacakṣus), he saw all things.
Sentient beings do not destroy the Dharma-eye; their objective realm has no inherent substance. The wisdom-eye, through its illusory manifestation, gives rise to the myriad realms.
Thus, one perceives the bodies of all Buddhas with mastery over existence and non-existence. Therefore, Meghashri said to Sudhana:
"I constantly see the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, even as many as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields. I know and recollect the objective realms of these Buddhas."
This is the Gate of Universal Vision through the Radiance of Wisdom.

Second, regarding the Bodhisattva Sea-Cloud (Sāgaramegha) seen in the country of Sāgaramukha, who realized the dwelling of the Ground of Practice (caryābhūmi): his natural precepts (prakṛtiśīla) were like the ocean.
He does not allow corpses of birth, cessation, and death to remain, making them the gateway to the ocean;

because he is able to transform the ocean of birth and death into the great ocean of wisdom, and constantly moistens sentient beings with this Dharma, he is named Sāgaramegha (Ocean Cloud). Because he has attained the light of the wisdom of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that corresponds to the characteristics of Mount Sumeru.
By contemplating the functioning of the faculties and their objects within the world, one attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).

One realizes that the ocean of suffering of ignorance (*avidyā*) arising through the twelve links of dependent origination is entirely the vast ocean of the nature (*dharmatā-samudra*) of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Apart from this ocean of birth and death, there is no other place for attaining Buddhahood. Thus, Haiyun said: "I have resided in this land for twelve years; because this ocean of nature is not limited."
It is immeasurable, yet it is fully endowed with the merit of wisdom; therefore, it is said that this ocean is exceedingly deep and vast, adorned with manifold jewels.
Ordinary beings constantly manifest the seven conditions of ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling, clinging to them without relinquishment.
By means of these, they bring about the three conditions of craving, grasping, and becoming. From these three conditions...
It forms the two conditions for birth, old age, sickness, and death in future lives; thus, one is tossed by the waves of manifold sufferings, circling without end.
Those of the Two Vehicles, studying through provisional means, moreover, become weary and abandon it, failing to give rise to great compassion.

Therefore, Haiyun directly uses fundamental sublime wisdom to suddenly illuminate that the essence, characteristics, and self-nature of dependently originated phenomena are without dependence, and thus suddenly becomes great wisdom.
It is an ocean. Regarding the statement that "this ocean produces great lotus clouds": it is through conduct free from defilement by means of wisdom (*jñāna*) that the great lotuses are produced.
*Nīla* here translates as "blue. Blue is the foremost of the five colors; the stem represents fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and thus the stem is made of blue jewels.
Because conduct is always in accord with wisdom, the flowers completely cover the great ocean. The *asuras* dwell within this ocean.
The water reaches halfway up his body. Because he acts with wisdom and does not sink into the sea of birth and death, the asuras grasp its stalk.
Because he bestows the various innate precepts through wisdom and washes away the defilements of the mind, the dragon kings shower it with scented water.
Because he responds through unconditioned, objectless compassion, the various spirit-kings pay him respectful homage. Because his wisdom is invincible, [he is thus honored].
The Buddha’s body is tall; he extends his right hand through the function of wisdom. He joins the seals of wisdom-action to rub the crown of my head.
With fundamental wisdom as the Universal Eye and discriminative wisdom as the sutra, he observes the faculties and objects of all sentient beings to establish various teachings.
Since sentient beings are inexhaustible, the teachings are likewise inexhaustible; therefore, it is said that upon each flower is the Buddha-body in its ultimate form.
The One at the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) extended his right hand and stroked my head, saying to me: "I shall preach to you the *Puyan Jing* (Sūtra of the Universal Eye).

Yet, even with ink as vast as the great ocean and flowers piled as high as Mount Sumeru, one could not record even a single chapter from this sūtra; nor could one record a single meaning within a chapter, or a single phrase within a meaning—not even a fraction of it.
For twelve hundred years, those who uphold this sūtra shall turn the wheel through skillful means and wisdom."
One shall attain liberation from all twelve hundred afflictions.
Third, regarding the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita at the village of Laṅkāpatha on the seashore, who has realized and dwells in the stage of cultivation:

having completed the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, he further contemplates the active manifestations and habitual tendencies of the six sense faculties, whereby they all become seeds of wisdom.
No longer lingering or obstructed, this is called "passing beyond sixty yojanas. Mount Laṅkā, situated in the Southern Sea, is lofty and steep, difficult to ascend;
yet now, within the ocean of birth and death, one suddenly transforms it into an ocean of wisdom. Having attained the path of transcendence, one dwells therein with patient endurance.
Unconfused by the demons of birth and death, he arrived at the coastal site of Laṅkā’s path and beheld the bhikṣu Sudhāna.
He saw this bhikṣu moving through the void, neither dwelling within the triple world nor dwelling outside of it.
Therefore, he comes and goes through the air; with the sound of the Dharma he transforms beings universally, and with the light of wisdom he shatters delusions.

Thus, the dragon kings produce thunder and flash lightning as offerings. Because he maintains humility and self-restraint through the practice of wisdom and compassion, the Garuḍa king takes the form of a youth, surrounded by celestial maidens, and together they join their palms in reverence. Through the ten pāramitās, he benefits sentient beings...
Therefore, this bhikṣu is honored by these ten kings. Because he has entered the gate of mastery in great wisdom, the two obstacles of affliction and knowledge cannot obstruct him.
All mirrors of false existence melt away wherever they touch, becoming equal to empty space. Thus, he says:
"In a single thought-moment, I have attained the unimpeded liberation door of universally and swiftly making offerings to all Buddhas."
He travels everywhere to the Buddha-fields of the ten directions; he passes through walls, crosses over barriers, enters the earth, and treads upon water as if they were empty space.
Fourth, in the country of Darbhikā, he meets the elder Megha and realizes the Dwelling of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*).
*Darbhikā* means "dissolution" (*pralaya*), signifying that from the holy teachings one dissolves all erroneous understandings. *Megha* means "cloud," signifying that it contains moisture.
The Rain of Dharma: Seeing Megha in the midst of a marketplace, surrounded by a thousand people, preaching the *Dharmaparyāya* on the Adornment of the Wheel of Syllables.
Since the three previous teachers were all bhikṣus, they represented the completion of supramundane merit; yet supramundane wisdom is not separate from the mundane world.
Therefore, Megha is a layman who enters the world without being defiled by it; thus, in the midst of the marketplace, his body of wisdom is sovereign, with both principal and retinue.
They intersect and interpenetrate; thus, a thousand people may circumambulate it. "Wheel" (*cakra*) carries the meaning of revolving in a circle.
By means of the dharma-gate in which a single name and a single sound lack intrinsic nature, they serve as the essence for immeasurable names and immeasurable sounds.

Thus, immeasurable names and immeasurable sounds are collectively a single syllable, and that single syllable is a single sound. Therefore, the one and the many revolve in a circle, mutually adorning one another.
Each and every worldly phenomenon (*laukika-dharma*) is entirely a supramundane phenomenon (*lokottara-dharma*); each and every supramundane phenomenon is entirely a worldly phenomenon.

When explaining that all phenomena exist, each and every one is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*); when explaining that all phenomena do not exist, they do not destroy their manifold characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the existence and non-existence of the ultimate and the conventional are perfectly transformed and mutually serve as adornments. By means of each and every phenomenon...

Because it is adorned by the simultaneous and perfect revolution of the differentiation of identity and difference, as well as formation and destruction, it is called the "Gate of the Adornment of Wheel-Syllables.
Since Megha possesses a conventional body and bodhicitta is the ultimate truth, and because the conventional truth must necessarily accord with the ultimate truth,
Megha, upon hearing that Sudhana had already generated the bodhicitta, immediately descended from his seat to pay homage, desiring to urge him forward.
Therefore, he said to Sudhana: "I know only this Dharma-gate of the *Ghoṣadatta-dhāraṇī*. *Dhāraṇī* is translated here as 'total retention' (*saṃgraha*).
This *Ghoṣadatta-dhāraṇī* is precisely the Gate of Adornment with the Wheel of Syllables."
Regarding the fifth dwelling, the "Abiding in the Means of Attaining Liberation through Seeing," which is the dwelling of the elder Muktaka:

because he dwells together with Megha amidst the laity, no specific country is mentioned. Since sentient beings in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are many, the wise take them as their forest of meditation (*dhyāna-vana*);
thus it is said that to the south there is a village named Vana-vāsin (Abiding in the Forest). It takes the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as...

This is the essence of dhyāna. Therefore, Sudhana traveled for twelve years before arriving. Previously, at the Sea of Clouds, he contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination and attained the supramundane mind.
Here, not destroying dependent origination and not clinging to dependent origination while traveling is the meaning of non-abiding.
Because the nature of the five aggregates is itself dhyāna, upon seeing liberation, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, for the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.

Therefore, he joined his palms. Because the essence of his concentration was profound, pervasive, and perfectly complete, he entered the *samādhi* of the *dhāraṇī* of revolving into boundless Buddha-fields of liberation.
Thus, in each of the ten directions, there appeared the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields.

"Revolve" (*xuan*) is synonymous with "whirlpool" (*xuán*); "whirlpool" carries the meaning of depth. "Ten" carries the meaning of fullness. This is because, within the *samādhi*, [he beheld] the Buddhas who are the fruit of his own wisdom.
Because all things manifest serenely from the cause of one’s own practice, the Elder said:

"When I entered samādhi, I saw the Dragon Sovereign King and ten other Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as ten leading Bodhisattvas. Since the Buddha is the resonance of one's own mind, when there is resonance in a single thought, there is a Buddha in that single thought;
when there is resonance in every thought, every thought is the Buddha. There is no external land apart from the mind. There is no mind apart from the land.
Regarding external Buddhas, he further says: "If I wish to see Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Peace and Bliss, and so forth, I see them all according to my thought.
Because the realm of all-encompassing wisdom, compassion, and myriad practices is fundamentally the nature of the Zen forest, which is inherently unimpeded, he says:
"I enter and emerge solely from this gate of liberation of unimpeded adornment."
Regarding the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja seen at the edge of Jambudvīpa who has realized the Stage of Right Mindfulness (*samyakcittatā-vihāra*):

because he has reached the ultimate limit of supramundane wisdom, he resides at the edge of Jambudvīpa. Having attained only mundane and supramundane great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he has not yet attained the great compassion that enters into the world and shares in its entanglements;
therefore, this bhikṣu is able to destroy all delusions through wisdom that is like the ocean. Thus it is said.
His name is Sāgaradhvaja. Walking meditation represents activity; samādhi represents stillness. This signifies that stillness exists based upon activity.

The side of the ground represents not dwelling within either stillness or activity, but rather moving with spontaneous mastery. Being free from inhalation and exhalation signifies that stillness accords with principle and activity accords with principle;
their nature is inherently pervasive and all-encompassing, without coming or going. Therefore, this bhikṣu is seen walking in meditation.
The earth-element enters into samādhi and becomes detached from inhalation and exhalation. Householders, lay devotees, and brahmins are those who practice worldly virtues;
the feet are their sphere of activity. Therefore, these three groups of beings are seen emerging from his feet and pervading the ten directions.
Kṣatriyas are of royal lineage, and brahmins are of pure conduct; the knees are the place where they exercise mastery over contraction and extension.
Because of mastery over pure wisdom, these two assemblies emerge from his knees. The waist is the place where worldly beings engage in desire;
the *ṛṣis*, who have severed desire, manifest through the illusion of wisdom (*jñāna-māyā*) to act like sentient beings while remaining personally free of desire.

Therefore, *ṛṣis* equal in number to the multitude of sentient beings emerge from his waist. The dragon signifies the rain of Dharma that moistens living beings; the ribs are the place of shelter and protection. Therefore—
The host of *nāgas* emerges from his flanks. The chest signifies the meaning of valor. The *svastika* rotates from all four sides; this signifies the inexhaustibility of the *brahmacarya*.

The *asura* signifies the meaning of not sinking; because one does not sink into the ocean of birth and death through diligent application of the myriad practices, the host of *asuras* emerges from the *svastika* on the chest.
This is for the purpose of transforming sentient beings without abandoning the various vehicles (*yāna*).

...the practice [of the Bodhisattvas]. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles turn their backs on the Buddha’s great function of compassion and wisdom, the assembly of the Two Vehicles emerges from his back.
"Shoulder" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of bearing a burden. Yakṣas and Rākṣasas have fearsome appearances, which signifies the meaning of protection.
Because they bear the great task and protect all wholesome qualities, the Yakṣas and others emerge from his shoulders. Kinnaras and Gandharvas are...
The musical deity: his abdomen contains all dharmas; because he constantly sings and praises all Buddha-dharmas, the *kiṃnaras* and others emerge from his abdomen.
The Wheel-Turning King has the significance of turning the wheel of Dharma; therefore, [the deities] emerge from his mouth.
They emerge from the mouth; because the solar disc dispels darkness, they emerge from the eyes.
Because Śakra is called the "Capable Lord" (*pati*) for dwelling in the Middle Way and leading sentient beings, Śakra emerges from between the eyebrows.

Because the practice of wisdom (*prajñācaryā*) is foremost within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), all Bodhisattvas emerge from the head. Because the fruit of wisdom (*jñānaphala*) is most supreme, all Buddhas emerge from the crown of the head.
He clearly understands that through the wisdom of emptiness, various bodies are produced like illusions;

he manifests emanations like clouds that fill the ten directions, accomplishing the teaching and adornment of sentient beings, yet his nature is identical to space and entirely devoid of thought or perception. Therefore, within meditative concentration, he manifests such a cloud-like array of bodies.
Furthermore, as for seeing all the pores of his body emit rays of light as numerous as motes of dust: this refers to the entire body.
This is always the unimpeded teaching-light of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

That Sudhana stood for one day up to six months and then another six days before Samudraketu emerged from meditative absorption signifies: one day and one night symbolize the fulfillment of *dāna* (generosity);

seven days and seven nights symbolize the fulfillment of the sevenfold ethical discipline (*śīla*); and half a month symbolizes the fulfillment of *kṣānti* (patience). Patience alone benefits oneself and does not yet benefit others.
This is the meaning of "half. One month symbolizes the fulfillment of diligence; six months symbolize the sixth stage (*vihāra*); and six days symbolize the perfection of the sixth *pāramitā*.

This is because one has merely attained pure loving-kindness (*maitrī*) but has not yet attained the skillful means (*upāya*) of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that acts in concert with sentient beings.
Therefore, Sāgaradhvaja said, "I know only this gate of the samādhi of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
As for the seventh, the place of the ocean tide where the upāsikā Śrīprabhā was seen to have realized the stage of non-retrogression:

it is called the "place of the ocean tide" because she manifested birth according to conditions without missing the proper time; it is called "universal adornment" because she dwells amidst birth and death through the ten thousand practices.
The garden takes great compassion free from defilement as its female lay devotee (upāsikā).

Appearing in a female form through a gentle and virtuous disposition, yet possessing no female mind, it is produced by the myriad practices of wisdom and compassion that serve the Buddhas and benefit sentient beings;
thus, one beholds the exquisite and wondrous features of Śūṣa’s countenance. The gardens, groves, palaces, ponds, and various articles are all adorned with jewels, arising from compassion and wisdom.
This is so. Therefore, Śūradatta said: "The Buddhas of the ten directions have all come to occupy these jeweled seats and preach the Dharma for me.

By manifesting eighty-four thousand afflictions as practicing the same path, they guide and lead me. I have realized that the nature of birth and death and the nature of Buddha-wisdom are fundamentally one and the same nature, and thus I am no longer subject to retreat or cowardice. For this reason, he said: 'The great assembly of eighty-four thousand is all here.'"
Udyāna traveled with me; we all attained non-retrogression regarding enlightenment. First, at the place of the three bhikṣus, I attained the supramundane mind—this is one.
Second, at the place of Megha Vimuktisamudrakūṭa, I attained both the mundane and supramundane minds.
Third, upon reaching this seventh stage, I entered worldly conduct out of compassion. These three all penetrate omniscience.
"O Sea, therefore I say that I have purified my brahmacarya under thirty Ganges-sands of Buddhas.

Because I am able to enter into birth-and-death to teach and transform sentient beings, I have realized that both birth-and-death and the practice of teaching sentient beings are all practices of nirvana—without arising or ceasing, ultimately peaceful and secure.
Therefore, I say that I know only this state of being free from sorrow and secure."
It is a banner.
At the eighth station, the Sea Tide Place (Sāgaratīra) in the country of Nalasura, one beholds the seer (ṛṣi) Vimalaghoṣa, who has realized the stage of youthful truth (kumārabhūmi).

By means of the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā), he initiates the activity of wisdom and unites it with the gate of compassion; only when these are fused into a single entity does [the realization] truly obtain.
The great function of non-action brings vast benefit without thought; it is like the surging of the tide, yet without effort.
Thus, he also dwells in the realm of the ocean tides. Nārada—here translated as "Not Lazy"—governs the world with the wisdom of effortless intelligence and tireless diligence.
Vemacitra—here translated as "Uttering a Terrifying Sound"—is named for a rishi because his speech crushes the heterodox. By means of wisdom...

He followed various paths yet held no divergent views; thus he was a seer (*ṛṣi*). The *pāṭala* tree resembles the *qiū* tree of this region, while the leaves of the *nyagrodha* tree resemble those of the persimmon.
Because he possessed the virtue of shading all beings with wisdom and compassion, the various adornments of the grove where the seer dwelt were visible:
the grass mat and the deer-skin robe were signs of his fewness of desires. By perfecting the myriad practices, he attained this state.

Therefore, the Rishi led ten thousand disciples while clad in deer skins; because the objects of the five sensory realms all return to the ground of wisdom, Sudhana prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the earth.

Because wisdom that is effortless cannot be shaken or moved, the Rishi said, "I have attained the liberation of the Invincible Banner," for he had realized that the realm of wisdom is all-pervasive. Thus, the Rishi took Sudhana by the hand. Well...

Vasumitra then sees himself traveling everywhere to the abodes of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields in the ten directions. Grasping the hand signifies the meaning of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
At the initial stage of the eighth [bhūmi], the "effortless wisdom" (*anābhoga-jñāna*), there is a fear that one might stagnate in quiescence and fail to spontaneously manifest wisdom and compassion;

therefore, one requires the empowerment of the Sage to stimulate and inspire them. Thus, by grasping the hand, one enters the Dharma through the Sage’s empowerment. Having entered the Dharma, one [proceeds] by oneself...
The power is always thus. It is like having crossed a river and no longer needing to carry the boat; therefore, one lets go of it and returns to one's original place.
Ninth is the village of Īśāna, where the Brahmin Jvalanānta (the "Heat-Fervent One") dwells as a son of the Dharma King.
*Īśāna* here is translated as "Long and Straight"; he dwells there because he gathers and transforms beings by extending the straight path and acting without any form of flattery or deceit.
Because his wisdom conformed with the heterodox, yet his power was able to overcome the poisonous heat of all afflictions and enter into divine function;

he manifested himself as conforming to the non-Buddhists by "roasting his body with five fires" to lead those following heterodoxy back to correct wisdom. Therefore, the Brahmin was named "Victorious Heat" (Jianre).

The mountain of blades symbolizes the power of the Dharma that destroys delusions; the mass of fire symbolizes the light of Vajra-wisdom. Through the realization of one's own nature, one attains liberation;
through the mastery of its power and function, one is free from fear. Thus, one is able to illuminate and sever the afflictions of sentient beings throughout the long night.

Therefore, when the Brahmin ascended that mountain of blades and cast himself into the mass of fire, he did so because the nature of adverse conditions is unfathomable; thus, Śūra exhorted him to virtue.
Sudhana ascended the mountain of blades and entered the mass of fire, yet he harbored doubts.

Because this power and function constitute an inconceivable realm that must be realized through direct experience (*pratyakṣa*), the devas, nāgas, and divine kings all praised the virtue of Jvalanāmukha from the sky, urging him not to doubt.
*Eṇī-bhara* means "stinking tree" in this language; because this nāga had previously damaged this tree in a past life, he was reborn with a head [resembling it].

He ascended this tree of stench; thus it was named after him. Because he entered realization through the union of wisdom, when Sudhana ascended the mountain of blades, he attained the Samādhi of Excellent Abiding before even reaching the summit;
and upon merely touching the mass of fire, he further attained the Samādhi of Tranquil Bliss.
By means of this single practice, according to the differing inclinations and desires of sentient beings, each perceives an inexhaustible variety.
The Section on Separate Practice is exactly as praised in the *Gaganagañja-paripṛcchā*. Therefore, it is said: "I have attained the liberation of the inexhaustible wheel.
Regarding the tenth [stage], the attainment of the empowerment-abode by the maiden Maitrīcaryā in the city of Siṃhavikrama:
she is called a "maiden" because her spontaneous great compassion is untainted by the habitual tendencies of attachment to birth; and she is "sovereign" because her compassion arises from wisdom.
Fearless. Therefore, his father was King Siṃhadhvaja. Because this abiding wisdom and compassion perfectly encompass the wisdom and compassion within the five stages, there is no other path;

thus, five hundred maidens serve as his attendants. Because he is able to abide where the Buddhas abide, containing the gates of cause and effect for the Buddhas across the five stages, he dwells in the Vairocana-kośa Palace through the practice of great compassion.
Relying on the teaching of the pure and white fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body as expounded by the Omniscient One, which covers and protects all sentient beings,
he sits upon a throne of Nāga-vijaya sandalwood feet, a golden-threaded net, and celestial robes.

Because this palace of wisdom and temple of compassion is the common place of entry for all sentient beings and the shared dwelling where Bodhisattvas of the five stages reside, he beholds immeasurable sentient beings.
He entered the royal palace. He took the luminous purity of the Dharma-body as the crystal floor; the sustaining power of pure conduct as the lapis lazuli pillars;
the protection of wisdom as the diamond walls; and the external adornment of the precepts as the Jāmbūnada gold ramparts.

Using the light of the teachings to illuminate the mundane world constitutes the windows and skylights. Because the mind is free from defilement and turbidity, his retribution-born skin is golden in color.

Because he uses wisdom to cover and protect sentient beings, his retribution-born eyes and hair are deep blue. Therefore, one sees within the hall such adornments as these, arranged according to reality.
Since a single dharma encompasses all dharmas and they enter into union at once, the realm of wisdom and its objects interpenetrate.

These are layered and inexhaustible. Therefore, the maiden caused Sudhana to observe, and he saw that within every single wall, every single pillar, and every single mirror-image, all the manifestations of the realms of all Buddhas were mutually contained.
The maiden said, "This is the Gate of Universal Adornment of Prajñāpāramitā; it is what I have [attained] from thirty-six Ganges-sands of Buddhas."
Regarding the attainment [of the goal] through each entering by way of different gates: taking one stage as encompassing all stages constitutes the Gate of Universal Adornment (*samalaṃkāra-mukha*).
Taking the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) makes thirty. The ten faiths (*śraddhā*) consist of believing in these three dharmas.

The ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the eleventh stage likewise involve only the mastery of these same three dharmas; there is no new dharma beyond them. Thus, they are accomplished through these three dharmas.
The six stages constitute thirty-six. Because these stages, in their progression, encompass all six positions, each individual stage possesses inexhaustible practices and vows.

Although their modes of activity differ, there is no distinction in the Dharma. These are the ways in which one enters through various gateways under as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in thirty-six Ganges Rivers.
The above ten spiritual friends clarify the manifestation of meditative contemplation through the clouds of virtue.
The gate of the Buddha-wisdom of one’s own mind universally perceiving the realms of all Buddhas;

the ocean-cloud gate of clearly contemplating the ocean of birth and death as the ocean of Buddha-lands originally pure through the twelve links of dependent origination; the gate of the well-abiding clear wisdom of the Dharma-body, which is sovereign, unimpeded, and transcends the mundane;
the ocean-cloud gate of Maitreya clearly abiding in the mundane while practicing cultivation, universally entering the gates of worldly letters and signs; and the gate of liberation’s clear body.

The Dharma-door of Samādhi wherein the self-nature of the myriad realms of Buddha-fields is contained; the Dharma-door of Unobstructed Supernatural Power wherein the luminosity of Sāgaramegha transcends entanglement yet manifests quiescent function;

the Dharma-door of Long-term Cultivation of Great Compassion wherein Śāntamati abides in the world; the Dharma-door of Manifesting Identity with the Evil through Effortless Wisdom wherein Viśvabhuja appears;

the Dharma-door of Gathering the Evil through Ascetic Practices wherein Jvalanāntaka subdues; and the Dharma-door of the Total Integration of All through the Fulfillment of Wisdom and the Perfection of Compassion wherein Maitrīyaśas acts.

This is the gateway of the simultaneous perfection of rank, wisdom, and compassion. From here below is established the gateway of the ten practices of self-benefit and benefit for others by the Ten Masters.

Although the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are not devoid of the practices of self-benefit and benefit for others, there is concern that one might enter the differentiated realms of the mundane world and lose mastery;
therefore, it is necessary to refine and temper them through the dharma-gate of the ten practices (*caryā*).
From the eleventh [stage] to the third eye, one beholds the bhikṣu Sudarśana, who has realized the practice of joy.

With the eye of wisdom (jñāna-cakṣus), one observes the faculties; with the dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus), one knows the dharmas; and with the eye of insight (prajñā-cakṣus), one discriminates between the correct and the false. These three are originally one; they are called three according to their respective functions.
If one lacks these three eyes, one is first deluded oneself—how could one be capable of benefiting others? Therefore, the country is named after them. Because the mind is detached from the world.

Only then is one fit to enter the world to share in its radiance and benefit all beings by transforming them so that strife is extinguished. Therefore, at the very beginning of his practice, he beholds bhikṣus;
through conduct that accords with worldly dust, they are as numerous as a forest, entering the cycle of birth and death to deliver all sentient beings and emerge from that cycle.

Furthermore, he causes sentient beings to give rise to the vow of great compassion and enter into the cycle of birth and death. Thus, through successive transmission, it is like one lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps;
those in darkness all become illumined, yet the light never comes to an end. This is the meaning of "coming and going. Therefore, one sees him walking back and forth in the forest.
Because he is able to practice the path, he appears in the prime of his youth; because his conduct is upright, his countenance is dignified.

Because he acts in accordance with the Way, his hair curls to the right without disorder. Because his wisdom is lofty and his virtue is perfected, there is a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) upon his crown.
Because his mind is pure and his wisdom is stainless, his skin is golden in color. Because his speech does not issue falsely, there are three lines upon his neck.

Because his wisdom is vast and his insight is broad, his forehead is wide, level, and symmetrical. Because he skillfully expounds the Dharma-gate of emptiness and non-substantiality, his lips and mouth are crimson and clean like the *bimba* fruit.
The fruit: this fruit is a red fruit from the south. Because his wisdom-karma is cool and refreshing, he bears the *svastika* on his chest.

Because he has fulfilled the practice of the seven factors of enlightenment, seven parts of his body—the two hands, the two shoulders, the two feet, and the male organ of the horse-king—are flat and full.

Because he teaches and filters all sentient beings, his fingers are webbed. Because his practice of gathering and sustaining life is universal, he is surrounded by the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas.
Because he transforms others according to their faculties, there is no fixed direction for him and no fixed dharma;
thus, the deities who preside over the directions rotate with him in every quarter to guide him. Because his conduct is untainted, the deities of his footsteps support him.
The lotus supports his feet; because he manifests wisdom through dhyāna, the earth deities reveal various treasure-troves.
Because the high becomes low, it is like the shifting of Mount Sumeru to signify humility; thus, the deity of Mount Sumeru bows his head in reverent salutation.

Because his speech is elegant and refined, causing others to find joy, "wind" signifies the meaning of verbal instruction, while "fragrant flowers" signify the meaning of finding joy. This is like the transformation of wind and earth into...
Contemplating this, the wind-spirit rains down exquisite fragrant flowers. Because they give rise to myriad virtues within the night of birth and death, the Night-Spirit is named "Spring Harmony.

Because their initial practice constitutes their youth, and because within a single practice they fully possess the three dharmas of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications—without departing from the Eightfold Noble Path—these constitute thirty-eight [stages]. By means of this...
Within this very life, there is no life that possesses a beginning, end, or middle. Thus, the *Sudarsana* says: "My years are few and my ordination is recent;
yet within this life, I have purified my brahmacarya under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-eight Ganges Rivers.
Because a single moment of delusion causes the three periods of time to interpenetrate in an instant, wisdom has no distance or proximity; it fully contains all within the dust of the present.
In the oceans of lands, it is therefore said that in some Buddha-fields one may practice the pure cultivation of Brahma-conduct for a single day and night,
and even in others, one may practice Brahma-conduct for unspeakable eons.
Twelfth, in the midst of a river island in the country of Renowned Fame (Yaśas), one sees the youth Īśvaraputra, who has realized the practice of bringing benefit to others.

Because the fragrance of his precepts is universally renowned throughout the land, and because he enters the marketplace with mastery, his undefiled precepts—like a flowing river—will inevitably enter the ocean of wisdom.
Therefore, the youth Īśvaraputra is at the river island; since all his playful activities are Buddha-works, one beholds him there.
The play of piling up sand, through the divine application of skillful means, enters the world and yet transcends it as the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*).
Like Sāgaramegha, taking the ocean of birth and death as identical to the ocean of wisdom as the essence of the precepts;

like the maritime captain, who does not abide on this shore or the other shore but ferries people across as the essence of the precepts; and like the night goddess Priyadarśanā, taking great compassion as the essence of the precepts—following [these examples].
The stages of advancement differ; however, as for the penetration of wisdom, it is fully present at every stage. Therefore, the Sovereign Lord said:

"I know all the dharma-gates of knowledge regarding crafts and supernormal powers. This includes knowing the world's systems of writing, calculation, seals (*mudrā*), realms (*dhātu*), locations (*sthāna*), medicine, arts, agriculture, commerce, the refinement of elixirs (*rasāyana*), and the skill of discerning auspicious marks, as well as the ability to teach according to the faculties [of beings]. "Realms" refers to the world-realms (*loka-dhātu*); "locations" refers to...

The dwelling place of sentient beings. Writing cures the obstacle of forgetting what has been learned; seals cure the obstacle of failing to maintain protection; medicine cures the obstacle of the disharmony of the four elements.
"Crafts" refers to technical skills: above, knowing celestial phenomena; below, knowing terrestrial geography; and in between, observing human sentiments.

Those who practice the vocations of the four classes of people and those who engage in the nine schools of thought all excel in their respective tasks, thereby curing the obstacle of lacking mastery in worldly affairs. Calculation refers to bodhi-... [text fragment]
The *saṃkhyā* method remedies the obstacle of doubt regarding taking and giving. The account presented here is largely the same as that in the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya-varga*).
However, it is the Bodhisattva who knows through the calculation of dharmas; this is not like the Buddha’s knowledge in that chapter, which is spontaneous and natural.

The laywoman Samudrapratisthānadarśanasampannā, who had realized the practice of non-opposition, was named "City" because her patience was like the ocean in its capacity to receive the hundred rivers;
she was called a "person" because she was fully endowed with all practices within that patience.

Because of these characteristics of patience, her physical appearance was seen to be upright and handsome, wearing plain white garments with her hair hanging loose; because she was complete in the ten thousand practices, she possessed ten thousand [virtues].
Surrounded by maidens, they open the gates with the Indra’s Net of the Wisdom of the Dharma-realm, encompassing the infinite within the subtle.

Furthermore, adding the vast mind of the power of aspiration of the Wisdom of the Dharma-realm, they cause all sentient beings of the ten directions to eat even a portion of food the size of a single atom, such that all obtain full satisfaction without diminishing it by even a hair's breadth. This food of a single atom is itself the measure of the Dharma-realm.
Because there is no obstruction from internal, external, middle, or peripheral limits regarding food, I am fully endowed with the liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit;
thus, I can take the food and drink within a single small vessel and universally bestow it upon infinite sentient beings, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
Because it is encompassed by the four immeasurable minds, infinite sentient beings enter through these four gates.
In the fourteenth [section], in the city of Great Flourishing (Daxing), he saw the lay practitioner (upāsaka) Mingzhi, who had realized the practice of being unyielding.

He was named "Great Flourishing" because he brought about great benefit through his diligence; he was called "Mingzhi" (Wisdom-Intelligence) because he observed the faculties and examined the dharmas; he was called a "lay practitioner" because he lived as a householder according to worldly customs;

and he was seen there because he dwelt amidst the bustling marketplace of birth and death through the practices of the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) and the seven factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga) without weariness. Thus, he saw him there.
Seated upon a tower of the seven precious jewels at the crossroads of the city, I have, through diligent practice, accumulated all manner of merit and severed all suffering and deprivation.
Therefore, the Wise One said: "I have attained the liberation door of the treasury of merit that arises according to one's will.
Since both material and Dharma gifts are born of the wisdom that realizes emptiness and non-reliance, immeasurable sentient beings come from various lands, each following [their own path].
Whatever they desired and requested, the householder looked up into the void, and everything required descended from the sky;
he then taught various dharmas according to their individual capacities. By means of the first dwelling, one first illuminates the Buddha-wisdom and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.

By means of the fourth dwelling, one subdues the delusions of the three realms and purifies Buddha-wisdom so that it manifests before one, thereby being born into the family of the Tathāgata. By means of the eighth dwelling, one is born into the [wisdom] of the Tathāgata’s non-...

The Family of Merit and Wisdom. Through the wisdom and compassion of the ten stages, one universally rescues others, ascends to the stage of consecration, and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.

Now, in the fourth practice, by contemplating the gate of the emptiness of phenomena, one realizes the liberation of dependent origination, remedies the residual habits of the three realms, and the wisdom of the Dharma-body manifests.
Furthermore, they are born into the family of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is said that the great assembly in this gathering has already been born into the family of the Tathāgata.
Fifteenth, in the city of the Lion’s Seat (Siṃhāsana), the Elder Ratnaśikhin is seen to realize the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.

He is called the "City of Fearlessness through Meditative Concentration" (*dhyāna-samādhi-abhaya-pura*), because the essence of concentration universally encompasses all practices, just as the body of the Elder Vimukta contains [all] within the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*).
The dust-motes and lands take the objective realm as following from the essence to constitute dhyāna.

This fifth stage takes the essence through its function, whereby all objective realms of the dust-motes are subsumed within a single dhyāna, reaching the pinnacle of the Dharma; therefore, it is named "Jewel Topknot" (Ratna-śikhin).

Because the essence of this practice is quiescent while its function is eternally constant, the marketplace of birth and death cannot cause any impairment. Thus, one sees him in the market; for within this dhyāna, the ten pāramitās are fully present.
And [it includes] the Eightfold Noble Path. Therefore, his residence—a ten-story pavilion—has eight gates.
Just as the first story provides food to represent *dāna* (generosity), so too does the highest story represent *jñāna* (wisdom) through the fullness of the Tathāgata.

These ten stories collectively encompass the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*) and comprehensively include the fruit of Buddhahood. They take the *dhyāna* of the non-abiding *dharmadhātu* as their essence; all are comprised within the ten *pāramitās* of *dhyāna*.

The *pāramitās* serve as adornments. Ratnaśikhin said: "Because in the past, during kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, when a Buddha entered a city, I performed various kinds of music and offered a single pellet of incense;
through the merit of this offering, I have now attained such a residence as this, having dedicated it toward three goals.

Here, "past kalpas as numerous as motes of dust" symbolizes transcending the mundane emotions and entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Musical sounds" symbolize the preaching of the Dharma. This clarifies that [the result] arises from concentration.

Wisdom. A single pellet of incense represents a single kind of meditative fragrance that possesses five aspects. The three states refer to constantly seeing the Buddha, constantly hearing the Dharma, and constantly being free from the suffering of poverty.
This means that while one has already attained the essence of concentration within the Ten Abodes, one now attains mastery over quiescence and function within the dhyāna-gate of the Ten Practices.
Regarding the attainment of the liberation of the treasury of immeasurable merit and virtue: through dhyāna...
It is the fulfillment of the ten thousand practices.
In the country of Shōkon (Sixteen Rattan Roots), one sees the Elder Fugen (Universal Eye) realizing the practice of Zengen (Subhūti).

Because his prajñā is profound and firm, penetrating to the very source of all phenomena, it is called a "country" after the way a rattan root grows deep down to the water's edge; because he possesses wisdom that knows all things universally, it is so named.
Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus), because the gates of wisdom are layered upon one another, lofty, and difficult to enter, he sees the city walls and battlements as towering and steep.

Because the wisdom of the three emptinesses (trīṇi śūnyatāni) sweeps away all boundaries, the thoroughfares are broad and level. When Universal Eye says, "I am skilled at healing all diseases," it signifies that he has studied under the masters of worldly medicine;
this also serves to symbolize the Dharma. For instance, the wind disorder (vāta-doṣa) symbolizes those who have many discursive thoughts (saṃjñā).
One treats [the former] with counting the breaths (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Those whose jaundice indicates an abundance of desire (*rāga*) are treated with the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*).
Those whose phlegm-fever indicates an abundance of delusion (*moha*) are treated with the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*).

Those whose possession by spirits indicates attachment to exquisite forms, failure to leave behind demonic activities and celestial retributive supernatural powers, are treated with the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatābhāvanā*). Those whose disease of sorcery-poison indicates having something to be attained (*upalambha*) [are treated accordingly].
The mind can give rise to various fetters, harms, and karmas. The disease of water is craving; the disease of fire is anger.
Diseases such as these can all be countered through the Dharma. Furthermore, my skill in compounding various perfumes refers to practicing worldly arts, which also serves to symbolize the Dharma.
Just as wisdom skillfully explains the fragrance of the teachings to permeate evil karma, so that all foul odors are transformed into the fragrance of wisdom. Pungent...
Tīraparṇī means "bank" in this language. This incense comes from the banks of the Indus River; it symbolizes that the river of the four wisdoms must enter the ocean of nature.
Upon smelling this fragrance of wisdom, one will surely reach the other shore. Aruṇavarti means "red-colored fragrance" in this language.
The fragrance of the manifestation of empty luminosity, wherein both mind and objects are liberated; the *ulūka-candana* fragrance. *Ulūka* is the name of a snake.
This snake is most venomous and constantly suffers from the heat of its own poison. When it coils its body around a *candana* tree, its poison is extinguished.

This represents the fragrance of hearing and expounding the Dharma that no phenomenon can be apprehended; it signifies the extinction of the heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*). I know this brings about [the liberation] of all beings.
Regarding "sentient beings universally seeing the gate of joy of all Buddhas": this means using wisdom to cause all objective realms to enter the realm of the Buddha.
As for the King Never-Tiring (Anantakṣaya-rāja) seen by Tārādhvaja in the city, who realized the practice of non-attachment: *Tārādhvaja* here translates as "Luminous Purity.
By means of supramundane luminous and pure wisdom, he entered worldly conduct of compassion, observing the faculties [of beings] and acting in concert with them. Not... [text fragment].
He falsely assumed the title of a city ruler. In the Sanskrit language, *anala* means "insatiable"; because he tirelessly brings benefit to sentient beings with sovereign ease, he is called a King.
Because he enters the world through the ten thousand practices, he is seen presiding over ten thousand ministers who manage the affairs of state together with him.
Because he employs the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to manifest adverse conditions for the sake of governance, one hundred thousand fierce soldiers behead all manner of evildoers.
The infliction of such punishments as gouging out eyes and other forms of immeasurable torture was ordered by the King.

When he commanded Sudhana to enter and observe the magnificent and sublime adornments of the palace, saying, "I am one who knows the liberation that is like an illusion," this clarified that these acts of punishment were all illusory manifestations of great compassion;

the King himself transformed into an evil person and further manifested fierce executioners to carry out the judicial proceedings. This was intended to cause real sentient beings to feel dread [and thus refrain from wrongdoing].
He severed evil; in reality, he did not inflict suffering or harm upon even a single mosquito or ant, let alone upon human beings.
Therefore, he experienced such magnificent adornments. This clarifies that if one indulges their passions to afflict and harm sentient beings, they shall surely fall into ruin.
Eighteenth, the city of Sublime Light (*Sudarśana*), where one encounters King Great Light (*Mahāprabha*) and realizes the practice that is difficult to attain.

This stage is called a "city" because it consists of the sublime, differentiated functions within non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*). It is called a "king" because it is the fundamental sovereign wisdom of non-effort.

By bringing to equilibrium and mastery the habitual tendencies of wisdom and compassion that were previously incomplete in the preceding stages, one finally enters the sublime function of non-effort; therefore, it is described as a place where one travels.

Gradually proceeding until reaching the city, because wisdom and compassion lacking in merit are difficult to bring into accord, even though he applied contemplation, he still longed for a sign of approval.
Thus, upon arriving at the city, he again inquired of the former residents.

Because they possessed the various practices distinguished by wisdom and compassion, he saw that the ground, trees, palaces, towers, and lotus ponds were all adorned with jewels. As for the length of the city—
It is ten *yojanas* in width; one *yojana* is equivalent to seventeen *li* in this region.

Furthermore, it is said that within the city there are ten billion streets, and between each street dwell immeasurable sentient beings. This could not be contained by the measurement of a worldly *yojana*;
rather, it is the great city of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and the inexhaustible thoroughfares where the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) intersect with one another.
Therefore, according to the faculties and karma of sentient beings, they perceive this city as variously different—broad or narrow, pure or defiled.
By means of this King of Wisdom, he universally demonstrates these principles, just as the eight trigrams and nine palaces all possess their respective methods.

The celestial phenomena of the upper direction, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the twelve double-hours, the branches and stems, the sun, moon, and five planets—all clearly manifest these dharmic signs for the human king.

The Dharma is employed to administer government decrees; the Awakened King takes it as a model for his teachings. Thus, when Sudhana praised the King, he compared him to the sky, wherein the noble ones manifest various dharma-gates like the constellations.
Through non-reliant wisdom, he enters into the minds of all sentient beings, sharing their same essence and having no distinct nature.
Sentient and insentient beings are of one single nature without duality; all follow the turning of wisdom and act accordingly.
This is the work of the Buddha. It is like a worldly sovereign who, when possessed of the Way, causes the hundred beasts to dance in harmony and the phoenixes and birds to appear in auspicious array;

even a commoner of supreme filial piety can move the ice of a pond so that fish leap forth or cause bamboo shoots to sprout from winter stalks. How much more so for one whose wisdom penetrates the source and whose conduct is equal to the Dharma-realm!
His benevolence encompasses all things; his spirit communes with all beings. He has no self-centered mind, taking instead the minds of all beings as his own mind.

It is like a *maṇi* jewel, which takes on the colors of whatever it encounters. Therefore, when the King entered the meditative state of "Great Benevolence Accordant with the World," the people of the city and countryside, along with the various birds and beasts, all came to pay him respectful homage.
The mountains, plains, grasses, trees, and even the ponds and springs all turned toward him in response.
The rivers and seas surged and poured before the King; all the celestial kings rained down offerings.

The seventh stage and this [eighth] are both royal stages, clarifying that the power of the wisdom of compassion functions differently according to the respective positions, yet there is no duality in the path.

Therefore, the seventh and eighth abodes are both situated at the place of the ocean tide. Thus, the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) of the seventh and the proper progression (*samyak-prasthāna*) of Avalokiteśvara meet in a single assembly.
One sees—whether it be a woman, a seer, a king, or a bodhisattva—which are symbols of differing capacities and functions.
Nineteenth: dwelling in the royal capital, one sees the laywoman (upāsikā) Acalā who has realized the practice of wholesome dharmas.

She takes sovereignty over the freedom of teaching the Dharma as her royal capital; she takes the untainted power of the Dharma as the laywoman Acalā; and she takes the mother of wisdom as... [the method].
"Protected by her father" means that her mind is untainted by sensory objects due to her humble compassion; thus it is said that she is a maiden protected by her parents.
When Sudhana enters the house and touches its halls, golden light shines forth and he immediately attains five hundred samādhi-doors;
this is because he is illuminated by the light of the teaching from the chamber of compassion, whereby he gains entry into the five hundred doors of the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*).
"Entering this samādhi like a fetus seven days old" means that through wisdom one enters into loving-kindness (*maitrī*), becoming gentle, harmonious, and joyful.

"All who see this woman have no defiled mind" means that because she is free from the karma of passionate attachment, her body lacks the marks of sexual desire, causing the minds of all who behold her to become upright.
She said: "In the past, during the time of the Buddha Viśvabhuja, I was a king named Vidyudatta."

As a princess, she beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs and gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Since that time, throughout all those kalpas, she has not even conceived a thought of desire, much less committed such an act.
Because she leads sentient beings by means of the perfection of vows and conduct arising from unconditioned wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), she is named Dīrghabāhu (Long-Armed).
Because her insight into the Path through wisdom is swift, she is named Vidyudatta (Lightning-Endowed). Because she cultivates compassion based on wisdom, [she is so named].

As the king’s daughter, in the eighth stage she was still stained by the habitual tendencies of sorrow; now that she has reached the ninth stage, those habitual tendencies have ceased to exist, and thus it is said that she is "without a mind of desire.
By means of the rank of Dharma Master, she overcomes the obstacle of not being masterful in preaching the Dharma.
Since one must be free from weariness, it is said: "I have attained the samādhi of seeking all dharmas without satiety."
In the city of Viśālā—Viśālā meaning "Birth of Joy"—he saw a renunciant, a wandering ascetic who had realized true practice.
The city was so named because, through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it universally benefited the common people, causing them all to experience joy.
He became a renunciant with wisdom equal to that of a Buddha; he manifested himself as one who shared the same false views as well as those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
To exhaustively engage in all such activities is called "universal conduct" (*sarvatraga*). Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi are also of this category.

Because ordinary practitioners have not yet entered the Dharma-realm where principle and phenomena interpenetrate, and where body and land are mutually pervasive through the gates of the Ten Mysteries and Six Characteristics, they are all considered "external paths" (*tīrthika*).
Now, this universal conduct—which benefits others by adapting to their various types—may resemble an external path, but it is not an external path. Sudhana...

In the middle of the night, he saw the grasses and trees on the mountain to the east of the city emitting light like the rising sun; this signifies that within the night of birth and death, there is the sun of great wisdom.

He saw practitioners on a level plateau at the summit of a mountain inhabited by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); the mountain summit represents the loftiness and excellence of wisdom, while the level plateau represents the impartiality of compassion.
To practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) upon this impartial abiding in wisdom and compassion is what the non-Buddhists claim they have realized.
The Bodhisattva practitioner in all stages manifests physical bodies in response to all phenomena through the penetration of wisdom;
these appear like echoes responding to sounds, yet they possess no substance that comes or goes. Below this, the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are established:

although the ten practices have accomplished worldly governance, transformation, and artistic skills, they have not yet been able to rely upon the unimpeded *dharmadhātu* of the Samantabhadra conduct of one's own Buddha-fruit.
Because one neither emerges from nor sinks into the ocean of birth and death at the gateway, the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are required. Twenty-one:

"The Vast Land" (Mahāviṣaya) refers to seeing the Elder who Sells Incense as the realization of the dedication for rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being.
It is called a "land" because it extensively gives rise to great vows; it is "vast" because it harmonizes wisdom and compassion, principle and phenomena, and nirvana and samsara.

The conceptualizations and discriminations of the defilement and purity of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are synthesized into a single pill. This mastery over both the general and the particular is called "Incense Seller.
Because one enters birth-and-death with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) yet remains unstained, one is a "layperson" (*upāsaka*).

One is also called "Blue Lotus," because the nature of incense has no fixed basis yet gives rise to the good and extinguishes the evil; this symbolizes that while the Great Vow has no fixed basis, its practice brings benefit to living beings.
The fragrance-king of fundamental wisdom arises from within ignorance; the fragrance of differentiated wisdom arises from the myriad objects.
Therefore, the Elder said: "I know the source of the fragrance-king and all other fragrances, and I also know the methods for blending them.
Among humans, there is a fragrance called Elephant-Treasury (*hastigarbha*), which is produced when dragons fight; if one is touched by this fragrance, the body becomes golden in color.

The first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) is symbolized by the dragon of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* contending with the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), thereby producing the fragrance of wisdom.

Sentient beings who enter this state immediately attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). On Mount Malaya there is ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*); if one anoints the body with it, one will not be burned even when entering fire.
This mountain is located within the territory of South India. It symbolizes the stage of "cultivating the ground" (*bhūmi-parikarma*) through the principle of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Anointing and polishing the essence of the precepts means that one cannot be burned by the fires of the three poisons. Within the ocean there is a fragrance called "Invincible" (*anabhibhūta*);

if it is used to anoint a drum, when its sound resounds, even the courageous enemies will retreat. This symbolizes that through the cultivation of practice, one dwells in the perfection of *dharma-kṣānti*, whereby evil adversaries naturally withdraw.
These ten kinds of fragrances represent the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), for they harmonize and integrate the ten [stages].

Abiding within the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), one brings mastery over the two gates of the ultimate and the conventional, as well as compassion and wisdom, thereby accomplishing the gate of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

This initial dedication enters the ocean of great compassion; fearing that the realization of wisdom might be neglected, the ten types of incense are used to symbolize the dharmas of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).
Because a single [ingredient] embodies all principles, it is represented by blended incense.
Regarding the twenty-second, the city of twenty-two-storied pavilions where the mariner Vasiṣṭha realizes the indestructible dedication:
in the low-lying lands of the Southern Sea, many people dwell in multi-storied buildings. Furthermore, the "pavilion" (lú) symbolizes wisdom. *Vasiṣṭha* means "sovereign" (*vaśitā*) in this context;
because he possesses the natural precepts and great compassion, he attains sovereignty while entering the ocean of birth and death, just as a boat dwells neither on this shore nor the other.
Because he ferries people across to the other shore and through the middle of the stream, he is called a boatman.

Because he delivers people across the ocean of birth and death by means of the precepts as the primary practice and its attendant myriad deeds, he is seen surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants on the seashore.
Because the ocean of birth and death is profoundly tranquil and unmoving, the boatman says, "I know all the jewel islands within the sea."

Taking the Tathāgatagarbha, which is both empty and non-empty, as knowing the location of the treasure; taking the nature-endowed virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges as knowing the types of treasure;

taking the awakening to Buddha-nature as knowing the seed of the treasure; and taking the penetration of the faculties of sentient beings as knowing the vessel for the treasure—by establishing teachings according to these faculties to manifest the virtue of wisdom, one brings forth all treasures. This is like the partial mastery of the Bodhisattvas in the Pure Land.

The Dragon realm, where purity and impurity have not yet been extinguished, is a place of difficulty for the Dragon Palace. The Śrāvaka, who can empty the three poisons, is a place of difficulty for the Yakṣa.
The Pratyekabuddha, who dwells in the ocean of Nirvāṇa where Buddha-wisdom does not manifest, is a place of difficulty for the Rākṣasa.

Because one takes the ocean of birth and death and accomplishes it as the gateway to the Dharma-realm, it is said: "I shall entirely avoid such difficulties as these. This is because one knows craving, grasping, and becoming.
One’s karma is like knowing the depth of whirlpools and eddies; the extent of emotional consciousness and conceptual thoughts is like the distance of waves and surges;
and the presence of affectionate attachment, joy, or anger is like the clarity or turbidity of the water’s color.

Furthermore, "knowing the movements of the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the divisions of time," means that one has mastered the subtle phenomena of yin and yang within the world to benefit others, and it also represents the distinct stages of teaching and practice.
This depends on the methods and procedures for maturing the faculties, as well as the duration of time—whether long or short.

Knowing whether the ship’s iron and wood are sturdy or brittle, and whether its mechanisms are stiff or smooth, represents the maturity or immaturity of the faculties, whether the three vehicles have turned back toward the Great Vehicle or not, and whether one is capable of entering the cycle of birth and death or not.
It is by means of these that merchants are transported to the Isle of Jewels to gather various treasures.
That Ratna leads them back to Jambudvīpa symbolizes following the rules of practice from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) through all subsequent stages.

Reaching the fulfillment of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) and returning to one’s original dwelling within the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to perform the practices of Samantabhadra signifies this.
"I have attained the practitioner of the Banner of Great Compassion" means that the nature-precept (*śīla*) of great compassion is unshakable and indestructible.
Twenty-third, in the city of Sukhāvatī, he saw the elder Anuttarajaya, who had realized the dedication that is equal to all Buddhas.
Because this elder was skilled in decisively resolving human affairs and was also skilled in preaching the Dharma such that it brought joy to people, the city was named Sukhāvatī.
Furthermore, because his practice of patience was supreme, he was given the name of the elder. He saw him in the Aśoka Grove to the east of the city, surrounded by immeasurable merchants.
Householders surround the Dharma-preacher; generating all manner of goodness through wisdom constitutes the eastern city gate.

Being able to practice forbearance so as to be free from sorrow and provide broad shade constitutes the grove. Using wisdom to transform ignorance and using goodness to exchange for evil constitutes the merchants.

Transforming the common people through virtue constitutes the householders—all of these are manifestations of the Dharma. I know that reaching all places constitutes the cultivation of the bodhisattva path.
Regarding the "Dharma-gate of Purity": it is because, like all Buddhas, one dedicates [merit] to all sentient beings such that there is no place where one's practice does not pervade.
