These three masters mentioned above were all laypeople; this signifies that dedication is the turning from the ultimate toward the conventional.
Twenty-fourth: In the city of Kaliṅga in the country of Śūna, one sees the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhahanu, who has realized the dedication that reaches all places.

"Śūna" means "valiant," and "Kaliṅga" means "strife. Because she enters the mundane world with diligence to extinguish the strife of the two views—of the mundane versus the ultimate, and of defilement versus purity—the country and city are named accordingly. Through her practice of compassion...

"Fatigue" refers to stretching the limbs. Because this stage is identical to the four abodes and the four grounds in emerging from the entanglements of the triple world and being born into the family of the Tathāgata, it represents the sign of transcending the mundane;
thus, it is the bhikṣu. The bhikṣu discards ornaments to manifest patience (*kṣānti*); the bhikṣuṇī manifests loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Being in the garden of King Prasenajit, the king represents wisdom (*prajñā*). This signifies that the stage of diligence (*vīrya*) unifies patience, wisdom, and loving-kindness, collectively encompassing the five [perfections].
The conduct of his station constitutes a single Dharma-realm.
He saw within the garden a flowering tree like the Pārijātaka of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, as well as various jeweled seats and jeweled grounds spread with kālintha garments.
Pārijātaka: this is translated as "Fragrance Pervading. The roots, flowers, branches, and leaves of this tree are all fragrant, and their scent pervades the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Kāliṅga: this is translated as "Fine Cotton Garment," which clarifies that his secondary environment (*upabhoga*) is fully perfected.
Seeing him at those various seats preaching various Dharmas to various assemblies clarifies that his practice of gathering and transforming beings proceeds directly [to its goal].

The assembly of those on the eleventh stage, who are adjacent to Buddhahood, is entirely encompassed therein. This is because a single stage pervades all five stages, and each individual stage pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

Through repeated refinement, they form the fifty-three dharmas and the hundred and ten cities—a gate of the inexhaustible Indra’s net, wherein the general and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and destruction are sovereignly interwoven.
Sudhana and the trees in the grove both circumambulated [the Bodhisattva] to the right.
The trees that surround this bhikṣuṇī are born from the retribution of her practice; they symbolize the universal compliance with patience, wisdom, and compassion.

When the bhikṣuṇī says, "I have attained the liberation of the realization of all-knowledge," she means that she is able to enter the ten gates of prajñā, such as the Universal Eye, relinquishment, and attainment.
That all phenomena are disintegrated is called "relinquishment" (śe), and that they are all perfected is called "attainment" (de). Thus, they are perfected and disintegrated simultaneously.
To destroy and then to establish is the relinquishing and attaining of the Universal Eye.
Twenty-fifth is the dedication of inexhaustible treasuries of merit, realized by seeing the woman Vasumitrā in a perilous land.
Because this woman is certain to dwell in a defiled and fearsome realm that is difficult for people to believe, she is named "Perilous Difficulty" (Kṣema).

Because one enters the realm of defilement through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) such that it all becomes a realm of wisdom, and because she dwells in the mundane world with great compassion while possessing great wisdom free from defilement, she is named "City Adorned with Jewels.
Vāsukī—translated here as "World-Friend" (Lokamitra)—acts as a teacher and friend to humans and devas; thus, the woman represents [this quality].
Abiding in reality, she does not realize [nirvana]; dwelling within the bonds of existence, she is not defiled. She manifests the practice of defiled dharmas, yet her mind is not defiled.

She manifests as a female body, yet within the true mark (lakṣaṇa), she is neither male nor female; she is regarded as a woman solely by virtue of the compassionate essence of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Vāsukī also says "exchanging wealth," meaning that she manifests worldly acts of sexual passion to exchange for wealth; this is precisely non-attachment.
And yet it is stained; though stained, it is unstained. This is the realm of Samantabhadra’s wisdom-illusion: one's own body is like an illusion, and the world is like a transformation.
There is no mind that stains an object, nor is there any object that can be stained. The mind has no self-nature, and objects likewise are fundamentally non-existent.

This is not something to be deliberated upon through worldly sentiments, nor is it the domain of those who act out of emotional views and deluded ignorance. It requires that wisdom penetrate the true source and that conduct be equal to the Dharma-realm.
Only then can one embody this Way. As for this woman who dwells in her own home north of the marketplace:
it signifies that the foolish, treacherous, and bustling marketplace—the great night of birth and death—is the bodhisattva’s own home; there is no other dwelling.

When Vāsukī says, "I have attained liberation at the limit of detachment," it means that by means of the King of Wisdom of the Dharma-realm, he abides in defilement yet remains stainless; such a person is truly capable of faith.
Upon entering, one immediately attains the joy of dhyāna; hence it is said that by briefly seeing me, one immediately leaves behind craving and attains the Samādhi of Joy.
Because wisdom arises from meditative concentration, one realizes the nature of sound; hence it is said that by briefly conversing with me, one immediately attains the Samādhi of Sound.
Grasping my hand signifies the meaning of seeking guidance and reception. Ascending my seat signifies the increase of signless wisdom. Contemplating me...
The blinking of the eyes signifies the meaning of seeing the Truths. Embracing me signifies the meaning of non-separation. Kissing my lips signifies the meaning of receiving instruction;

this clarifies that all who draw near enter the gateway of omniscience. Unlike those of the three vehicles who merely seek liberation from entanglements, they do not reach the realm of the King of Wisdom within the Dharma-realm, which is both defiled and stainless. They spontaneously benefit sentient beings, being neither bound nor liberated. This is...

It is the state of being eternally free from desire. Furthermore, it is said that in the past, during the time of a Buddha, Mañjuśrī exhorted me to resolve to attain enlightenment and give a single precious coin.
Thus, I attained this liberation. Mañjuśrī’s exhortation symbolizes that concentration arises from wisdom; the precious coin symbolizes that concentration can perfectly penetrate all phenomena.
Resolving to attain enlightenment is the departure from desire; giving up the coin is the departure from greed. Although a single coin is small, it...
To be able to relinquish that which one holds most dear is no different from giving much; this is the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
Twenty-sixth, in the City of Skillful Deliverance, he saw the householder Viśvantara (Vaiśravaṇa), who had realized the dedication of all roots of goodness in accordance with firmness.
"Viśvantara" means "encompassing," signifying the vastness of wisdom that encompasses all. One...

This is the ultimate nature of all phenomena. When a lay practitioner establishes a stupa-chamber and installs a sandalwood throne without placing an image upon it, the intent is to clarify that all Buddhas and sentient beings possess no marks of arising or ceasing.

Through skillful means, he uses the sandalwood throne and stupa as representations to cause others to know that the nature and characteristics of their own bodies are like the signless primordial Buddha upon the throne.
One must realize that this nature is like space and penetrate these characteristics as being like a transformation.
I have opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which is without beginning and without end, without present and without past;

therefore, I say that by opening the gate of the stupa, I have attained the Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Buddha-seed and the liberation of non-parinirvāṇa, whereby I constantly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Twenty-seventh, seeing Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva on Mount Potalaka, one realizes the dedication that accords with all sentient beings.
"Potalaka" means "White Small Flower" (*kumuda*); this mountain produces many of these flowers, and the Bodhisattva’s humble and compassionate conduct is like them.
Avalokiteśvara is the embodiment of great compassion for the sake of benefiting beings within the ocean of birth and death.
Together with the wondrous principle of Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-body and the myriad practices of Samantabhadra’s Wisdom-body, these three factors constitute the virtue of Vairocana.
If one translates [Avalokiteśvara] as "Contemplating the World," then it refers to the mastery over the wisdom and principles of both the mundane and supramundane realms;

this would thus be subsumed under the sixth gate of Prajñā, rather than being the gate of expedient means and great compassion (mahākaruṇā). Therefore, we know that the old translation rendered it as "Contemplating the World."

The sound was thus. The Bodhisattva dwelt on Mount Śvetaketu (Small White Flower Mountain) to demonstrate to sentient beings that they should not commit even minor evils nor abandon even minor virtues.

He saw that within the rocky valleys to the west, springs flowed with crystalline clarity, the forests were lush and verdant, and fragrant grasses, soft and supple, spread across the ground in a clockwise spiral.
The west is the region of slaughter, punishment, and cruelty, where the Bodhisattva must carry out the transformative work of compassion.

His great compassion reaches its ultimate limit; he benefits sentient beings according to their needs and does not dwell upon his own karmic retribution. Thus, he dwells amidst the crags, valleys, and defiled realms of sentient beings:

the flowing springs represent the crystal clarity of his compassionate heart; the forest represents the dense shade of his meritorious kindness; the fragrant herbs represent his eloquent words that delight people;
and the clockwise spirals represent sentient beings’ harmonious transformation. Behold Avalokiteśvara seated in the full lotus posture upon a diamond rock.
As for the seated Bodhisattvas sitting upon jewel stones: this symbolizes that Vajra-wisdom accords with compassion; their wondrous functions intermingle yet remain unmoving.

When it says, "The Bodhisattva declares: 'I have accomplished the liberation of the practice of great compassion,'" it clarifies that Avalokiteśvara is the very embodiment of the great compassion of all Buddhas of the past and present.
Therefore, from the stages below up to the tenth bhūmi, none depart from the gateway of great compassion.
In this stage, mundane great compassion is brought to fulfillment; hence it is said that "accomplishment" is attained.

As for the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin (Universal Progress), who comes from the void to the Cakravāḍa mountains, causing the earth to shake in six ways and emitting bodily radiance that outshines the light of the sun, moon, and all the devas—rendering their lights like a mass of ink—he proceeds to the abode of Avalokiteśvara because he possesses right wisdom that is non-reliant. Thus, he is called Samantagāmin.

They come from emptiness. The Cakravāḍa Mountains are the retributive environment falsely grasped by sentient beings; because they are manifested through wisdom and thus false attachments dissolve, they tremble.
Because the light of untainted wisdom cannot be reached by the light of worldly karmic retribution, it is like a mass of ink.
Because he who has correctly entered the path of great wisdom returns to the station of compassion by increasing its brilliance, he proceeds to the abode of Avalokiteśvara.

Twenty-eighth: regarding the Bodhisattva Samyaktvaniyata’s dedication of merit upon realizing the aspect of True Suchness (Tathatā), because wisdom and compassion are non-dual in essence, they reside together on Mount Śvetaketu.
Samyaktvaniyata said: "I come from the world-system of Wondrous Treasury in the eastern direction."
Regarding the liberation of swift practice described in the *Pumen* (Universal Gate) chapter attained by the Buddha Universally Victorious Birth (*Samantavijaya-janman*):
because the treasury of one’s own wondrous wisdom-essence is unborn yet constantly giving birth, it constitutes the World of the Wondrous Treasury in the East.

Because the differentiated, illusion-like wisdom-body arises from fundamental wisdom, it possesses a nature of no coming yet resonates throughout the ten directions; this is the "swift" [liberation] attained by the Buddha Universally Victorious Birth.
This refers to swift movement. It has already been as many *kalpas* as atoms since departing from that place. In each and every thought-moment, he takes steps as numerous as atoms;

in each and every step, he traverses Buddha-lands as numerous as atoms. As for his making offerings to each and every Buddha with exquisite requisites, it is because the nature of wisdom is inherently all-pervasive;
thus, without being swift, he proceeds, transcending the limits of conceptual thought. Therefore, in a single thought-moment, he passes through as many Buddha-lands as those atoms.

By means of the seal of non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), one transcends the functioning of karma which is like an illusion; accomplished without effort, this constitutes "wondrous equipment.
Twenty-ninth: At the city of Drōṇa-pati, seeing the Great Deity, one realizes unbound and unattached liberation and dedicates [the merit].
Drōṇa-pati here means "Gate of Existence" (*sadvāra*); because the rank of the Dharma Master possesses great Dharma-gates, it is called "Opening and Penetrating."
Sentient beings call this place a city. Because their wisdom is like that of the heavens, they manifest both good and evil; rewards and punishments accord with the timing.
Constantly responding to the myriad phenomena through non-thought and non-action, they serve as celestial deities.

Within this realm’s heaven and earth, all those known as the spirits of heaven, earth, sun, moon, the five planets, great mountains and rivers, the Five Peaks, the Four Rivers, the seas, and the altars of soil and grain, are all the manifested bodies of Bodhisattvas.

This is not something that can be accomplished by the powers of worldly spirits or deities. That Mahādeva extends his four hands and takes the waters of the four oceans to wash his face symbolizes the use of the four *saṃgrahavastu* (means of integration) to carefully observe sentient beings and gather them in.

To speak of "accomplishing the liberation of the cloud-net" means that with the great compassion-cloud, he universally rains down the net of the teachings to filter and rescue sentient beings. Mahādeva manifests his golden...

The silver, the seven treasures, and all the various articles of offering were gathered like mountains and bestowed upon Sudhana, so that he might gather in sentient beings through the practice of giving (*dāna*).
This clarifies that the great compassion born of non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) is like an illusion; its karmic activity is inexhaustible and never depleted.
Regarding the thirty [deities] who witness the Bodhimanda and the Earth Goddess dwelling in peace, who realize the immeasurable dedications equal to the Dharma-realm:
in this stage, one unifies the five dharmas of bodhi, prajñā, rati, compassion, and wisdom, and through their complete perfection, they constitute the Bodhimanda.
With compassion abiding below, they give rise to all dharma-gates; bearing and nurturing sentient beings, they are the Earth Goddess, as opposed to the celestial deities mentioned previously.

This is the sublime function of pure wisdom; this earth deity is the very embodiment of great compassion. Because its essence is eternally active yet eternally quiescent, it is called "Abiding in Peace" (Anju).

While heaven moves, the earth is still; like an elephant, its wisdom and compassion cover and sustain all. It nurtures beings as if they were its own private charge, thereby bringing about transformation.
To see a million earth deities, such as Anju, all emitting light and causing the great earth to tremble everywhere clarifies this point.

Compassion and wisdom reach fulfillment here; the karmic activities of defilement and purity have ceased. Regarding the statement that "dwelling securely, he presses the earth with his feet, and immeasurable (*asaṃkhyeya*) treasuries of jewels spontaneously surge forth":
this symbolizes that the treasury of the Great Compassionate Mind-Ground can manifest clearly in its entirety, its divine functions fully prepared through effortless spontaneity.
Regarding the statement "I have attained the liberation of the indestructible treasury of wisdom": this is because [he] follows compassion...
When wisdom arises, it is indestructible; yet within the activities of the *dharmadhātu*, there is no wisdom that is not contained and no compassion that is not fulfilled.
Therefore, it is called a "Treasury" (*garbha*). Those who, prior to world-ages as numerous as motes of dust, served various Buddhas and attained this liberation, possess infinite great compassion;
thus, although they have realized the Way and entered *parinirvāṇa*, these are all simply the household affairs of that which has neither beginning nor end.
Thirty-first is the night goddess Vasanti, seen in the city of Kapilavastu, who has realized the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).

"Kapila" means yellow; this city was named after an ancient sage with yellow hair, signifying that wisdom accords with the Middle Way and representing the auspicious color of the central palace. "Vasanti" means she presides over the springtime.

The presiding goddess represents the emergence of the myriad practices from the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). The Night Goddess represents the great wisdom of the night of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
From this point downward, there are nine Night Goddesses and one Gopā; all are of the female class of worldly beings.

They represent the Bodhisattva’s great compassion, which, like a woman giving birth to and raising children, is never weary. Because they occupy the rank of spiritual deities, they maintain and uphold [the Dharma].
She protects and sustains the world. Although her own body does not depart from the Buddha’s assembly, she is likewise unimpeded in manifesting her form throughout the ten directions.

That the night goddess wears crimson robes, a Brahma-crown, and necklaces, with all the constellations brilliantly arrayed upon her body, symbolizes that the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) universally possesses the qualities of all ten stages;
thus, the wisdom of the differentiation of great compassion illuminates everything with complete perfection. Night...
The deity said: "I have attained the liberation of the Dharma-light that shatters the darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings.
During times of night, dense clouds, wind and rain, or when roaming among thieves;

whether on mountains, at the sea, or in the perils of the wilderness—whether I manifest as a boatman, a sea deity, a king of fish or turtles, or as a beautiful bird, a sacred tree, a dwelling, or a level path."

The manifestation of the sun, moon, stars, and lightning to cause all sentient beings to leave behind the fear of darkness clarifies the detailed and comprehensive nature of the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
To say that she has constantly manifested in female form throughout kalpas as numerous as dust motes to cultivate this Dharma clarifies the profound depth of her great compassion;
it shows that she does not seek to transcend the world, for within the fundamental realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), there is no world to be transcended.
Regarding the night goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā, who attained the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*) while beholding the Bodhimanda:
because she abides in the world with great compassion without departing from the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), she is likewise present at the Bodhimanda.

When she says, "I have attained the bliss of tranquil meditation and am extensively roaming in limited liberation," it is because the essence of the precepts is fundamentally meditation; the nature of all objective realms is itself...

Dhyāna. Its nature is inherently pervasive. To speak of "protecting and saving sentient beings with an unmoving single mind while practicing the first dhyāna," and so on, up to "extinguishing the feverish afflictions of sentient beings while practicing the fourth dhyāna," clarifies that the essence of the Dharma-body precept is inherently constant and stable. It perpetually accords with the function of compassion;
gathering and transforming beings according to their capacities—all these are gates of dhyāna. Although they are the same as the practices of the dhyāna heavens, there is no longing for them.
The phrase "the mind that delights in the tranquility of dhyāna" and "feeling weary of and detaching from birth-and-death while practicing the three dhyānas" is an error of the translator.
It should read, "by nature detached from birth-and-death while practicing the three dhyānas."
To the right of the Bodhimaṇḍa, one sees the night goddess Rātridevatā Priyanayanā-vilokita-sattvā, who has realized the Bhūmi of Radiant Illumination (Prabhākārī).

The right side represents the station of compassion; it clarifies that she initiates practice through bodhicitta. Her perfection of patience and loving-kindness is indicated by her "joyful eyes" (*priyanayanā*), which are the mark of patient and compassionate love.
Her "observation" (*vilokita*) signifies that she does not abandon sentient beings. From every single pore of the night goddess’s body, there issue forth...
The manifestation of clouds of bodies fills the ten directions; this "explaining the characteristics of the ten pāramitās" clarifies that the transformative activities reach everywhere.
It states that all the requisites for the dhyāna-pāramitā are precisely the individual stillnesses of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and wisdom.
Furthermore, from each and every pore, there emerge immeasurable clouds of bodies of sentient beings.

As for the clouds of bodies resembling those of the various heavenly and human kings that pervade the ten directions, these represent the gathering of similar types and common activities in every place.

That such clouds of bodies appear before all sentient beings and proclaim their own various teachings on emanation through both sentient and insentient sounds clarifies that the wisdom-function of the *dharmadhātu* is one and the same for both sentient and insentient beings.
Because its essential nature is thus, the manifested form-body is unimpeded and inexhaustible.
It is said that the Universal Monarch of antiquity was Mañjuśrī, that my own night goddess is Samantabhadra, and that the King’s precious consort is none other than myself.
The manifestation arises from fundamental wisdom to exercise differentiated functions and practice great compassion, without being limited by kalpas.
For when one cultivates the supramundane, it manifests in a single thought-moment; yet, in practicing great compassion, there is no end to time.
34. As for this Night Goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā, who has realized the stage of Jvalanprabhā within this assembly:
because her wisdom and compassion are perfected at this level, she is born into the family of the Tathāgata and never departs from bodhi; therefore, she is present in this assembly.
One sees this Night Goddess, throughout all worlds, in all realms of existence, and at all times, acting in accordance with all sentient beings.

Those who are universally transformed and delivered through skillful means by means of their physical forms, speech, conduct, and understanding do so because they have attained the liberation of manifesting everywhere throughout all worlds to discipline sentient beings.
The night goddess recounted that during the past Perfectly Pure Kalpa, as many Buddhas as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru appeared.
At that time, a universal monarch was born by transformation from a lotus; the king had one...
That the woman was none other than my own self means that because the essence of wisdom is perfectly pure, it is called an eon (*kalpa*);

because the fruits of wisdom resulting from the progressive distinctions within diligence are as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field, there are Buddhas as many as those atoms; because wisdom is untainted, the King was born from a lotus; and because he attained the union of compassion and wisdom.

Therefore, the royal daughter was none other than myself. At that time, the lotus emitting light ten times to make known the appearance of a Buddha symbolized the perfection of the wisdom of the ten *pāramitās*.

To say that this liberation was obtained from one hundred and ten past Buddhas, and further to cite all the Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a world-system, indicates the mutual interpenetration of cause and effect across the ten stages (*bhūmis*) and the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*).
For the sake of one hundred and ten Buddhas, through the pervasiveness of fulfilling wisdom and practice, one's own mind is as the Buddha; one's conduct is entirely as the Buddha;
one's vision is entirely as the Buddha. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single thing that is not the Buddha.

For the sake of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, if even a single dharma or a single object were not the Buddha, that would be a false view. During those kalpas and at the time of those Buddhas, I may have been a night...
Deities may manifest as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) or even as courtesans; the courtesan symbolizes the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*).

Thus, all such bodies symbolize the practices (*caryā*) undertaken according to their respective stages within the state of Buddhahood. The Buddhas whom they serve all symbolize the fruits (*phala*) realized according to those respective stages.

Therefore, when the characteristics of practice and fruit coincide, the Buddhas naturally correspond with one another. If one perceives anything apart from one's own practice and one's own fruit, [it is not the true manifestation].
This is not right view. Even if one were to force oneself to see it, it would merely be a temporary manifestation and not the actual Buddha.
Not far from here, one will see the night goddess Silent Sound Ocean, who has realized the Difficult-to-Conquer stage (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

At this level, she cultivates worldly arts and crafts through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet without departing from the essence of bodhi and her diligent practice, she possesses skillful means.
It is possible. Therefore, not far from here, tranquility is the essence of concentration (*samādhi*), and the ocean of sound is its function.

This illustrates that while the substance of concentration is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), its resonance is universal. This night goddess is the mother of the aforementioned Night Goddess Universal Savior;

she symbolizes that the essence of concentration can give rise to the practice of diligence. If all practices were not rooted in concentration, they would eventually lead to exhaustion. Thus, I have attained...

Regarding the liberation "The Birth in Every Thought-Moment of Vast and Great Joy-Adornments": this clarifies that the joy of dhyāna is all-pervasive, and that principle and practice mutually adorn one another to bring about the vast benefit of sentient beings.
As for the statement that this liberation was attained by making offerings in the past to ten Buddhas, such as Dharmadhātunirghoṣa, who are non-retrogressive:
this signifies that within the stage of the first bhūmi, one fully cultivates the practices and fruits of all ten bhūmis before attaining it.
Furthermore, the subsequent rebirth in this Sahā world to make offerings to the four Buddhas, namely Kāśyapa, Vipaśyin, and so forth,
represents the fruits of the stages from the first to the fourth bhūmi prior to the fifth bhūmi.
It is also said that within this kalpa, one shall make offerings to all future Buddhas, as well as to all worlds throughout kalpa after kalpa.

Regarding the phrase "I shall make offerings to all future Buddhas who exist therein": this clarifies that the essential nature of dhyāna is perfect and that the three periods of time are of a single limit (*ekānta*).
It is like water or a mirror in the world, or like a dry vessel in space, which universally contains all images. The Buddhas to whom one makes offerings are the fruits within this practice.
Even if explained in terms of conventional phenomena (*vastu*), it does not contradict this symbolic teaching (*dharmanirukti*), because the Buddhas perceived as others are also one's own wisdom.
It is through mutual correspondence and by practicing in accordance with it that one may perceive them.
Among the assemblies of the thirty-six Buddhas, those who see the deity "Increasing the Protection of All Cities" realize the Stage of Manifestation (Abhimukhī-bhūmi).
It is named for its divine power, which consists of the internal wisdom-force that increases the bodhicitta and protects the city of sentient beings' minds.
When the night goddess says, "I have attained the liberation of the profound, sovereign, and wondrous sound," it clarifies that a single sound pervades the entire dharma-realm;
being without substance and without discrimination, it can transform all dharmas to teach and transform sentient beings through all-encompassing wisdom.
All these are attained with manifest mastery. It is said that after passing through world-systems and as many eons as atoms, one attains this liberation.
The first Buddha was named Dharma-ocean Thunder-voice Radiance King (*Dharmasāgaragarjitasvararāja*). After that Buddha had passed into extinction, there was a king who left the household life;
it is because he was able to transform all the various names and phrases, as numerous as the atoms of all worldly sentient beings, into a single totality...

The ocean of the sounds of Prajñā is called the world-system of Transcending Dusty Kalpas. Taking fundamental wisdom as the first Buddha, taking the mastery of preaching the Dharma to destroy delusions as the name of the Buddha, and taking the perfection of wisdom that has emerged from the entanglements and the disappearance of discursive observation that has emerged from the entanglements as the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
taking the manifestation of the wisdom of the three emptinesses as the King’s renunciation of the world, and arising through the wisdom of emptiness.

Out of compassion for the world, the princess also became a nun. When the Dharma was about to perish, there were many who divided it into a thousand schools and engaged in disputes that would lead to the extinction of the Buddha-dharma;
[the princess] possessed the wisdom of clarity regarding emptiness but had not yet fully realized it, thus entering into worldly great compassion.

Furthermore, by mentioning that she made offerings to a hundred Buddhas, she demonstrated that within the sixth bhūmi, she fully cultivated the superior progress and mutual integration of the ten bhūmis.

Regarding the result, it does not reach the characteristics of the fruit of the eleventh stage because the gate of the wisdom of emptiness is not yet the conduct of Samantabhadra entering the realm of entanglements;
thus, among the ten concentrations, the thirty bodhisattvas of the wisdom of emptiness all enter the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka), yet they do not see the body of Samantabhadra.
Sāgaradhvaja’s entry into the concentration of cessation also symbolizes this wisdom of emptiness.

The thirty-seventh night goddess, Puṣpābhikīrṇā (Flower-Sprinkler), who attained the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*) within the assembly of the Buddha’s retinue, symbolizes the entry into the cycle of birth and death through skillful means (*upāya*) while remaining within the state beyond birth and death, thereby universally performing all practices. Just as in the previous stage, she enters the realm of entanglement to benefit worldly beings;
this is like the laywoman Śreṣṭhidāraka (or Śreṣṭhin), for whom the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) were all practiced in concert with her path.

Therefore, it is called "The Tree Flower in Full Bloom. When the Night Goddess said, "I know the liberation of the Radiance of Vast Joy Born from [the Dharma]," she clarified that the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) have all been thoroughly penetrated.

She further stated that in the past, King Dharmasvaravyūha had five hundred ministers, sixty thousand court ladies, and seven hundred princes; at that time, the king established a great assembly for giving.
There was a daughter of a householder named Ratnaprabhā, who was present in the assembly together with sixty young maidens.
That king was none other than Vairocana; that daughter Ratnaprabhā was myself. In this evil age of manifold sufferings, she represents the ground of practicing compassion.
The king represents wisdom. The five hundred great ministers represent the simultaneous practice of the five stages. The sixty thousand court ladies—
The manifest grief represents the pervasion of the six realms of existence. The seven hundred princes represent the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
The maiden Radiance (*Prabhāvatī*) represents compassion. The assembly of sixty maidens represents that the compassion of the six stages is all in union with wisdom.

That king is Vairocana himself; he represents wisdom acting as the fruit of conduct within the mundane world. Therefore, Vairocana Buddha’s lotus crown, bracelets, and armlets are likewise his mundane body.

Among the thirty-eight sites of practice, the night goddess who has realized the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*)—named "Great Vow and Power of Diligence Who Protects All Sentient Beings"—manifests as a deity because she benefits beings spontaneously through the power of her original vows by means of non-effortful wisdom (*anabhoga-jñāna*).
Her sitting upon the lion throne within the "Mani-Jewel-Treasury" palace, which universally manifests all palaces, symbolizes the absence of... [text truncated].
Within merit and wisdom, the function of stainless wisdom manifests universally in all places.

As for seeing the manifestation of bodies as reflections of the sun, moon, and stars, and causing all sentient beings to universally behold these various bodies according to their own minds—this is the manifestation of the essence of wisdom in response.

The Night Spirit said: "As for my attainment of the liberation that teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they may give rise to roots of goodness, it is because through the wisdom of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*), all roots of goodness arise spontaneously.
To illustrate the Bodhisattva’s wheel of wisdom, it is like the sun traveling through the sky, where there is neither day nor night;
it is like a phantom person dwelling in the world, free from sorrow, joy, and the like. With these metaphors, she answered his inquiry regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Regarding the question of "long or short," this clarifies that the liberation of a bodhisattva cannot be measured by the duration of time.

It cites how, in the past, when the Buddha Dharmacakraghoṣagaganapradīparāja sat at the site of enlightenment for a full hundred years, the Crown Prince Suprabha—who possessed the twenty-eight marks—rescued those in prison; subsequently, during the final five hundred years, he practiced [the path].
The Brahma-practitioner possesses effortless wisdom that universally illuminates like an echo yet remains without dependence; this constitutes Buddhahood.

Within the first stage, the fulfillment of the ten stages and the hundred *pāramitās* for a period of one hundred years signifies the King, who represents wisdom. The Prince represents the practice of compassion;

the prison represents the realm of compassion. The five hundred years of renunciation and cultivation represent departing from the house of effortful application (*sābhoga*) into the state of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).

He penetrates all five stages; however, because he has not yet fulfilled the fourfold causes and effects of the ninth and tenth bhūmis, the Prince possesses only twenty-eight marks, lacking four of the thirty-two major marks.
Thirty-ninth: The Night Goddess Wondrous Virtue Perfect Light (*Lakṣmīparipūrṇaprabhā*), who realized the Stage of Good Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*) while at the Lumbinī Garden.
"Lumbinī" is translated here as "Victory of Joy"; it is the garden where the Buddha was born. It is called a garden because it brings joy to sentient beings through the Dharma.

The Night Goddess is so named because her wondrous wisdom is perfected on the Stage of Good Wisdom and she skillfully expounds the teachings. She enumerates ten kinds of treasuries of birth (*janma-kośa*).

Born into the family of the Buddhas, yet saying, "I have attained this liberation of sovereign birth from immeasurable kalpas ago," and claiming to have already attained great effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), one is about to ascend to receive the office of a Buddha;

training in this stage and attaining eloquence in preaching the Dharma is called "receiving birth while dwelling in the womb. After a hundred years have passed, the World-Honored One is truly born here.
He likewise manifests birth in every Lumbinī grove throughout the trichiliocosm,
and he also manifests his birth within every single atom of all worlds in the ten directions. Having ascended from this stage to the tenth bhūmi over the course of a hundred years,
he descends as a spirit in a single thought-moment, for the essence of his non-conceptual wisdom is like space and like an illusion.
Pervading the entire *dharmadhātu* without any interval of coming or going, it arises in all places.
As for the celestial maidens who, bearing various offerings, wait before the *pi-lo-cha* tree for the Buddha’s descent from heaven:
*pi-lo-cha* means "lofty and manifest," signifying the Buddha’s virtue; it expresses that when a sage acts, all things behold him. Thus it is said.

In the past, during the Kalpa of Delight (*Ratnāvatī*), when eighty *nayuta* of Buddhas appeared, the king’s queen and two billion court ladies went to the Golden Flower Garden (*Suvarṇapuṣpa-udyāna*), where she gave birth to the Bodhisattva by grasping a tree. At that time, the wet nurse was none other than myself;
having come from the eighth stage of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), I served those eighty *nayuta* of Buddhas with compassion.
Filled with the joy of the Dharma through the two modes of wisdom, he was accompanied by two hundred million court ladies and the king’s consort.
Because he gave rise to great wisdom by means of great compassion, he was born grasping a tree. The wet nurse also felt sorrow for his body.
Regarding the forty [instances] of seeing the maiden Gopā in the city of Kapilavastu as she realizes the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*):

the yellow city symbolizes that the essence and function of the two virtues of wisdom and compassion are all-pervasive. It nurtures and sustains all phenomena while remaining without intrinsic substance;

it is like the soil of the *wùjǐ* (earth element), which presides over all four seasons without being restricted to any single season. Because wisdom and compassion have no sequence of priority, this city is the same as that of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

In the middle [section], Gopā—here translated as "Guardian of the Ground"—symbolizes the protection of the ground of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). She was the third consort when the Tathāgata was a crown prince;

she symbolizes the joy of the Dharma of loving-kindness and compassion, rather than being a wife for the five worldly desires. As stated later in the text, she has been the Buddha’s consort for a long time;
this symbolizes that wisdom and compassion are never separated. Her husband is the realization of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), and her essence is...
Pervading the ten directions, it cannot be discussed in terms of material obstruction, nor can it be understood through physical form. It manifests as a human being to demonstrate the ways of humans;
it manifests in celestial realms to share the customs of devas; and it appears in the various distinctions of the hells and the animal realm.
It cannot be known by a single mode of action, nor can it be understood by a single body. This is because the body of Samantabhadra’s conduct is such by the nature of the Dharma. Regarding this—
Ten gates are established to praise its virtues: 1. The gate of the essence of wisdom being without dependence, yet manifesting forms according to the capacity of the vessel.

2. The gate of these very forms being like reflections, their nature free from worldly dust. 3. The gate of the reflections of wisdom being fundamentally non-existent, while the vessel appears according to the mind.

4. The gate of wisdom having no "this" or "that," responding to conditions like an echo. 5. The gate of sentient beings’ deluded perceptions, wherein wisdom has no active agency. 6. The gate of wisdom being without... [text incomplete]
The gates of arising according to dreams and illusions; the gate of arising like an illusion, which is not the conceptualization of desire;

the gate of manifesting in response throughout the ten directions through the power of vows like empty space; the gate of unconditioned great compassion that penetrates the mundane to benefit sentient beings;

and the gate of wisdom pervading all conscious beings, wherein the conventional observation is eternally true. These ten dharma-gates are the practice of Gopā. At that time, the Universal Manifestation Dharma...
Furthermore, within the Hall of Increasing Radiance, the spirit Anuttaraguṇa and ten thousand spirits who preside over palaces came to welcome Sudhana.
The ten thousand signify the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*). The spirits who preside over palaces signify the protection and sheltering of compassion.
Their coming to welcome him signifies the meeting of wisdom and compassion. He saw Gopā surrounded by eighty-four thousand court ladies; and as for those court ladies...
The women were all born from royal lineages, representing the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
They all practiced together with compassion, yet that compassion was born from wisdom. Gopā said, "In the past, I was the daughter of an elder named Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Prince was named Śrīdhararāja, who is none other than the present Tathāgata. I entered into marriage with the Prince."
The ritual of going together to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma symbolizes that within this stage, wisdom and compassion are in perfect accord and never separated.
The fifty Buddhas seen at that time, who surpass the sun and moon and so forth, symbolize that all five stages are the fruits of practice.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas, the eight classes of beings including devas and nāgas, and the various deities of earth, wind, water, and fire symbolize the hosts of protectors among the six realms.

This refers to the universal nature of the practices of birth. At that time, although I had attained the samādhis and liberations for observing all bodhisattvas after already passing through kalpas as numerous as atoms, I was still unable to fully know the practices of the bodhisattvas.

Because the practices of Samantabhadra are fundamentally inexhaustible, and in order to cause the Great Being Dharmamegha to ascend into the gateway of the Samantabhadra practices of the eleventh stage, he was consecrated within the Ten Samādhis.
The Great Being at the Summit does not see the body of Samantabhadra. These ten masters below represent the practices of Samantabhadra within the eleven stages (bhūmis).
[Verse] 41: In this world, one sees Lady Māyā, realizing that the illusory manifestation of birth arises from compassion.
The Buddha-gate represents the realm of great compassion that encompasses all within this world, without distinction of distance, proximity, internal or external, or cardinal directions.
Māyā—here translated as "Queen of Heaven"—represents great compassion that dwells eternally in the world without effort;

she is the Mother of the Tathāgata, representing how great wisdom is born through the illusion of great compassion. Within this gateway of the Dharma-realm, there are eight habitual practices of compassion and wisdom known as the [Six] Pāramitās and two further perfections.

First, the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) is the householder woman Śreṣṭhadattā, who cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*); yet in the eighth stage, a portion of non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) manifests.

This constitutes the gate of cultivating wisdom from the basis of compassion. Second, the tenth stage is the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja, who represents the gate of the perfection of both wisdom and compassion.
Third, the seventh practice (*caryā*) is King Atṛpta, who represents the skillful means (*upāya*) of compassion.
1. The Gate of the Great Light King (Mahāprabharāja) in the eighth stage, who practices compassion through the practice of non-action.
2. The Gate of the seventh and eighth stages, where the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Samantagambhīraśubhavyūha assemble; this is the gate of the non-dual perfection of compassion and wisdom. 3.
The Gate of the tree-flower deity (Pārijātaka) in the seventh stage, who universally manifests the arousal of great compassion. 4. The [Gate] of the tenth... [text truncated]
The daughter Dìgōubā (Dharmodgatā) is the gateway of universal inclusion within the *dharmadhātu*, wherein compassion and wisdom are perfected.

Eighth, this very Mother of Buddhas is named the Gateway of Spontaneous Arising of Wisdom through the Illusory Manifestation of Compassion, whereby one attains Buddhahood and enters the inexhaustible conduct of Samantabhadra.
Prior to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), great vows of compassion arise from fundamental wisdom and involve cultivation and nurturing through practice. After the tenth stage, [they become spontaneous].
When all merit is perfected, it consists purely of compassion as the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.

Because one manifests a body of wisdom through the illusory power of compassion to benefit sentient beings without ceasing, this is what constitutes "birth" as a Buddha. The City-Ruling Spirit Ratnanetra exhorted Sudhana to guard the city of his own mind.
The host of deities of the Lotus Wondrous Virtue Body praised the body of Māyā, and the light from her ear-ornaments entered the crown of Sudhana’s head.
Furthermore, the Rākṣasa King who guards the Dharma Hall commanded Sudhana to contemplate his own body and mind as being like a dream or a shadow while seeking a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Here, the "jewel eye" symbolizes compassion and the "wisdom eye" in its midst; the "light from the ear" symbolizes the sound of the teaching.
*Rākṣasa* is translated here as "The Terrifying. It symbolizes the devouring of sentient beings by ignorance and the three poisons.
Taking these three groups of dharmas as the preliminary expedient means (*upāya*) for the eleven stages, one is led into the Great Conduct of Samantabhadra.

When Sudhana received and practiced this teaching, he immediately saw a precious lotus emerge from the earth, upon which Māyā appeared, manifesting infinite forms of activity identical to those of all sentient beings.
"Body" clarifies that there is no inherent self-nature in body or mind; this is the vision of the phantom-born body produced through compassion and wisdom.

Māyā said, "The characteristics of my body remain as they were, yet it can contain oceans of bodhisattva assemblies as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, all of whom move about freely within my womb;
some even traverse a trichiliocosm in a single step. This refers to Samantabhadra the Great...

The ocean of compassionate conduct is vast and inexhaustible, equal to space. Regarding the statement, "I have been the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time," this refers to the wisdom that spontaneously benefits sentient beings;
all such wisdom is born from the Mother of Great Compassion. This is what is meant by being "born as a Buddha," and it does not necessarily refer to [possessing] the thirty-two marks of a great man.
When all Buddhas are about to attain enlightenment, they emit light from their navels which illuminates my body.
This refers to the region of the navel among the parts of the body, where vital energy (*prāṇa*) arises and circulates through the upper and lower [parts].

Because it is able to cause growth and development, this is the meaning of compassion (*karuṇā*). It is manifested within compassion, just as the light between the eyebrows manifests wisdom (*jñāna*).

When it is said that "from inconceivable kalpas of antiquity, one has attained this illusory liberation of wisdom," it clarifies that it cannot be measured by duration—whether long or short—and that one must transcend such numerical reckoning.
It is only when the wisdom that exhausts all afflictions (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests that one truly knows; therefore, only a Buddha can know the number of these kalpas.
When the various masters below this point also say, "I know only this, and cannot know anything beyond," they clarify that within the general there is the particular.
This is not like those prior to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), who remain obstructed and fail to reach realization.
42. As for the Thirty-three Heavens, they behold the daughter of the Heavenly King Right Mindfulness (Samyaksmṛti), named Sovereign Light of the Celestial Lord (*Devendra-prabhā*).

She is the one who realizes that wisdom and compassion are sovereign and that all phenomena are never lost from right mindfulness; she is the gateway of immediate presence. In the preceding "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-paṭala*), the son of the gods Right Mindfulness was designated as the King.
Furthermore, there is this daughter, who represents non-thought (*asmṛti*) and spontaneously functioning wisdom and compassion, manifesting divine transformations without fixed direction.

To be sovereign as a deva or a king is not a matter of physical location. When the goddess says, "I have attained the liberation of unimpeded mindfulness," she means that the duration of the kalpas of the three periods of time is clearly perceived in a single thought-moment, as if it were presently manifest before her. This is because, through the wisdom of non-thought, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus.
When she says, "All the Buddhas who appeared throughout the kalpas of those intermediate eons, I have made offerings to all of them," this does not imply a long duration of time.
The states of being near, intermediate, distant, or long-term are encompassed in a single thought-moment by the wisdom-realm that is timeless; this is not achieved through deliberate effort.
From here on, the fact that the common worldly stream is not distinguished by divine marks or extraordinary features indicates that the supramundane path is fulfilled.
It is only feared that the practice for benefiting sentient beings may not be vast or sovereign, and that there remains no further mind seeking liberation apart from defilement or purity.
Merely by boarding the ship of the Dharma-nature and hoisting the sail of great compassion, with great wisdom as the helmsman,
one follows the wind of original vows to unfurl the net of the *pāramitās*. Thus, one traverses the ocean of birth and death to filter out the fish of those with attachments,
placing them upon the shore of non-reliant wisdom and dwelling in the jeweled hall of the *dharmadhātu*, just as in the Maitreya Pavilion below.
Forty-third: In the city of Kapilavastu, one sees the youth and teacher Viśvāmitra, who has realized the Dharma that pervades the ten directions and serves as a model for the world.
His yellow-colored city symbolizes not departing from the Middle Way. His conduct and governance follow secular classics; this youth-teacher is like Zhongni (Confucius) of this region.
Zhongni’s head was shaped like an inverted roof, resembling the summit of Mount Niqiu, which is low in the center and slopes downward.
This is for the sake of the name. It signifies that he emerged from a humble station to enlighten the ignorant. Confucius was born in Yanzhou, within the domain of the mountain trigram (Gén).

His image is that of a young boy in the state of *méng* (ignorance), yet he is positioned above the lunar mansion of *Jiǎo* (the Horns), presiding over the gate of manifold goodness; thus he was born under the influence of the *Jiǎo* qi and was no ordinary person of the world.
That he universally befriended those who did not speak, yet commanded Sudhana to visit various masters of arts, clarifies the method of the true teacher and model.

The Rectifier does not personally instruct; he entrusts the task to an Assistant Instructor. However, matters that cannot be decided must be referred to him. When virtue is manifested, it does not remain solitary; it will surely have neighbors.
Thus, the Assistant aids and assists in the realization of his transformation.
Regarding the forty-fourth, the youth Viśvāmitra-putra (Son of All Arts), who realized the gate of the wisdom of characters that pervades the ten directions:
this youth Viśvāmitra-putra was a disciple of Samantabhadra, similar to Yan Hui [Yan Yuan]. He is said to have attained the liberation of "skillfully knowing all arts.
He constantly recited and maintained the forty-two letters of the alphabet, thereby entering immeasurable gates of *prajñāpāramitā*. By means of this—
All phonemes encompass all written characters; therefore, to hold one character is to hold all characters, and to hold all characters is to hold one character—this is the gateway of Prajñā.
When pronouncing the syllable *A*, one enters the gate of the *pāramitā* of the non-differentiated realm of the Bodhisattva’s majestic power.
*A* here means "non-existence," for it signifies the realization that all things are empty and non-existent.

This is the Dharma of the Tathāgata; it is the realm of the Bodhisattva’s undifferentiated majestic power (*prabhāva*). When pronouncing the syllable *ta*, one enters the gate of the *pāramitā* of the realm of infinite differentiation.
This "many" (*bahu*) refers to the realm of Samantabhadra’s differentiated wisdom and conduct.

Forty-fifth is the Upāsikā Bhadraśrī, who has realized all worldly matters of right and wrong, fortune and misfortune, as well as the various arts, techniques, sorcery, and methods for benefiting living beings through extensive discourse. There is no phenomenon she does not understand; thus she is named Bhadraśrī.

Dwelling amidst the dust of the world to benefit sentient beings, she may appear as one who extensively discourses on worldly divination and profound prognostication for those who have not yet attained realization, or she may appear as a skilled physician with medicinal prescriptions.
He rescued the world from its insecurity. He discerned precious objects to distinguish the false from the true, and edited names and phrases to explain the meaning of the texts.
Among those of rare talent and profound wisdom, there were none who did not attain universal illumination. Ghosts, spirits, and all manner of malevolent forces were all able to be subdued by him.

Possessing the ocean of wisdom of Samantabhadra and the Dharma-body of Mañjuśrī, he personally dwells in the state of Buddhahood. His spiritual transformations pervade the myriad phenomena, reaching everywhere without limit; there is nowhere he does not go, yet he leaves no trace of his activity.
This is not so. As it is said, "The Buddha takes the Dharma as his body. Because he has thoroughly penetrated all dharmas, there is no dharma he does not know and no dharma he does not penetrate;
only then can he be the Teacher of Gods and Humans. If one seeks only transcendence, then everything is entirely absent. This is the path of the Two Vehicles;
however, because the Dharma has no place of reliance, the body likewise has no reliance. Although it pervades all phenomena, it possesses no self-substance of its own.
Therefore, he said, "I have attained only this liberation of the field of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) that is without dependence.
Forty-sixth: In the city of *Udaka-kṣetra*, one sees the elder *Dṛḍha-vimukti* realizing the gate of liberation called "Pure Recollection of Non-attachment in the World.
*Udaka-kṣetra* symbolizes the moisture of wisdom and virtue that nourishes people; *Dṛḍha* symbolizes tireless effort in benefiting sentient beings. By means of these...
The adornment of all mindfulness by means of signless wisdom is such that one remains mindful of all phenomena while being inherently unattached; this is liberation.
This is the forty-seventh gate, the "Gate of the Radiance of Pure Wisdom for Abiding in the World," as realized by the Elder Sun-Moon (Candrasūrya) in the City of Fertile Fields (Kṣetrabhūmi).
The skillful means and great compassion of this assembly are of one essence and non-dual with the previously mentioned signless liberation;
therefore, it is also located in the City of Fertile Fields (*Uṣita*). In the ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, and ten stages, the seventh and eighth positions are mutually integrated.
In these eleven stages, the sixth and seventh positions are of one essence; this is the dynamic form of their progressive advancement. By means of the light of great compassion, they shatter...
The delusions of sentient beings are the liberation of the radiance of pure wisdom.

Regarding the forty-eighth [chapter], "Birth in the City," it describes seeing the elder Anabhibhūsenā (Unconquerable Army) and attaining the gate of inexhaustible marks within the realization of the markless dharma.
It is called the city of birth through great vows and manifold practices; it surpasses all demons of birth and death, and its hairs are without [defilement].
O Jayasena, because all mental objects and states of mind are entirely the inexhaustible marks of the Buddha, they are the inexhaustible marks within the markless.
Regarding the forty-ninth gate, the "Gate of the Manifest Speech of Verification by the Most Quiescent Brahmin Seen in the Village of the Dharma-Cluster": the Dharma...

The "village" (*grāma*) symbolizes the rank of a Dharma Master, taking the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the village. "Utmost tranquility" symbolizes the station of the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*):
though dwelling in the mundane, one is not mundane; though amidst clamor, one is not clamorous. "Sincere vows" refers to those who have attained liberation:
since all speech is inherently true by nature, both person and phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*), and there is no false speech.

The "Fifty Gateways of the Wondrous Intentional Flower" (pañcāśan-manojña-puṣpa-dvāra) reveal that the boy Guṇākara and the girl Guṇavatī manifest the state where wisdom and compassion are perfected and dwell in the world as a magical appearance (māyā-vihāra). The "Wondrous Intentional Flower" signifies wondrous conduct within wisdom;

the boy and girl signify being free from desire and defilement, gentle, humble, and compliant. Because their wisdom and compassion are perfectly balanced, it is stated in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata": [text follows].

The Extraordinary Samantabhadra is likewise thoroughly penetrated. When the boys and girls say, "We have attained the liberation of dwelling in illusion," it means that they have realized that both the realm of the Buddha and the realm of sentient beings are produced as illusory manifestations of wisdom. They dwell within the realm of illusion, which is neither real nor unreal.

Mind and objects are entirely fused; essence and appearance are unimpeded; body and land interpenetrate; light and shadow multiply in layers; and their substance penetrates through both the holy and the ordinary. Their nature...

It encompasses both the past and the present; it abides eternally in the world yet has no point of dependence. Therefore, it is further said that the self-nature of illusory phenomena is inconceivable.
Below this, the text points to Maitreya’s attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood within a single lifetime. This "single lifetime" is the birth of non-birth;
it is not a birth characterized by the sequence of the three periods of time. The three dharmas of Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra pervade the fifty [chapters].
The essence of the causal and resultant stages does not exist as some separate phenomenon apart from these fifty-one stages.
It is through the power of inconceivable roots of goodness that the fifty-first virtue gives rise to the possessor of virtue, causing Sudhana’s body to become supple and lustrous,
thereby pointing toward the nature of the Great Adornment Garden of Vairocana’s Treasury in the Country of Sāgaratīra.
Regarding the gate of Maitreya Bodhisattva within the vast multi-storied pavilions attaining the fruit of Buddhahood in one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*):
the "shore of the ocean" symbolizes ascending toward the fruit of Buddhahood in one more birth, standing at the shore of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

The "adorned garden" symbolizes entering into the wisdom and compassion regarding birth and death to adorn the fruit of Buddhahood. *Vairocana*—here translated as "various lights"—symbolizes differentiated wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*). *Cakravartin*.
This is called "Universal Illumination," which symbolizes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

This pavilion symbolizes the Dharma-realm’s essence and function—the Wisdom of Universal Radiance—which accomplishes all myriad practices and extensively benefits all sentient beings; for this reason, its dimensions are equal to empty space.
All worlds and sentient beings dwell within it, cohabiting and moving about therein without being aware of it, just as when Sudhana entered this pavilion.

The various worlds seen within the pavilion are explained in detail according to the sutras. This pavilion is formed through the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, his great compassion for benefiting sentient beings, and his great vows;
it dwells within the garden of birth and death of all living beings. Therefore, it is said to be born from skillful means and born from merit and wisdom.
It arises without a place of coming and ceases without a place of going—all of these are...
The wisdom that abides as an illusion within the marks of arising and ceasing is, in turn, like the arising and ceasing produced by the karmic power of sentient beings;
it is entirely devoid of any essence or characteristics of coming or going. This is called the "Vairocana-Adorned-Treasury Pavilion.

Maitreya—here translated as "The Compassionate One"—was prophesied by the World-Honored One as one who is in his final birth before attaining Buddhahood. This refers to the fruit of Buddhahood after one more lifetime. It is, in fact, the wisdom of the illusory abiding of the dharma-realm.
In every realm, within every atom, an inexhaustible ocean of Buddhas eternally abides as a single path; it is without birth or death, and without past, present, or future.

Yet, through the Great Practices of Samantabhadra, in accordance with the timing and needs of sentient beings, he manifests such events as attaining Buddhahood, entering Nirvana, and receiving predictions of future enlightenment.
Therefore, while the World-Honored One’s traces of transformation have not yet ended, Maitreya is shown to reside in the Tuṣita Heaven.

In reality, Maitreya is already equal to all Buddhas without distinction. Devasaṃbhava extols at length the virtues of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) Maitreya, causing Sudhana to draw near to and serve him.
Yet, he states that one should not practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) with a limited mind;
rather, one who dwells in the ten stages (daśabhūmi), purifies Buddha-lands, and serves spiritual friends must clarify these six perfections.
The ten stages are all but a partial portion of the supramundane; pure vision has not yet been extinguished, and the universal conduct of Samantabhadra has not yet been perfected.

They are not identical to the body of merit and the ocean of fruition of the marks of reward of Vairocana Buddha, which is fully endowed with the ocean of blessings consisting of various features such as the jeweled crown, necklaces, bracelets, and armlets.
Rather, they merely attain equality with the supramundane transformation Buddhas who have discarded all ornaments and loathe the body of birth and death. This is...
Therefore, when the eleventh stage is perfected, one is instructed to enter the gateway of the *dharmadhātu* and realize the essence of the fundamental fruit.
One penetrates the state of the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, which is the original source of ignorance. Thus, one naturally possesses the retributive marks of boundless merit;

furthermore, this is augmented by the infinite adornments of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) accomplished through the ocean of the diverse wisdoms of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows. Yet, one does not allow this to remain merely as a causal attraction.
The mundane transformation realm is a gateway of practice with finite limits.
At this point, Sudhana prostrated himself before the pavilion and praised it with various methods of eulogy, extolling it as the dwelling place of a Great Sage endowed with immeasurable merit.
This clarifies the ocean of the Buddha’s fruition; even though one praises it, there is no end to it. Maitreya Bodhisattva [then] departed from his separate...
Regarding those who have come from other realms to join the great assembly and extol the virtues of Sudhana, as well as those who extensively praise the merits of the bodhicitta:
they are said to have "come from elsewhere" because they do not abide in their own karmic retribution, but rather employ worldly means to gather and transform sentient beings.

Furthermore, all the supernatural powers and the myriad practices of a bodhisattva—which turn the ocean of afflictions into the ocean of omniscience—have the bodhicitta as their very foundation. The bodhi-...

The mind is without support; wisdom is also without support. All that is performed is without a basis for abiding. The myriad practices are like transformations; benefiting sentient beings is like an illusion.
The powers of the spiritual faculties and supernatural abilities are like the moon in the sky appearing universally in all waters—all these are the functional efficacy of the bodhicitta.
If one attains anything without relying upon the bodhicitta, it is not one's own true dharma. Therefore, the bodhi...
The merit of focusing the mind is inconceivable. As for Maitreya snapping his fingers and the gate of the pavilion opening immediately:
snapping the fingers signifies the removal of defilements (*rajas*), and the sound signifies shaking and awakening.

When defilements are removed and attachments perish, the gateway of wisdom opens of its own accord. Once Sudhana has entered, the gate closes again; this is because delusion has vanished and wisdom has manifested.
"Open. Wisdom has no internal or external, no entering or exiting, no delusion or awakening; this is called "returning to closure," meaning it returns entirely to the source.
To see that within the pavilion it is vast and immeasurable, identical to empty space, refers to the immeasurability of the realm of wisdom.

That all its adornments are made of jewels signifies that the compassionate practices and vows of wisdom are all noble and precious. As for all the miraculous transformations and realms contained therein—

He also beheld the deeds and practices of Maitreya throughout the three periods of time, as well as the Buddhas and spiritual friends whom Maitreya had served in the past—all of whom had expounded the various Dharmas for Sudhana.
Through the realm of the wisdom of the Dharma-body, this is the natural and eternal state: there is nothing that is not numinous and no dharma that is not wondrous.
This is the realm of divine transformation, wherein the three periods of time—past, present, and future—do not shift by even a single thought-moment.
Therefore, one perceives the events of the three periods of time. Because the nature of the three periods is perfect, he speaks with constant fervor;
thus, it is heard that he was taught the Dharma by the Buddhas of the past. As for Maitreya’s own withdrawal of his supernormal powers such that the manifested realms no longer appear:

this is because the self-nature of all dharmas is like a dream, like an illusion, and like a shadow; like a reflected image, they are both eternally present and eternally dissolved, eternally one and eternally different.

It causes one to know the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that it follows conditions; yet, though it follows conditions, it is the natural law that it returns to its own nature.
He said to Sudhana: "When I attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), you and Mañjuśrī shall both behold me. This signifies the convergence of the three [times].
Since there is no distinction between past and present wisdom, the Buddhas of the three periods of time see one another simultaneously. Therefore, this liberation-gate is so named.
It is the treasury of adornment consisting of unforgetting mindfulness that enters all realms throughout the three periods of time.
As for the statement, "I was born into a brahmin family in the village of Kuṭi in the kingdom of Mālava," *Mālava* means "highly elevated" and *Kuṭi* means "many houses.
This signifies that his wisdom is highly elevated while his conduct is vast and manifold; furthermore, it indicates birth from a pure lineage.
As for the fifty-second [chapter], where Maitreya causes Sudhana to see his first spiritual friend, Mañjuśrī: this clarifies that the ultimate fruit is identical to the cause.

This is because at the time of initial faith, the gate of the universal radiance wisdom—where quiescence and function are eternally present—is devoid of the distinctions of past and present, the three periods of time, or beginning, end, entry, and exit.
Thus, after traveling through one hundred and ten cities in the *Sudhana-avadāna*, he arrives in the country of Samantamukha.
Those who wish to behold Mañjuśrī should, at one time, universally seal all the dharmas previously cultivated.
These one hundred and ten cities are the realm of the single Dharma-realm shared by the Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings;
this is the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) land, the place where Mañjuśrī dwells. From afar, Mañjuśrī extends his right hand across one hundred and ten *yojanas* to touch Sudhana.

Sudhana praised his ability to give rise to such vows and practices, and how he had been taken into the care of various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), thereby enabling him to accomplish incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Dharma-gates and enter the site of Samantabhadra’s practice (*caryā-maṇḍala*). By touching his head with his hand, [the teacher] signified the identity of cause and effect;
by traveling one hundred and ten *yojana*, it signified that he had already transcended the causes and effects of the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*), and was thus led to enter.
The "Samantabhadra’s Place of Practice" (Samantabhadra-maṇḍala) refers to the constant practice of Samantabhadra after one has attained the fruit of Buddhahood.

As for Mañjuśrī placing Sudhana in his own dwelling and then withdrawing him so that he no longer appears, this clarifies that after attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, there is no difference between that state and the time of being an ordinary person.
Because the Buddha-dharma is fundamentally non-existent after one has attained Buddhahood, it does not manifest.
As for Sudhana’s vision of as many spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as there are atoms in the great trichiliocosm, this is because his Dharma-body wisdom is coextensive with the Dharma-realm;
thus he perceives all universally, and none of them differs from the essence of Mañjuśrī.

In the fifty-third [chapter], when Sudhana, before the seat of the Tathāgata Vajragarbha at the Bodhimaṇḍa, gave rise to a mind as vast as the realm of empty space, he then beheld Samantabhadra seated upon a precious lotus throne before the Tathāgata.

This was because, following the fruit of Buddhahood, one ultimately does not depart from the wondrous principle of bodhi—the wisdom of Vajragarbha—contained within that very initial mind of faith; thus it arose.
This is the gate of the constant practice of the *Indra-jāla* (Indra’s Net) of the Dharma-realm.
When Samantabhadra extends his right hand and strokes the crown of Sudhana’s head, Sudhana immediately attains the samādhi-gates as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields.
Just as he strokes Sudhana’s crown here, so too does the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra do so at the abodes of all Buddhas within every single atom of every world throughout the ten directions.

In the same way, he also patted Sudhana on the crown of his head; that all the dharma-gates obtained were identical [to his own] clarifies that the dharma-realm is eternal, the fruit of Buddhahood is eternal, and it is only through the mutual correspondence of the marks and the practice of Samantabhadra that one attains the already perfected, ancient fruits of all Buddhas.
The ancient practices of Samantabhadra also clarify that the fulfillment of conduct does not depart from its cause; time does not shift, and wisdom does not differ.
When Sudhana takes a single step within the lands in a pore of Samantabhadra’s body, he passes through worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many lands.
Even if he were to travel in this manner for all future eons, he could still not know the sequential order of the oceans of lands within a single pore—the oceans of lands.

The limits of all the distinctions within the oceans of lands, the universal entry into the oceans of lands, and the formation and destruction of the oceans of lands, as well as the limits of the oceans of Buddhas and the oceans of bodhisattva assemblies—all these cannot be known;
such is the nature of the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s vast and inexhaustible realm of conduct. At that time, Sudhana attained the various practices of Samantabhadra.
The ocean of vows is equal to that of Samantabhadra and equal to that of all Buddhas.

With a single body filling all worlds, their lands, practices, perfect awakenings, spiritual powers, wheels of Dharma, eloquence, great compassion, and inconceivable liberation and mastery are entirely equal.
This clarifies the inexhaustible ocean of conduct throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions.
This is that which the Buddhas have practiced together; it is the ultimate path, wherein there is no further view of either attaining or not attaining Buddhahood.
