Postscript to the Carved Edition of the *Compendium of the Essential Points of the Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka*.
When I first read the "Samantabhadra Samādhi" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I was filled with great doubt and alarm.

Upon reaching the "Brahmacarya" chapter, where it is taught that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind, my heart involuntarily stirred. On another day, I read the biography of Master Li [Li Tongxuan], which mentions a commentary of forty fascicles that accords with this teaching;
though I have not yet been able to see it, I truly rejoice in this privately. The biography states: The Master’s name was Tongxuan. He was of the Tang...
He was a member of the imperial clan. He had a handsome beard and mustache, bright eyes and brows, and lips as red as vermilion with a complexion as purple as a ripe plum.

He wore a crown of birch bark and a long skirt of hempen cloth; his sleeves were wide and his waist was loose, and he went barefoot. In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, he arrived at Yuxian in Taiyuan.

There was a man named Gao Xiannu who marveled at him and took him into his quarters. Every morning he consumed nothing but ten dates and one *baiye* (cypress-leaf) cake. He remained in deep meditation.

Jingchong was reclusive and never associated with others. After more than three years had passed, he moved to the side of an ancient Buddha hall belonging to the Ma clan and built an earthen hut to dwell in.
He sat in a constant meditative posture throughout the day. Ten years later, he suddenly took his scriptures and books upon his back and set out on a journey.

After traveling twenty li, he happened upon a tiger blocking the road; it lay submissive and docile before him. The elder stroked it and said, "I am about to compose a treatise to explain the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*."
He asked, "Can this sutra serve as a place for you to dwell? Thereupon, he slung the sutra-casket over his back and followed him.
Upon reaching the front of an earthen cave at the foot of Mount Shenfu, he knelt and halted. He then took the casket and placed it inside the cave; the tiger tucked its tail and departed.

The cave was brilliant and pure, measuring six or seven *zhou* in width, with a circular opening above and below that matched its proportions; it seemed almost as if fashioned by heaven. The elder reached out and—
Hao’s mind was in profound accord with the Buddha’s wisdom; every night, white light would issue from his mouth to serve as a lamp.
At that time, there were suddenly two women of exquisite and peerless beauty, both with their heads veiled in white cloths, who daily drew water for the elder and prepared the incense.
He provided paper and ink. Every day between the hours of the Rabbit (卯) and the Dragon (辰), he prepared pure offerings and placed them before the Elder.

Once the meal was finished, he would remove the vessels and depart; no one could fathom where he went. This continued for five years. When his discourse was concluded, he suddenly vanished without a trace.
In the twenty-eighth year of the Kaiyuan era, when the Elder was ninety-five years old, he went out one day and said to the villagers, "May you all dwell in peace. I am about to..."
"Let us return. They then turned back. That evening, smoke and clouds gathered and spread, and the rocky valleys shook and trembled. Two white cranes soared through the sky, crying out mournfully;
other birds and beasts filled the mountains with their sorrowful calls. The next day, the villagers went together to visit him, only to find that he had passed away while sitting upright.
Viewed from this, it is clear that the Elder was a person who, within the assembly of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhāsa*), had mounted his vow to propagate the Dharma.
Wuxing formerly possessed a set of woodblocks for this treatise, which had already been destroyed by fire. Furthermore, the printed copies at various monasteries were all incomplete and damaged.
After searching for them for a long time, the Zen Master Dazong of Zhenru Temple said to me with a smile:
"In the past, I obtained a single copy that remained entirely intact. It was lent to Liurong Yu'an over ten years ago; now that Yu'an has passed away, his disciples..."
He returned to me. "How could I have delayed you? I said, greatly rejoicing. I immediately reimbursed him for his original expenses. He carried the texts into the mountains;

they comprised one hundred and twenty fascicles in total, their jade-like brilliance shining resplendently. Yet within barely ten days, the old hall of Yuyan was consumed by fire and reduced to ashes. Alas!
When the Dharma-treasure dwells in the world, there are surely divine guardians who protect it with such skill. Thus it was.

Thus, with a purified mind and in profound contemplation, I beheld the Elder taking the treasury of the inexhaustible Dharma-realm—the immovable wisdom-treasure inherent in the fundamental nature of all people—and manifesting it perfectly and instantaneously.
Its flames surged and its light soared, penetrating beyond the reach of words. At that moment, my sorrow and joy were immeasurable;
I immediately desired to transmit this to others so that all might see it for themselves. Yet, as I turned my gaze toward the bound volumes piled upon the desks, they were too numerous to count.

I have now used this to moderate its profuse expressions and condense its universal meanings, modeling it after the structural momentum of the *Threefold Cycle* (*San-zhou*). I have organized it into three fascicles and titled it *Zuan-yao* (Essential Compendium). It is like a person of six or eight feet standing before a mirror of only a few inches; while their dignified bearing and demeanor can still be observed, they remain incomplete. However, as it has not yet been carved for printing, it has remained stored in my bookcase for thirty years.

Regarding the *Wen-xuan*: ... [The text continues with the description of the *Wen-xuan*] ... it was compiled by Xiao Tong during the Liang dynasty. Its scope is vast, its categories are numerous, and its contents are exhaustive. Yet, because the work is so extensive, those who seek to study it often find it difficult to grasp the essential points. Consequently, many scholars abandon it midway.

I have therefore selected and edited the most significant passages from within it, arranging them according to genre and theme to facilitate understanding. This work is intended to serve as a guide for those who wish to enter the great ocean of literary excellence. It is not merely a collection of elegant phrases, but a systematic introduction to the principles of composition and the spirit of the ancients. May it serve as a lamp for future generations. Master Lu of Wutai harmonized his Way with the fundamental vehicle of the teachings and harbored a profound resolve for its propagation and protection. Yesterday, upon returning from Taichang, he spoke of this compilation;
it perfectly accorded with his great aspiration, and he subsequently donated pure gold so that these verses could be completed as a magnificent undertaking.

To the Elder Gong, this was what is called a meeting, as rare as once in a thousand years, occurring as if day and night were one. Formerly, Chan Master Puan Xu, upon reading the preface to this treatise, [was moved].
When the fundamental ground is reached, affective attachments vanish; when the essence of mind is known, one merges with the Great Enlightenment. Consequently, he said:
"The Elder has brought down a resounding blow at the very beginning of the sutra; the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all casually shattered to pieces.

He even went so far as to say, "Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī study together with me; what is this 'Eggplant' (a derogatory term for Śāriputra) that Sudhana is? I, however, say that Puan has lost sight of what was before while looking toward what is behind; he is utterly lacking in discernment.
One should know that every character, every phrase, and every sentence herein is the vajra-staff with which the Elder struck our hearts and pounded our vision.
When a scholar who has mastered the texts rouses themselves without sparing their own person, charging through the brunt of battle and facing the sharpest blades to carve out a new livelihood,
they thereby offer a profound repayment for the Elder’s kindness.

To expand a single phrase into hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of phrases—even this would not yet be considered extensive; [to encompass] all hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions...
To take a single phrase as one sentence would still not constitute brevity. My friend Wucan possesses the ability to expand and condense;
yet he declined to do so for both, instead selecting the forty-fascicle *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* by the Great Being Zao Bo (Dharmakṣema) and abbreviating it into three volumes.

This balance between expansion and brevity is perfectly suited, and its meaning is already complete. Moreover, even before the Great Being Zao Bo had lifted his pen, he had already reached the very marrow of the matter.
"Courage! All is contained therein. As for those who possess it, they are merely people who have reduced the Dharma to mere words.
I, however, say to them: "You have not yet seen that there is nothing to be studied."
